cgst-s1.plainEnglish: **Section 1 — short title, extent and commencement.** The CGST Act extends to the whole of India and came into force on notified dates — most provisions from **1 July 2017**, a few (registration machinery) from 22 June 2017, and TDS/TCS (sections 51/52) from 1 October 2018.

cgst-s2.plainEnglish:
**Section 2 is the dictionary of the CGST Act** — 120-plus defined terms. A GST
position almost always turns on a definition, so read the section text for the
exact words. The ones that decide the most disputes:

- **"aggregate turnover" (2(6))** — PAN-level, all-India, taxable + exempt +
  export + inter-State supplies, **less** taxes and inward RCM. Drives the
  registration threshold, composition, e-invoicing, QRMP and audit limits.
- **"business" (2(17))** — very wide; includes activities "whether or not for
  pecuniary benefit" and anything "incidental or ancillary".
- **"consideration" (2(31))** and **"supply"** (section 7) — the two together
  decide whether GST applies at all.
- **"goods" (2(52))** — every kind of movable property, including actionable
  claims and growing crops, **excluding** money and securities.
- **"services" (2(102))** — anything other than goods, money and securities;
  includes activities relating to the use of money for a consideration.
- **"input", "input service", "capital goods", "input tax", "input tax credit"**
  (2(59)/(60)/(19)/(62)/(63)) — the ITC vocabulary.
- **"place of business" (2(85))**, **"fixed establishment"**, **"location of
  supplier / recipient"** — the registration and place-of-supply vocabulary.
- **"reverse charge" (2(98))**, **"non-taxable supply" (2(78))**, **"exempt
  supply" (2(47))**, **"taxable supply" (2(108))**.
- **"related persons"** (Explanation to section 15), **"distinct persons"**
  (section 25(4)) — valuation and cross-charge.

complianceChecklist.item: When applying any section, substitute the section 2 definition of each key term
Check the amendment history of the specific definition clause you rely on
Compute 'aggregate turnover' correctly (PAN-level, exclude taxes and inward RCM)

keyConcepts.note: PAN-level, all-India — the trigger for threshold, composition, e-invoicing, QRMP and audit — s.2(6).
Goods = movable property (not money / securities); services = everything else (not money / securities). Schedule II resolves the boundary for a supply.
A deposit is not 'consideration' unless and until the supplier applies it as consideration for the supply — proviso to s.2(31).

cgst-s2.practicalNotes:
Two practical habits: (1) when reading any operative section, keep section 2 open
and substitute the defined meaning; (2) note the **carve-outs inside a
definition** (e.g. "aggregate turnover" excludes inward RCM; "goods" excludes
money and securities; "consideration" excludes a deposit unless applied as
consideration).

Several definitions were **amended with retrospective effect** (e.g. "supply" and
Schedule III items, "OIDAR", "online money gaming", "specified actionable claim")
— check the amendment history / effective date on the specific clause.

faqs.q: Does 'aggregate turnover' include the tax I collect?
faqs.a: No. Aggregate turnover excludes CGST, SGST, UTGST, IGST and cess, and excludes the value of inward supplies on which you pay tax under reverse charge. It **includes** exempt supplies, exports and inter-State supplies.

faqs.q: Are securities 'goods' or 'services'?
faqs.a: Neither. 'Goods' and 'services' both exclude money and securities. Dealing in securities is outside GST, though related activities (brokerage, DP charges) are taxable services.

faqs.q: Is a refundable security deposit taxable?
faqs.a: Not on receipt — a deposit is not consideration unless the supplier applies it towards a supply. If it is later adjusted against dues, GST applies at that point.

commonMistakes: Testing thresholds on State-level rather than PAN-level turnover
Treating a deposit as taxable consideration on receipt
Overlooking carve-outs inside a definition

The Board may fix the jurisdiction of each.

cgst-s6.plainEnglish: **Section 6 — cross-empowerment.** A **State / UT tax officer** is deemed a proper officer for CGST purposes (and vice versa) so that a single authority handles a taxpayer for both taxes. Where a proper officer under the SGST/UTGST Act has initiated proceedings on a subject-matter, the CGST officer shall **not** initiate on the same subject-matter, and vice versa. An order by one is subject to appeal / review only under that Act.

cgst-s6.practicalNotes: Section 6(2)(b) — the bar on **parallel proceedings** by Central and State authorities on the same subject-matter for the same period is a frequent litigation ground; if you have a State audit / SCN running, a fresh Central SCN on the same issue can be challenged.

faqs.q: Can both the Central and State GST departments audit me for the same period?
faqs.a: They can each administer you, but section 6(2)(b) bars **both** from initiating proceedings on the **same subject-matter**. Cross-notices on the same issue and period are routinely stayed by High Courts.

cgst-s7.plainEnglish:
**Section 7 defines "supply" — the single event that GST is charged on.**

- **7(1)(a)** — all forms of supply of goods or services for a **consideration**
  in the course or furtherance of business (sale, transfer, barter, exchange,
  licence, rental, lease, disposal).
- **7(1)(b)** — **import of services** for a consideration, whether or not in the
  course of business.
- **7(1)(c)** — activities in **Schedule I** (deemed supply **without**
  consideration): permanent transfer of business assets on which ITC was taken;
  supply between related / distinct persons in the course of business (with a
  50,000-per-year gift carve-out for employer→employee); principal↔agent
  supplies; import of services from a related person.
- **7(1A)** — where an activity is a supply, whether it is a supply of **goods**
  or of **services** is decided by **Schedule II**.
- **7(2)** — **Schedule III** activities are treated as **neither** a supply of
  goods nor of services (employee services to employer, court / MP-MLA
  functions, funeral, sale of land, sale of completed building, actionable
  claims other than specified actionable claims, high-seas sales, sale of
  warehoused goods before clearance, and — from Oct 2023 — the specified
  co-insurance / re-insurance arrangements).
- **7(3)** — the Government may notify a transaction to be a supply of goods and
  not services, or vice versa.

complianceChecklist.item: Screen every receipt / transaction for whether it is a supply before charging or not charging GST
Identify distinct-person supplies (branch transfers, HO→branch services, guarantees) and value them under Rule 28
Check Schedule III before treating land / completed-building / actionable-claim dealings as taxable
Document employee cost-recoveries against CBIC Circular 178/10/2022

keyConcepts.note: Any payment (money or otherwise) or the monetary value of an act or forbearance, for the inducement of a supply — s.2(31).
Trade, commerce, manufacture, profession, vocation etc., whether or not for pecuniary benefit, and incidental / ancillary activities — s.2(17).
Barter and exchange are supplies; value is then determined under section 15 read with the valuation rules.

cgst-s7.practicalNotes:
Test any transaction against section 7 first: **is there a supply at all?** Only
then ask place, time and value.

The three most litigated areas: (i) "in the course or furtherance of business" for
one-off asset sales and recoveries from employees; (ii) Schedule I distinct-person
supplies (branch transfers, corporate guarantees, secondment); (iii) whether
something is goods or services (software, works contract, food, intangibles).

Schedule III para 5 (sale of land and completed buildings) keeps real estate
outside GST once the completion certificate is issued or first occupation
happens.

examples.title: Recovery from employees
examples.scenario: A company recovers a nominal amount from employees for canteen food and for notice-pay shortfall.
working: Canteen: recovery is generally not 'in the course or furtherance of business' where it is a statutory / welfare arrangement — Circulars and AARs treat pure cost recovery as outside supply
Notice pay: CBIC Circular 178/10/2022 clarifies that notice-pay recovery is not a taxable supply (it is a consequence of breach, not a supply of 'agreeing to tolerate an act')
examples.result: No GST on either, on the CBIC's own clarification — but keep the arrangement documented as cost recovery / employment terms.

flowchart.title: Is this transaction a 'supply' under GST?

nodes.text: You have a transaction involving goods, services or money
Is it listed in Schedule III (employee↔employer, sale of land / completed building, actionable claims, etc.)?
Not a supply — outside GST entirely.
Is there consideration?
Is it in the course or furtherance of business (or an import of service)?
Is it a Schedule I activity (distinct/related persons, business-asset transfer with ITC, principal↔agent)?
It is a supply. Use Schedule II to decide goods vs services, then place, time and value.

faqs.q: Is a stock transfer between two GSTINs of the same company a supply?
faqs.a: Yes. Section 7(1)(c) with Schedule I para 2 makes supplies between **distinct persons** (s.25(4)/(5)) a supply even without consideration, when made in the course of business.

faqs.q: Is the sale of a building liable to GST?
faqs.a: Not once the completion certificate is issued or first occupation has taken place — Schedule III para 5. Sale before that (an under-construction unit) is a taxable supply of construction service.

faqs.q: Is a corporate guarantee given to a group company a supply?
faqs.a: Yes — it is a supply of service between related persons under Schedule I, and Rule 28(2) prescribes a value (1% of the guarantee amount or the actual consideration, whichever is higher).

commonMistakes: Charging GST on sale of land or of a completed building
Ignoring GST on inter-branch (distinct person) service flows and guarantees
Treating every employee recovery as a taxable 'tolerating an act' service
Overlooking that import of services can be a supply even outside business (7(1)(b))

caseLaw.name: Union of India v. Mohit Minerals Pvt Ltd
caseLaw.citation: (2022) 10 SCC 700 / 2022 (61) GSTL 257 (SC) / [2022] 138 taxmann.com 331 (SC), Civil Appeal Nos. 1390-1394 of 2022 and connected matters, decided 19-05-2022
caseLaw.facts: Levy of IGST on ocean freight on a reverse-charge basis on the Indian importer, where the importer had already paid IGST on the CIF value of goods.
caseLaw.issue: Validity of the reverse-charge levy on ocean freight; the binding nature of GST Council recommendations.
caseLaw.held: The reverse-charge levy on ocean freight was struck down as it amounted to double taxation and the importer was not the recipient of the transportation service. GST Council recommendations are recommendatory, not binding on Parliament or the States.
caseLaw.effect: Ocean-freight RCM on CIF imports is not payable. The wider observation on the non-binding nature of Council recommendations is frequently cited.

caseLaw.name: Torrent Power Ltd. v. Union of India
caseLaw.citation: R/Special Civil Application No. 12175 of 2024 & connected matters (Gujarat High Court), decided 14-08-2026
caseLaw.facts: Holding companies gave corporate guarantees to banks for their subsidiaries, mostly without a commission. They argued this was a shareholder / investment act, not a supply, and that a guarantee is an actionable claim outside the levy.
caseLaw.issue: Whether a corporate guarantee by a holding company for its subsidiary, without consideration, is a taxable supply.
caseLaw.held: Yes. Holding and subsidiary are related persons, so furnishing the guarantee is a supply of service 'in the course of business' under section 7(1)(a) read with Schedule I even without consideration; safeguarding a subsidiary's financial interest is 'business' under section 2(17), and volume / continuity / profit motive are immaterial. A corporate guarantee is not an 'actionable claim' excluded by Schedule III — a guarantor's liability is contingent and secondary, not a direct right to a debt. A share pledge securing the guarantee does not take it outside the levy. (The court separately read down 'whichever is higher' in Rule 28(2) and barred the 1% for pre-26.10.2023 periods — see section 15.)
caseLaw.effect: Inter-company guarantees are within GST as related-party supplies, with or without a fee. Argue the valuation and the retrospective points (section 15 / Rule 28), not the existence of a supply. Gujarat HC — persuasive elsewhere; a Revenue SLP is expected.

caseLaw.name: C.C., C.E. & S.T. v. Northern Operating Systems Pvt Ltd
caseLaw.citation: (2022) 5 SCC 362 / [2022] 138 taxmann.com 359 (SC), Civil Appeal Nos. 2289-2293 of 2021, decided 19-05-2022 (a service-tax ruling applied to GST reverse charge)
caseLaw.facts: A foreign group company seconded employees to its Indian affiliate; the secondees worked under the Indian entity's control but stayed on the foreign company's payroll, and the Indian entity reimbursed the salary cost with no mark-up. A service-tax demand treated this as a 'manpower recruitment or supply agency service' from the foreign company.
caseLaw.issue: Whether cross-border secondment of employees is a supply of manpower service to the Indian entity (taxable under reverse charge), and whether the extended limitation applied.
caseLaw.held: On the merits — yes. Looking at the economic substance rather than the form, the foreign company supplied manpower to the Indian entity, which is the service recipient and liable under reverse charge; the secondees remaining on the foreign payroll and the absence of a mark-up do not change this. On limitation — the extended period was not invokable, as the assessee held a bona fide belief and there was no wilful suppression; the demand was confined to the normal period.
caseLaw.effect: Secondment of employees from an overseas group company to an Indian entity attracts GST under RCM as an import of manpower supply service, on the cost reimbursed (CBIC Circular 210/2024-GST later clarified valuation — where the Indian entity has full ITC, the value may be taken as declared, possibly Nil). Separately, a strong precedent that a bona fide interpretational belief defeats the extended period.

caseLaw.name: Skill Lotto Solutions Pvt Ltd v. Union of India
caseLaw.citation: (2021) 2 SCC 55 / 2020 SCC OnLine SC 990 / [2020] 122 taxmann.com 49 (SC), W.P.(C) No. 961 of 2018, decided 03-12-2020
caseLaw.facts: A lottery agent challenged the levy of GST on lottery — arguing that a lottery is an actionable claim (excluded from 'goods') and that charging GST on the full face value of the ticket (without deducting the prize money) was unconstitutional.
caseLaw.issue: Is GST on lottery valid, and can it be charged on the face value of the ticket?
caseLaw.held: The definition of 'goods' in section 2(52) expressly includes actionable claims, and Schedule III excludes only betting/gambling/lottery in part — the legislature is competent to tax lottery. Levy on the face value of the ticket is valid; the prize money is not a permissible deduction.
caseLaw.effect: The constitutional foundation for taxing lottery, betting, gambling and (under GST 2.0) online money gaming as 'specified actionable claims' at 40% on the full face value / deposit.

caseLaw.name: State of West Bengal v. Calcutta Club Ltd
caseLaw.citation: (2019) 19 SCC 107 / 2019 SCC OnLine SC 1291 / [2019] 110 taxmann.com 47 (SC), Civil Appeal No. 4184 of 2009, decided 03-10-2019
caseLaw.facts: Whether a members' club supplying food, drink or facilities to its own members makes a 'sale' / 'service' — the doctrine of mutuality says a person cannot trade with himself.
caseLaw.issue: Are supplies by an incorporated members' club to its members taxable?
caseLaw.held: The doctrine of mutuality survived the 46th Constitutional Amendment; supplies by a members' club to its members were not a 'sale of goods' or a taxable 'service' in the pre-GST regime.
caseLaw.effect: Largely NEUTRALISED for GST — section 7(1)(aa), inserted by the Finance Act 2021 with retrospective effect from 01.07.2017, deems a club / association and its members to be distinct persons, so supplies by a club to its members ARE taxable under GST. Calcutta Club still matters for pre-GST periods and as interpretive background.

instrumentsExplained.gist: Notified Finance Act 2025 changes relating to Schedule III (specified actionable claims / warehoused-goods definitions) with retrospective effect from 01.07.2017.

cgst-s8.plainEnglish:
**Section 8 tells you how to tax a bundle of supplies.**

- **Composite supply** — two or more taxable supplies naturally bundled and
  supplied together in the ordinary course of business, one of which is the
  **principal supply**. Tax the **whole bundle at the rate of the principal
  supply**. (Example: goods + transit insurance + freight → rate of the goods.)
- **Mixed supply** — two or more independent supplies made together for a single
  price, not naturally bundled. Tax the **whole bundle at the highest rate**
  among the items. (Example: a hamper of chocolates, dry fruits, aerated drinks
  and a decorative box → highest applicable rate.)

complianceChecklist.item: For every bundled offering, classify as composite or mixed and document why
Composite: charge the principal-supply rate on the whole value
Mixed: charge the highest applicable rate on the whole value

keyConcepts.note: The predominant element of a composite supply, to which the other supplies are ancillary — s.2(90).
Not a statutory term — drawn from the pre-GST 'bundled service' jurisprudence; look at trade practice and customer perception.

cgst-s8.practicalNotes:
The distinction turns on whether the elements are **naturally bundled** — judged
by industry practice, customer expectation, whether elements can be supplied
separately, and advertising. Get it wrong and either you under-charge (mixed
treated as composite) or over-charge (composite treated as mixed).

Works contracts and restaurant service are separately defined as composite
supplies of **service** in Schedule II, so section 8 is not needed for them.

examples.title: Composite vs mixed
examples.scenario: (a) A dealer sells a laptop with a pre-loaded OS, one-year on-site warranty and delivery, for a single price. (b) A retailer sells a gift pack of a bottle of wine (28%), chocolates (18%) and a mug (18%) for 2,000.
working: (a) Naturally bundled around the laptop → composite supply; principal supply = laptop → tax the whole at the laptop rate
(b) Independent items sold together for one price, not naturally bundled → mixed supply → tax the whole 2,000 at 28% (highest)
examples.result: (a) laptop rate on the whole; (b) 28% on the whole gift pack.

faqs.q: How do I decide composite vs mixed?
faqs.a: Ask whether the elements are naturally bundled and supplied together in the ordinary course of business. If yes and there is a clear principal supply → composite (principal-supply rate). If they are independent and just packaged together for one price → mixed (highest rate).

commonMistakes: Splitting a composite supply into parts and charging different rates
Treating a genuine mixed supply as composite and charging the lower rate

cgst-s9.plainEnglish:
**Section 9 is the charging section for CGST.**

- **9(1)** — CGST is levied on all intra-State supplies (except supply of
  alcoholic liquor for human consumption) on the **value under section 15**, at
  rates notified (0.125% to 20% CGST; effective GST rates 0 / 5 / 12 / 18 / 28%
  plus special rates), collected in the prescribed manner, paid by the
  **taxable person**.
- **9(2)** — CGST on petroleum crude, high-speed diesel, motor spirit, natural
  gas and aviation turbine fuel is levied **from a date to be notified** by the
  Government on the Council's recommendation (currently outside GST).
- **9(3)** — **reverse charge**: the Government may notify categories of supply
  where the **recipient** pays the tax (e.g. GTA, legal services from an
  advocate, director's services, sponsorship, import of services, security
  services).
- **9(4)** — reverse charge on supplies from an **unregistered** supplier to a
  registered person, for notified classes (currently limited — mainly promoter /
  real-estate inward supplies).
- **9(5)** — for notified services supplied **through an electronic commerce
  operator** (passenger transport, accommodation, restaurant service, house-
  keeping), the **ECO** pays the tax as if it were the supplier.

complianceChecklist.item: Maintain the current RCM list (Notif 13/2017-CT(R) and 4/2017-CT(R), as amended)
Identify RCM inward supplies each month and pay the tax in cash in GSTR-3B Table 3.1(d)
Issue self-invoices and payment vouchers for RCM from unregistered suppliers
Claim ITC of RCM tax paid, subject to sections 16 and 17
E-commerce operators: pay tax under section 9(5) on notified services routed through the platform

keyConcepts.note: Liability to pay tax on the recipient instead of the supplier — s.2(98).
A person who owns / operates / manages a digital platform for electronic commerce — s.2(45).
A person registered or liable to be registered under section 22 or section 24 — s.2(107).

cgst-s9.practicalNotes:
Under RCM the recipient pays tax in **cash** (not by using ITC), then takes ITC
of that tax in the same or a later month subject to section 16. Issue a
**self-invoice** under section 31(3)(f) for RCM inward supplies from unregistered
suppliers, and a **payment voucher** under section 31(3)(g).

The RCM list is in Notification 13/2017-CT(R) (services) and 4/2017-CT(R) (goods),
each as amended — keep the current version.

examples.title: RCM on legal services
examples.scenario: A private limited company (turnover 3 crore) receives legal advice from an advocate and is billed 1,00,000 without GST.
working: Legal services by an advocate to a business entity → RCM under Notif 13/2017-CT(R)
Company pays IGST/CGST+SGST @18% = 18,000 in cash through GSTR-3B (Table 3.1(d))
Company takes ITC of 18,000 in Table 4(A)(3), subject to section 16 / 17
examples.result: Net cash cost is nil if the ITC is fully eligible; the tax is only a timing / cash-flow item.

flowchart.title: Who pays the GST — supplier or recipient?

nodes.text: You have received a taxable supply of goods or services
Is it a notified reverse-charge supply (GTA, advocate, director, sponsorship, import of service, security, etc. — Notif 13/2017 or 4/2017)?
You (the recipient) pay GST in cash, issue a self-invoice if the supplier is unregistered, then claim ITC.
Is it a section 9(5) service supplied through an e-commerce operator (cab, stay, restaurant, housekeeping)?
The e-commerce operator pays the GST as if it were the supplier.
Forward charge — the supplier charges and pays the GST.

faqs.q: Can I pay reverse-charge tax using my ITC balance?
faqs.a: No. Reverse-charge tax must be paid in cash through the electronic cash ledger. You then take ITC of that tax (subject to sections 16 and 17).

faqs.q: Is section 9(4) RCM on all purchases from unregistered dealers?
faqs.a: No. The broad 9(4) levy was suspended and then replaced with a targeted version — it now applies only to notified classes (principally certain inward supplies of real-estate promoters). Ordinary purchases from unregistered persons are not under RCM.

faqs.q: Petrol and diesel — are they under GST?
faqs.a: They are within the GST framework (section 9(2)) but the levy is 'from a date to be notified'. Until then they remain under VAT / Central Excise and carry no GST and no ITC.

commonMistakes: Paying RCM tax by debiting the credit ledger instead of cash
Not issuing self-invoices for RCM from unregistered suppliers
Missing RCM on director's remuneration, sponsorship, or import of services
Claiming ITC on petrol / diesel purchases

caseLaw.name: Union of India v. Mohit Minerals Pvt Ltd
caseLaw.citation: (2022) 10 SCC 700 / 2022 (61) GSTL 257 (SC) / [2022] 138 taxmann.com 331 (SC), Civil Appeal Nos. 1390-1394 of 2022 and connected matters, decided 19-05-2022
caseLaw.facts: RCM levy on ocean freight on the Indian importer under a section 9(3) notification.
caseLaw.issue: Whether the importer could be made to pay tax under RCM on a service it did not receive.
caseLaw.held: The levy was unconstitutional to that extent; recommendations of the GST Council are not binding.
caseLaw.effect: No ocean-freight RCM on CIF imports; a leading authority on the scope of section 9(3) notifications.

instrumentsExplained.gist: Notified Finance (No. 2) Act 2024 changes across the CGST Act; for section 9, related to the levy framework and Explanation on 'specified actionable claims'.

cgst-s10.plainEnglish:
**Section 10 is the composition scheme** — a simplified, low-rate, low-compliance
option for small taxpayers.

**Eligibility** — aggregate turnover in the preceding financial year up to
**1.5 crore** (75 lakh for specified special-category States). A separate
**10(2A)** scheme covers service providers / mixed suppliers up to **50 lakh**
turnover.

**Rates** — 1% (manufacturers and traders — 0.5% CGST + 0.5% SGST), 5% for
restaurant service (2.5% + 2.5%), 6% under the 10(2A) service scheme (3% + 3%).
A trader pays 1% on **taxable** turnover only; a manufacturer / restaurant pays
on total turnover in the State.

**Cannot** — make inter-State outward supplies; supply through an e-commerce
operator that collects TCS; supply non-taxable goods; be a casual / non-resident
taxable person; manufacture notified goods (pan masala, ice cream, tobacco,
aerated water, etc.).

**Consequences** — no ITC; no tax collected from customers; issue a **bill of
supply**, not a tax invoice; file **CMP-08** quarterly and **GSTR-4** annually.

complianceChecklist.item: Confirm preceding-year aggregate turnover is within the limit
File CMP-02 before the financial year begins (or opt in Part B of REG-01 as a new registrant)
Pay the ITC-03 amount on stock and note the credit-ledger lapse
Issue bills of supply with 'composition taxable person, not eligible to collect tax on supplies'
Pay RCM tax at normal rates in cash
File CMP-08 quarterly (by the 18th) and GSTR-4 annually (by 30 June)
On crossing the limit, file CMP-04 within 7 days and switch to normal with ITC-01

keyConcepts.note: All-India PAN-level turnover of taxable, exempt, export and inter-State supplies, excluding taxes and inward RCM — s.2(6).
The document a composition taxpayer / exempt supplier issues instead of a tax invoice — no tax shown — Rule 49.

cgst-s10.practicalNotes:
Opt in with **CMP-02** before the start of the year; a new registrant opts in
Part B of REG-01. On opting in, pay the ITC-03 amount on stock and let the credit
ledger lapse.

RCM still applies — a composition taxpayer pays reverse-charge tax at the
**normal** rate (not the composition rate) and gets no ITC of it.

If turnover crosses the limit mid-year, composition ends **from the day** of
crossing; file **CMP-04** within 7 days and switch to normal, claiming ITC on
stock via ITC-01.

examples.title: Trader composition tax
examples.scenario: A trader in Maharashtra under composition has, in a quarter, total turnover of 30,00,000 of which 4,00,000 is exempt goods.
working: Taxable turnover = 26,00,000
Tax @1% on taxable turnover = 26,000 (13,000 CGST + 13,000 SGST)
examples.result: Pay 26,000 through CMP-08 for the quarter; no tax charged to customers, no ITC.

flowchart.title: Can I be under the composition scheme?

nodes.text: Check the preceding year's aggregate turnover (all-India, PAN level)
Is turnover within 1.5 crore (goods) / 50 lakh (10(2A) services)?
Not eligible — register / continue as a normal taxpayer.
Do you make any inter-State outward supply, or supply through a TCS e-commerce operator, or manufacture notified goods (pan masala, ice cream, tobacco...)?
Are you a casual / non-resident taxable person, or supplying non-taxable goods?
Eligible. File CMP-02, pay ITC-03 on stock, issue bills of supply, file CMP-08 + GSTR-4.

faqs.q: Can a composition dealer make inter-State sales?
faqs.a: No. Any inter-State outward supply disqualifies the composition scheme. Inter-State **purchases** are allowed.

faqs.q: Does a composition taxpayer pay RCM?
faqs.a: Yes, at the normal rate, in cash, with no ITC. Composition is only about **outward** tax.

faqs.q: Can a composition supplier sell on Amazon / Flipkart?
faqs.a: Not where the platform is required to collect TCS. Supply through such an e-commerce operator disqualifies composition (a limited relaxation exists for goods suppliers making intra-State supply through ECO, subject to conditions).

commonMistakes: Making an inter-State sale while under composition
Collecting tax from customers on a bill of supply
Paying RCM at the composition rate instead of the normal rate
Continuing under composition after crossing the turnover limit

instrumentsExplained.gist: Raised the composition turnover limit for goods to 1.5 crore (75 lakh for special-category States) from 01.04.2019.

forms.purpose: Intimation to opt into the composition scheme.
forms.when: Before the start of the financial year

forms.purpose: Quarterly statement-cum-challan of composition tax.
forms.when: 18th of the month after the quarter

forms.purpose: Annual return of a composition taxpayer.
Intimation of withdrawal from composition (voluntary or on crossing the limit).

cgst-s11.plainEnglish:
**Section 11 is the exemption power.** The Government, on the Council's
recommendation, may by **notification** exempt goods or services — wholly or
partly, absolutely or conditionally, generally or for a class — where it is in
the public interest. It may also exempt by **special order** in exceptional
circumstances, and may issue an explanation within one year that is
retrospective.

Key points:
- An **absolute** (unconditional) exemption is **mandatory** — the supplier must
  not charge tax and cannot claim ITC on the exempt supply.
- A **conditional** exemption can be availed or not, unless it is the only rate.
- Exempt supplies drag in section 17 apportionment and can block composition /
  registration reliefs differently.

complianceChecklist.item: Work from the current consolidated 12/2017 and 2/2017 CT(R) notifications
Check each exemption entry's conditions before applying it
Do not claim ITC on inputs used for absolutely-exempt supplies; apportion common ITC
Issue a bill of supply (not a tax invoice) for exempt outward supplies

keyConcepts.note: Nil-rated, wholly exempt under s.11 / s.6 of IGST, or non-taxable supply — s.2(47).
A supply not leviable to tax under the CGST/IGST Act (e.g. alcoholic liquor, petroleum until notified) — s.2(78).

cgst-s11.practicalNotes:
The core exemption notifications are **12/2017-CT(R)** (services) and
**2/2017-CT(R)** (goods), each heavily amended — always work from the current
consolidated version and check the entry conditions.

"Nil-rated", "wholly exempt" and "non-taxable" all count as **exempt supply** for
ITC apportionment. Zero-rated supply (exports / SEZ) is different — it carries
full ITC.

faqs.q: Can I choose to pay tax on a supply that is exempt?
faqs.a: If the exemption is **absolute** (no conditions), no — you must not charge tax. If it is **conditional**, you may choose not to satisfy the condition and pay tax instead, unless that is the only tariff entry.

faqs.q: Does an exempt supply affect my ITC?
faqs.a: Yes. ITC attributable to exempt supplies is not available; common ITC must be apportioned under section 17 read with Rule 42 / 43.

commonMistakes: Charging tax on an absolutely-exempt supply
Claiming full ITC while making exempt supplies
Confusing zero-rated (exports, full ITC) with exempt (no ITC)

instrumentsExplained.gist: The master exemption notification for services (as amended).

cgst-s11a.plainEnglish:
**Section 11A (inserted by the Finance (No. 2) Act 2024) gives the Government
power not to recover GST that was not levied or was short-levied because of a
general practice.**

Where, due to a **generally prevalent trade practice**, tax was not being paid
(or was under-paid) on a supply, the Government may, on the Council's
recommendation, direct by notification that the tax **need not be paid** for the
past period. It does **not** entitle anyone to a **refund** of tax already paid
in line with the correct position.

This is the GST equivalent of the old section 11C of the Central Excise Act — a
one-time regularisation tool for industry-wide interpretation errors.

complianceChecklist.item: Check for a section 11A notification before conceding a past-period demand arising from an industry-wide practice

Defined term — tap in the text to see the definition.
