cgst-s11a.practicalNotes:
Relevant where a sector receives a favourable clarification after years of a
different practice — an 11A notification can close the past exposure without
individual litigation. Track whether a notification has issued for your sector's
issue before conceding a past demand.

faqs.q: Can I claim a refund under section 11A?
faqs.a: No. Section 11A only regularises non-payment / short-payment caused by a general practice; it expressly does not allow a refund of tax that was correctly paid.

commonMistakes: Assuming section 11A allows a refund of tax already paid

instrumentsExplained.gist: Notified section 11A from a date appointed under the Finance (No. 2) Act 2024.

cgst-s12.plainEnglish:
**Section 12 fixes the time of supply of goods — the point at which the tax
becomes payable.**

- **Forward charge (12(2))** — the **earlier** of (a) the date of issue of the
  invoice, or the last date on which it was required to be issued under
  section 31, and (b) the date of receipt of payment. By Notification
  66/2017-CT, tax on **advances for goods** is **not** payable — so effectively
  it is the invoice date / last date for issue.
- **Reverse charge (12(3))** — the **earliest** of (a) date of receipt of goods,
  (b) date of payment, or (c) 30 days from the supplier's invoice. If none can
  be determined, the date of entry in the recipient's books.
- **Vouchers (12(4))** — date of issue if the supply is identifiable at that
  point; otherwise the date of redemption.
- **Residual (12(5))** — date of filing the return, or of payment of tax.
- **Interest / late fee / penalty additions (12(6))** — time of supply is the
  date the supplier receives that addition.

complianceChecklist.item: Issue the tax invoice for goods on or before removal / delivery (section 31(1))
Recognise output tax on goods by the invoice date (advances not taxed)
For RCM goods, book the tax by the earliest of receipt / payment / 30 days from supplier's invoice

keyConcepts.note: The point fixed by sections 12–14 at which the liability to pay GST arises.
The earlier of the entry of payment in the books or the credit to the bank account — Explanation to s.12/13.

cgst-s12.practicalNotes:
For most sellers of goods on forward charge the practical answer is simply the
**invoice date**, because advances are not taxed and the invoice must be issued
on or before removal / delivery (section 31(1)).

The 30-day RCM trigger (12(3)(c)) is the one people forget — if goods are
received but not paid for and the supplier's invoice is more than 30 days old,
RCM tax is due even though no cash has moved.

examples.title: Advance for goods
examples.scenario: A manufacturer receives 5,00,000 advance on 10 May for goods to be delivered and invoiced on 20 June.
working: Advance received for goods → Notification 66/2017-CT: no tax on the advance
Time of supply = invoice date 20 June (or last date for issue, if earlier)
examples.result: GST is payable in the June return, on the full value, at the invoice date.

faqs.q: Do I pay GST on advances received for goods?
faqs.a: No. Notification 66/2017-CT exempts every registered person (other than a composition taxpayer) from paying tax on advances for **goods** — tax is due at the invoice / removal stage. Advances for **services** are still taxed (section 13).

faqs.q: When does RCM on goods trigger if I haven't paid the supplier?
faqs.a: On the earliest of receipt of goods, payment, or **30 days from the supplier's invoice date**. So an unpaid RCM purchase still attracts tax 30 days after the invoice.

commonMistakes: Paying GST on advances for goods (no longer required)
Missing the 30-day RCM trigger on unpaid purchases
Delaying the invoice beyond removal and shifting the tax point incorrectly

instrumentsExplained.gist: Exempts registered persons (other than composition) from paying GST on advances received for supply of goods — tax is due only at the invoice stage.

cgst-s13.plainEnglish:
**Section 13 fixes the time of supply of services.**

- **Forward charge (13(2))** — if the invoice is issued **within 30 days** of
  completion of service (45 days for banks / NBFCs): the **earlier** of invoice
  date and payment date. If the invoice is **not** issued in time: the **earlier**
  of completion of service and payment date. If neither works: the date the
  recipient shows it in the books.
- **Reverse charge (13(3))** — the **earlier** of (a) date of payment, or
  (b) **60 days** from the supplier's invoice date. If neither can be
  determined, date of entry in the recipient's books. For **associated
  enterprises** where the supplier is outside India — the earlier of the book
  entry date and the payment date.
- **Vouchers, residual, additions** — as in section 12.

complianceChecklist.item: Issue service invoices within 30 days of completion (45 days for banks / NBFCs)
Issue a receipt voucher and pay GST on advances for services
For RCM services, book the tax by the earlier of payment or 60 days from the supplier's invoice
For continuous supply, invoice by the due date of payment / completion of the event (section 31(5))

keyConcepts.note: Service supplied continuously / recurrently under a contract for a period exceeding 3 months with periodic payment obligations — s.2(33); invoice timing follows section 31(5).
As defined in section 92A of the Income-tax Act — a special RCM time-of-supply rule applies for imported services from them.

cgst-s13.practicalNotes:
Unlike goods, **advances for services are taxable** — receipt of an advance is a
time of supply, and a **receipt voucher** (section 31(3)(d)) must be issued.

The 30-day invoice window (section 31(2) read with Rule 47) is what keeps the
"invoice date" as the practical time of supply. Miss it and the tax point shifts
back to the **completion of service**, which can pull a liability into an earlier
period.

For imported services, RCM time of supply is the earlier of payment or **60 days**
from the foreign supplier's invoice.

examples.title: Advance for a service
examples.scenario: A consultant receives 2,00,000 advance on 5 April for a project completed and invoiced on 30 June.
working: Advance for a service → time of supply for the advance is 5 April
Issue a receipt voucher; pay GST on 2,00,000 in the April return
Balance value → time of supply on the invoice / completion in June
examples.result: GST on the advance is due in April; the rest in June.

faqs.q: Are advances for services taxable?
faqs.a: Yes. Receipt of an advance for a service is a time of supply. Issue a receipt voucher and pay GST on the advance; adjust it when the final invoice is raised.

faqs.q: What happens if I raise the service invoice after 30 days?
faqs.a: The time of supply shifts to the **date of completion of the service** (or the earlier payment date). This can move the liability into an earlier tax period and attract interest.

commonMistakes: Not paying GST on advances for services
Raising service invoices late and mis-timing the liability
Using the 60-day RCM window for goods (it is 30 days for goods, 60 for services)

forms.purpose: Issued on receipt of an advance for a supply — section 31(3)(d).
Issued when an advance is refunded and no supply is made — section 31(3)(e).

cgst-s14.plainEnglish:
**Section 14 decides which rate applies when the GST rate changes** and the
supply straddles the change date.

For each supply, look at three events: **(1)** supply of goods / completion of
service, **(2)** issue of invoice, **(3)** receipt of payment.

- If the supply is **before** the rate change: the **new rate** applies only if
  **both** invoice and payment are after the change; otherwise the **old rate**.
- If the supply is **after** the rate change: the **old rate** applies only if
  **both** invoice and payment are before the change; otherwise the **new rate**.

In short — the rate is fixed by whichever **two of the three events** fall on the
same side of the change date.

complianceChecklist.item: On any notified rate change, list open advances, un-invoiced supplies and unpaid invoices
Apply the two-out-of-three test (supply / invoice / payment) to fix the rate for each
Re-price contracts and POs to reflect the new rate where the contract is tax-exclusive

keyConcepts.note: Defined term — tap in the text to see the definition.
Defined term — tap in the text to see the definition.
Defined term — tap in the text to see the definition.

cgst-s14.practicalNotes:
Payment is treated as received on the date of book entry or bank credit,
**whichever is earlier**; but if the bank credit is more than 4 working days
after the rate change, the date of credit is taken.

This section matters at every GST Council rate revision (e.g. the 2022 rate
rationalisation, GST 2.0). Map open orders, advances and pending invoices to the
change date before it takes effect.

examples.title: Rate change straddle
examples.scenario: Rate on a product goes from 12% to 18% on 1 October. Goods are supplied on 25 September; invoice raised 3 October; payment received 10 October.
working: Supply (25 Sep) is before the change
Invoice (3 Oct) and payment (10 Oct) are both after the change
Rule: supply before change → new rate applies only if both invoice and payment are after — they are
examples.result: 18% (the new rate) applies.

faqs.q: Rate changed mid-contract. Which rate for the part already invoiced?
faqs.a: Apply section 14 supply by supply / invoice by invoice. For each, see whether at least two of {supply, invoice, payment} fall before or after the change and apply that rate.

commonMistakes: Applying the invoice-date rate mechanically without the section 14 test
Ignoring the 4-working-day rule for bank credits around the change date

cgst-s15.plainEnglish:
**Section 15 is the valuation section — how much GST is charged on.**

**15(1)** — the value is the **transaction value**: the price actually paid or
payable, where supplier and recipient are **not related** and price is the
**sole consideration**.

**15(2) — inclusions.** The value **includes**:
- any taxes, duties, cesses, fees (other than GST itself and the compensation
  cess if charged separately);
- amounts the supplier is liable to pay but which the recipient has paid;
- **incidental expenses** — packing, commission, and anything charged before /
  at the time of supply;
- **interest, late fee or penalty for delayed payment** of consideration;
- **subsidies** directly linked to the price (excluding Government subsidies).

**15(3) — exclusions (discounts).** A discount is excluded if:
- given **before or at the time of supply** and recorded in the invoice; or
- given **after supply**, if agreed **before / at the time of supply**, linked to
  specific invoices, **and** the recipient reverses the proportionate ITC.

**15(4)** — where 15(1) does not apply (related parties, non-monetary
consideration), value is determined under the **valuation rules** (Rules 27–35).
**15(5)** — the Government may notify supplies to be valued in a prescribed
manner (e.g. lottery, second-hand goods, TCS-inclusive value).

complianceChecklist.item: Build the invoice value with all section 15(2) inclusions (non-GST taxes, incidental charges, price-linked subsidies, interest for delay)
Only net off discounts that meet the section 15(3) tests; issue section 34 credit notes for post-sale discounts
Ensure buyers reverse ITC on excluded post-sale discounts
Value related-party / branch supplies under Rule 28 (use the full-ITC proviso where available)
Use Rule 33 for genuine pure-agent reimbursements and keep the documentation

keyConcepts.note: The price actually paid or payable for the supply where the parties are unrelated and price is the sole consideration — s.15(1).
Officers / directors of one another's business, employer-employee, holding-subsidiary, common control, etc. — Explanation to s.15.
A recipient of supply who incurs expenditure on behalf of the customer and is reimbursed at actuals — Rule 33; such reimbursements are excluded from value.

cgst-s15.practicalNotes:
**TCS under the Income-tax Act** forms part of the value (Circular 76/50/2018 as
amended — TCS is on a tax-inclusive value but not itself included after the 2019
clarification); **TDS** does not.

**Post-sale discounts** are the biggest valuation trap. To exclude them you need
a **pre-agreed scheme**, a link to specific invoices, and an **ITC reversal by
the buyer** — usually done through a **credit note** under section 34. A pure
quantity / turnover discount announced later does not reduce value.

**Related-party / branch** supplies: Rule 28 — open market value, or 90% of the
downstream sale price for goods to be sold as such, **or**, where the recipient
is eligible for full ITC, **any value declared in the invoice is deemed to be
the open market value**. This last proviso removes most branch-transfer
valuation disputes.

examples.title: Post-sale (secondary) discount
examples.scenario: A distributor is given a 2% year-end volume rebate on 1 crore of purchases. The scheme was announced at the start of the year and is linked to the year's invoices.
working: Discount agreed before / at the time of supply and linked to invoices → can be excluded from value
Supplier issues a credit note under section 34 for 2,00,000 + GST
Distributor reverses the proportionate ITC
examples.result: Value is reduced by 2,00,000; if any condition fails, the discount cannot be netted and the credit note is a financial (no-GST) credit note.

examples.title: Branch transfer with full-ITC recipient
examples.scenario: Head office transfers goods to its branch in another State; the branch can claim full ITC.
working: Rule 28 second proviso: where the recipient is eligible for full ITC, the invoice value is deemed to be the open market value
examples.result: Any reasonable value declared on the branch-transfer invoice is accepted; no separate valuation exercise needed.

flowchart.title: How do I value this supply?

nodes.text: Identify the price actually paid or payable for the supply
Are the supplier and recipient related, or is price not the sole consideration?
Value under Rules 27–31 (open market value / 90% rule / cost + 10% / best judgement). Rule 28 proviso: full-ITC recipient → invoice value accepted.
Add: non-GST taxes, recipient-borne supplier liabilities, incidental charges, interest for delay, price-linked subsidies. Any discount?
Is the discount recorded on the invoice, OR pre-agreed + invoice-linked + buyer reverses ITC?
Discount cannot be deducted — value stays gross; issue only a financial credit note.
Value = transaction value with the section 15(2) additions and section 15(3) discounts.

faqs.q: Is interest on delayed payment from a customer taxable?
faqs.a: Yes. Section 15(2)(d) includes interest, late fee or penalty for delayed payment of consideration in the value, at the rate applicable to the underlying supply. Raise a debit note / invoice for it when received.

faqs.q: Do I add TDS deducted by my customer to the value?
faqs.a: No. TDS (income-tax or GST) is a mode of recovery, not part of the consideration. TCS collected by you under the Income-tax Act is a different question — see Circular 76/50/2018 as amended.

faqs.q: Can I reduce value for a discount I decide to give after the sale?
faqs.a: Only if the discount was agreed **before or at the time of the supply**, is linked to specific invoices, and the buyer reverses the proportionate ITC. A discount thought of later cannot reduce the taxable value.

faqs.q: How do I value free samples / buy-one-get-one?
faqs.a: Free samples are not a supply for consideration (value nil) but ITC on them is blocked under section 17(5)(h). 'Buy one get one' is one supply of two items for a single price — value the whole and ITC is not affected (Circular 92/11/2019).

commonMistakes: Not adding freight / packing / installation charged separately to the invoice value
Netting off turnover discounts decided after the sale
Forgetting GST on interest / penalty recovered from customers for late payment
Under-valuing branch transfers without using the Rule 28 full-ITC proviso
Claiming ITC on free samples (blocked by 17(5)(h))

caseLaw.name: Torrent Power Ltd. v. Union of India
caseLaw.citation: R/Special Civil Application No. 12175 of 2024 & connected matters (Gujarat High Court), decided 14-08-2026
caseLaw.facts: Holding companies gave corporate guarantees to banks for their subsidiaries' borrowings, mostly without any commission. The department levied GST on a deemed value of 1% per annum of the guaranteed amount under Rule 28(2) — including for guarantees executed before Rule 28(2) came in (26.10.2023) and for pre-GST guarantees — and issued section 74 SCNs alleging suppression. The vires of section 15(4), Rule 28(2) and CBIC Circulars 204/16/2023 and 225/19/2024-GST were challenged.
caseLaw.issue: Whether a corporate guarantee without consideration is a taxable supply, whether the Rule 28(2) '1% per annum or actual consideration, whichever is higher' valuation is valid, and whether it can apply retrospectively.
caseLaw.held: A corporate guarantee by a holding company for its subsidiary, even without consideration, is a supply of service between related persons (section 7(1)(a) with Schedule I); it is 'business' under section 2(17) and is not an actionable claim excluded by Schedule III. Time of supply is annual under section 13(2)(c); it is not a continuous supply. Section 15(4) is intra vires. Rule 28(2) is upheld, but the words 'whichever is higher' are struck down as arbitrary (Article 14 / 19(1)(g)) — value is the actual consideration where there is one, otherwise the deemed 1%. The 1% deemed value cannot be levied for any period before 26.10.2023 (impermissible retroactive levy), though it applies from that date if the guarantee continues. Section 74 SCNs premised only on 'non-declaration' in a genuine interpretational dispute were quashed. Circulars 204/16/2023 and 225/19/2024-GST set aside to the extent inconsistent.
caseLaw.effect: Where a guarantee commission is actually charged, value it at that amount — the department cannot force the deemed 1% on top. No 1% demand for periods before 26.10.2023. Gujarat HC — binding in Gujarat, persuasive elsewhere; a Revenue SLP is expected, so confirm the position and any stay.

caseLaw.name: Union of India v. Bombay Tyre International Ltd
caseLaw.facts: Central Excise valuation — what post-manufacturing expenses form part of assessable value.
caseLaw.issue: Scope of 'transaction value' and permissible deductions.
caseLaw.held: Only expenses up to the point of sale / removal form part of value; post-sale transport and certain trade discounts are deductible.
caseLaw.effect: Foundational reasoning still cited for the treatment of freight, discounts and incidental expenses under GST valuation.

instrumentsExplained.gist: Notified Finance Act 2025 changes to section 15 (relating to the discount / credit-note mechanism and value of exempt supply) from 01.10.2025.

forms.purpose: Reduces the value / tax of an earlier invoice — used for post-sale discounts, returns and deficiencies; must be declared in GSTR-1.

cgst-s16.plainEnglish:
**Section 16 is the gateway to input tax credit (ITC).** It sets out who may take
credit, the conditions every claim must satisfy, and the outer time limit.

**Sub-section (1) — entitlement.** A registered person may take credit of the
input tax on inward supplies of goods or services used, or intended to be used,
in the course or furtherance of business. The credit is posted to the electronic
credit ledger.

**Sub-section (2) — the conditions (all must be met).**
- (a) possession of a tax invoice / debit note / other prescribed document;
- (aa) the supplier has reported that document in GSTR-1 / IFF and it appears in
  the recipient's GSTR-2B;
- (b) the goods or services have been received (bill-to / ship-to deliveries
  count);
- (ba) the ITC has not been restricted in the recipient's GSTR-2B under
  section 38;
- (c) the tax has actually been paid to the Government; and
- (d) the recipient has furnished the GSTR-3B return.
First proviso: for goods received in lots, credit is taken on receipt of the last
lot. Second proviso: if the recipient does not pay the supplier the value plus
tax within 180 days of the invoice date, an equal amount of ITC must be reversed
with interest, and re-availed when payment is finally made (reverse-charge
supplies are excluded).

**Sub-section (3) — depreciation.** No ITC on the tax component of capital goods
if income-tax depreciation has been claimed on that tax.

**Sub-section (4) — time limit.** ITC on an invoice or debit note cannot be taken
after 30 November following the end of the financial year to which it pertains,
or the date of filing the annual return, whichever is earlier. For a debit note
the relevant year is the year of the debit note itself (position from
01.01.2021).

**Sub-section (5) — one-time relaxation.** For FY 2017-18 to 2020-21, ITC could be
taken in any GSTR-3B filed up to 30 November 2021 (inserted by the Finance (No. 2)
Act 2024, with retrospective effect from 01.07.2017).

**Sub-section (6).** Where a cancelled registration is later revoked, ITC for the
intervening period may be taken in a return filed within 30 days of the
revocation order.

complianceChecklist.item: Hold a valid tax invoice / debit note / bill of entry / ISD invoice for every ITC claim
Reconcile the purchase register to GSTR-2B each month before filing GSTR-3B
Claim ITC only to the extent reflected in GSTR-2B (clause (aa) + Rule 36(4))
Confirm the goods / services have been received (last lot for instalments)
Track supplier payments; reverse ITC with interest where value + tax is unpaid for 180 days
Re-avail reversed ITC in the month the supplier is paid
Claim all pending ITC for a financial year by the GSTR-3B for October of the next year
Do not claim income-tax depreciation on the tax component of capitalised capital goods

keyConcepts.note: CGST / SGST / UTGST / IGST and cess charged on inward supplies — section 2(62).
The ledger ITC is credited to and output tax is paid from — section 49, Rule 86.
Goods capitalised in the books and used in the course of business — section 2(19).
The static auto-drafted ITC statement generated on the 14th; the reference for clauses (aa) and (ba).

cgst-s16.practicalNotes:
**GSTR-2B is the ceiling.** Since 01.01.2022, clause (aa) with Rule 36(4) means
you can claim only what appears in GSTR-2B. Reconcile the purchase register to
2B every month and chase suppliers for missing invoices well before the
section 16(4) deadline.

**"Actually paid" (clause (c)).** Departments deny ITC to bona fide recipients
when the supplier defaults on payment of tax. Several High Courts have granted
relief where the recipient holds a valid invoice, has paid the supplier, and the
supplier was registered at the time — but the Supreme Court has not settled the
point. Keep proof of payment to the supplier and of the supplier's registration
status.

**180-day reversal.** Track creditor ageing. Reverse the ITC in Table 4(B)(2) of
GSTR-3B for the month the 180 days expire, with interest under section 50(3);
re-avail in Table 4(A)(5) in the month you pay. There is no fresh time limit on
re-availment.

**The 30-November cut-off is hard.** The GSTR-3B for October (filed by 20
November) is normally the last return before the deadline for the previous
financial year's invoices.

examples.title: 180-day reversal and re-availment
examples.scenario: X Ltd receives services worth 10,00,000 plus 1,80,000 IGST on 5 April 2024 and takes ITC of 1,80,000 in April's GSTR-3B. The supplier is not paid by 2 October 2024 (180 days). Payment is made in January 2025.
working: Day 180 falls in October 2024 → reverse 1,80,000 in GSTR-3B for Oct 2024, Table 4(B)(2)
Interest @18% p.a. under s.50(3) from the May-2024 return due date to the Oct-2024 return date
January 2025: supplier paid → re-avail 1,80,000 in Jan GSTR-3B, Table 4(A)(5)
examples.result: The credit is only a timing loss plus interest, provided the supplier is eventually paid.

examples.title: Missing the time limit
examples.scenario: An invoice dated 15 March 2024 (FY 2023-24) is discovered unclaimed in December 2024.
working: FY 2023-24 → deadline is 30 November 2024, or filing of the FY 2023-24 annual return, whichever is earlier
Last practical return before 30 Nov 2024 is GSTR-3B for October 2024
examples.result: The ITC has already lapsed — it could only have been claimed up to the October 2024 GSTR-3B.

examples.title: Depreciation on the tax component
examples.scenario: Y buys a machine for 50,00,000 plus 9,00,000 GST.
working: If Y capitalises 59,00,000 and claims income-tax depreciation on 59,00,000, section 16(3) blocks the 9,00,000 ITC
If Y capitalises only 50,00,000 and depreciates 50,00,000, the 9,00,000 is available as ITC
examples.result: Capitalise the cost net of GST and take the tax as ITC — do not depreciate the tax.

flowchart.title: Can I take ITC on this invoice?

nodes.text: You hold a tax invoice / debit note / prescribed document for a business inward supply
Is it in your GSTR-2B and not flagged / restricted?
Wait — cannot claim until it appears in 2B. Follow up with the supplier.
Have you received the goods / services? (last lot, if in instalments)
Is the supply blocked by section 17(5), or used for exempt / personal purposes?
No full ITC — the credit is blocked, or must be apportioned under section 17.
Is it within 30 November following the FY (or the annual-return date)?
Time-barred under section 16(4) — the credit lapses.
Will you pay the supplier (value + tax) within 180 days?
Take the ITC in GSTR-3B Table 4(A)(5).
Take it now, reverse with interest at day 180, re-avail when you pay.

faqs.q: Can I take ITC if the supplier has not paid the tax to the Government?
faqs.a: Clause (c) of section 16(2) requires the tax to have been *actually paid*. Departments deny ITC when the supplier defaults. Several High Courts have granted relief to bona fide recipients who hold a valid invoice and have paid the supplier, but the Supreme Court has not settled the question. Keep proof of payment to the supplier and of the supplier's registration status at the time of supply.

faqs.q: Is there a time limit for ITC on a debit note?
faqs.a: Yes. Since 01.01.2021 the relevant financial year for a debit note is the year of the **debit note itself**, not the year of the original invoice. A debit note dated May 2024 for a 2022 invoice therefore carries a 30 November 2025 deadline.

faqs.q: Does the 180-day payment rule apply to reverse-charge supplies?
faqs.a: No. The second proviso to section 16(2) expressly excludes supplies on which tax is payable on reverse charge.

faqs.q: I received goods in five instalments against one invoice. When do I take credit?
faqs.a: On receipt of the last instalment — first proviso to section 16(2).

faqs.q: Registration was cancelled and later restored. What about ITC for the gap?
faqs.a: Sub-section (6) lets you take that ITC in a return filed within 30 days of the revocation order, provided the credit was not otherwise time-barred on the date of the cancellation order.

commonMistakes: Claiming provisional ITC on invoices not yet in GSTR-2B
Missing the 30 November cut-off and losing genuine credit
Forgetting the 180-day reversal on old creditors, then facing interest and penalty in audit
Applying a debit note's time limit by reference to the original invoice year (the pre-2021 position)
Capitalising GST on plant and machinery and also claiming depreciation on it
Claiming full ITC where the input is partly for exempt or personal use — that is a section 17 apportionment, not a section 16 question

caseLaw.name: Union of India v. Bharti Airtel Ltd
caseLaw.citation: (2022) 4 SCC 328 / [2021] 131 taxmann.com 319 (SC), Civil Appeal No. 6520 of 2021, decided 28-10-2021
caseLaw.facts: Airtel sought to rectify GSTR-3B of Jul–Sep 2017 to claim under-reported ITC after GSTR-2A data became available.
caseLaw.issue: Whether a filed GSTR-3B can be reopened / rectified to claim ITC of an earlier period.
caseLaw.held: GSTR-3B is a valid return; rectification of a filed GSTR-3B to add earlier-period ITC is not permitted. The remedy is to claim in a subsequent period's return.
caseLaw.effect: You cannot reopen a filed GSTR-3B — claim missed ITC in a later return within the section 16(4) limit.

caseLaw.name: Suncraft Energy Pvt Ltd v. Assistant Commissioner, State Tax
caseLaw.citation: 2023 (79) GSTL 156 (Cal), MAT No. 1218 of 2023, decided 02-08-2023; Revenue SLP (C) Nos. 27827-27828/2023 dismissed by the Supreme Court on 14-12-2023 (by a speaking order — relief confined to non-exceptional cases)
caseLaw.facts: ITC was denied to the recipient because of a GSTR-2A mismatch / supplier non-payment, without any action against the supplier.
caseLaw.issue: Can ITC be reversed in the recipient's hands for the supplier's default without first proceeding against the supplier?
caseLaw.held: Where the recipient holds a valid invoice, has paid the supplier and the supplier was registered, ITC cannot be denied mechanically; the department must first proceed against the supplier and can recover from the recipient only in exceptional cases (missing / non-existent supplier, collusion, closure of business).
caseLaw.effect: Gives bona fide recipients a defence against automatic section 16(2)(c) denials. The SC's dismissal of the Revenue SLP (14-12-2023) affirms it, subject to the 'exceptional cases' carve-out.

caseLaw.name: D.Y. Beathel Enterprises v. State Tax Officer
caseLaw.facts: ITC was recovered from the recipient where the supplier had collected but not paid the tax; the supplier was not examined.
caseLaw.issue: Recovery from the recipient without joining / examining the defaulting supplier.
caseLaw.held: The recovery was set aside; the department must examine and proceed against the supplier before recovering from the recipient.
caseLaw.effect: Supplier must be joined before ITC is recovered from a bona fide recipient.

caseLaw.name: State of Karnataka v. Ecom Gill Coffee Trading Pvt Ltd
caseLaw.citation: 2023 INSC 212 / (2023) 4 SCC 340 / [2023] 148 taxmann.com 330 (SC), Civil Appeal No. 230 of 2023, decided 13-03-2023
caseLaw.facts: Purchasing dealers claimed ITC under the KVAT Act on the strength of tax invoices and cheque payments; the sellers were untraceable / had not paid the tax.
caseLaw.issue: What must a purchasing dealer prove to claim input tax credit on a purchase?
caseLaw.held: The burden of proving a genuine transaction — actual physical movement and receipt of the goods, the identity and capacity of the seller — is on the purchasing dealer. A tax invoice and payment by cheque alone are not enough; the dealer must furnish the transporter details, freight payment, delivery evidence, etc.
caseLaw.effect: Applied to GST — a valid invoice + GSTR-2B is the entry point, but if genuineness is questioned the recipient must be able to prove actual receipt. Keep transport, e-way bill, weighbridge and delivery records.

caseLaw.name: ALD Automotive Pvt Ltd v. Commercial Tax Officer
caseLaw.citation: (2019) 13 SCC 225 / 2018 SCC OnLine SC 1945 / [2018] 99 taxmann.com 202 (SC), decided 12-10-2018
caseLaw.facts: ITC under the TNVAT Act was claimed beyond the statutory time limit for making the claim.
caseLaw.issue: Is the time limit for claiming input tax credit mandatory or merely procedural?
caseLaw.held: Input tax credit is a concession created by statute; a registered person can claim it only within the period and on the conditions the statute lays down. The time limit is mandatory, not directory.
caseLaw.effect: Reinforces that the section 16(4) 'thirtieth day of November' cut-off is a hard limit — missed credit is lost (subject only to the retrospective section 16(5)/(6) windows).

caseLaw.name: Jayam & Co. v. Assistant Commissioner
caseLaw.facts: A TNVAT provision restricting / reversing input tax credit was challenged as taking away a vested right.
caseLaw.issue: Is input tax credit a right that the legislature cannot curtail?
caseLaw.held: ITC is a form of concession / benefit granted by the statute. It is not an absolute or constitutional right; the legislature may impose conditions, restrictions and even withdraw it, and the conditions must be strictly complied with.
caseLaw.effect: The foundational statement relied on whenever ITC conditions (16(2)(aa)/(ba)/(c), Rule 36(4), Rule 86A/86B) are challenged — the conditions are valid and must be met exactly.

instrumentsExplained.gist: Brought clause (aa) of section 16(2) into force from 01.01.2022, making GSTR-2B the basis for ITC.
Notified the Finance Act 2022 ITC changes — omission of 'or section 43A' from clause (c), the November-30 wording in sub-section (4), and clause (ba) — from 01.10.2022.
Notified sub-sections (5) and (6) of section 16 (the retrospective relaxations for FY 2017-18 to 2020-21 and for revoked cancellations) from 27.09.2024.
Notified the CGST (Amendment) Act 2018 change to the Explanation on receipt of goods / services (bill-to / ship-to for services) from 01.02.2019.
Notified the Finance Act 2023 substitution in the second proviso — 'paid by him along with interest payable under section 50' — from 01.10.2023.

advisories.ref: Advisory — GSTR-2B is the basis for ITC
advisories.gist: From January 2022 ITC in GSTR-3B Table 4 is auto-populated from GSTR-2B and any excess must be explained; reconcile the purchase register to 2B, not 2A, before filing.

advisories.ref: Advisory — hard-locking of auto-populated GSTR-3B ITC
advisories.gist: GSTN has moved in phases towards restricting manual edits to the auto-drafted ITC figures in GSTR-3B; report differences through the reclaim / reversal statement rather than by overriding Table 4.

advisories.ref: Advisory — Electronic Credit and Re-claimed Statement
advisories.gist: An opening balance of ITC 'reversed and available for re-claim' had to be reported once; thereafter Table 4(B)(2) reversals and 4(A)(5) / 4(D)(1) re-claims are tracked in the statement.

forms.purpose: Static, auto-drafted statement of ITC available for the month; the reference for eligible credit.
Summary return where ITC is claimed (Table 4A) and reversed (Table 4B), and output tax is paid.
Statement of inputs / capital goods sent to and received from a job worker.

cgst-s17.plainEnglish:
**Section 17 restricts ITC in two situations and then lists the credits that are
blocked outright.**

**Sub-sections (1) and (2) — apportionment.** Where inputs are used partly for
business and partly for other purposes (1), or partly for taxable / zero-rated
supplies and partly for exempt supplies (2), credit is restricted to the part
attributable to business / taxable use. Rules 42 (inputs and input services) and
43 (capital goods) prescribe the monthly and annual working.

**Sub-section (3) — value of exempt supply.** "Exempt supply" for this purpose
includes reverse-charge inward supplies, transactions in securities, sale of land
and (subject to Schedule II para 5(b)) sale of building. By later amendment the
value of duty-credit scrips and certain warehoused-goods / high-seas transactions
are excluded from the exempt-supply figure.

**Sub-section (4) — banking companies / NBFCs.** May either follow Rules 42/43 or
take a flat 50% of eligible ITC each month (the 50% option is irrevocable for the
year and the 50% lapses).

**Sub-section (5) — blocked credits.** ITC is **not** available on, broadly:
motor vehicles for transport of persons (≤13 seats) and vessels / aircraft, with
carve-outs for further supply, passenger transport, driving training and goods
transport; related services (insurance, repair, leasing) of those vehicles; food
and beverages, outdoor catering, beauty treatment, health services, club and
fitness membership, life and health insurance (unless obligatory or for onward
supply); works contract services and goods / services for construction of
immovable property on own account (other than plant and machinery); travel
benefits to employees on leave; goods lost, stolen, destroyed, written off or
given as gifts / free samples; tax paid under sections 74 (pre-FY 2024-25), 129
and 130; and CSR expenditure (from 01.10.2023).

**Sub-section (6).** The Government may prescribe the manner of the sub-section
(1)/(2) attribution — done through Rules 42 and 43.

complianceChecklist.item: Identify credit that is exclusively for exempt supply (T2) or non-business use (T3) and reverse it in full
Run the Rule 42 / 43 working every month on common credit
Do the annual Rule 42 / 43 true-up by 30 November of the next financial year
Reverse ITC on any inventory write-off, loss, destruction, gift or free sample in the month it occurs
Exclude blocked-credit invoices (17(5)) from ITC at source
Banks / NBFCs: lock the 50% option at the start of the year and apply it consistently

keyConcepts.note: Nil-rated, wholly exempt, non-taxable supply, and (for s.17) RCM inward supplies, securities, land and building — s.2(47) as expanded by s.17(3).
Defined in the Explanation to s.17 — excludes land, buildings, civil structures, telecom towers and outside-factory pipelines.
A contract for building / construction / fabrication etc. of immovable property where transfer of property in goods is involved — s.2(119).

cgst-s17.practicalNotes:
**Rule 42 / 43 is a two-step exercise.** Compute a provisional reversal every
month based on that month's exempt turnover ratio, then a final annual reversal
by 30 November of the next year; the difference carries interest if the annual
figure is higher.

**"Plant and machinery" is defined** in the Explanation to section 17 — apparatus,
equipment and machinery fixed to earth by foundation or structural support, used
for making outward supplies, **excluding** land, building or other civil
structures, telecom towers and pipelines laid outside the factory. This is the
line that decides construction-ITC disputes.

**17(5)(c) and (d) — construction.** ITC is blocked on works-contract services
and on goods / services used to construct immovable property "on his own
account", except plant and machinery. *Safari Retreats* (SC, 2024) held a
building can be "plant" on a functionality test — but the **Finance Act 2025
retrospectively amended 17(5)(d)** ("plant **and** machinery" for "plant **or**
machinery", w.e.f. 01.07.2017) to take a let-out building outside "plant". Unless
that amendment is struck down, a construction-ITC claim on a building now rests
on challenging the retrospective amendment. See Case law.

**Reversal on write-off / loss.** Book any inventory write-off, destruction or
free issue against a monthly ITC reversal — a very common audit pick-up.

examples.title: Rule 42 monthly reversal
examples.scenario: A registered person has common ITC (not exclusively for taxable or exempt use) of 5,00,000 in a month. Total turnover 2 crore, of which exempt turnover is 40 lakh.
working: Reversal for the month (D1) = 20% x 5,00,000 = 1,00,000
Plus 5% deemed reversal (D2) for non-business use on the common credit
examples.result: Reverse 1,00,000 (D1) + 25,000 (D2) = 1,25,000 in GSTR-3B Table 4(B)(1); true up annually by 30 November.

examples.title: Blocked credit — car for management
examples.scenario: A manufacturing company buys a 5-seater car for the use of its directors and pays 3,00,000 GST.
working: Motor vehicle for transport of persons with ≤13 seats → s.17(5)(a)
No carve-out (not further supply / passenger transport / driving school)
examples.result: The 3,00,000 ITC is fully blocked. Repair, insurance and leasing of that car are also blocked under s.17(5)(ab).

flowchart.title: Is my ITC blocked or restricted under section 17?

nodes.text: You have ITC on an eligible inward supply (section 16 conditions met)
Is the supply in the section 17(5) blocked list (car, food, construction, insurance, CSR, gifts, write-offs...)?
No ITC — reverse fully (or don't claim). Check the carve-outs in 17(5)(a)/(b).
Is the input used partly for exempt supply or partly for non-business / personal purposes?
Restrict the credit — apply Rule 42 (inputs / input services) or Rule 43 (capital goods), monthly and annually.
Full ITC available (subject to the 50% option if you are a bank / NBFC).

faqs.q: Is ITC on a goods carriage (truck) blocked?
faqs.a: No. Section 17(5)(a) blocks motor vehicles for **transport of persons** with seating capacity up to 13. Goods carriages are outside the block, so ITC on trucks and on their insurance and repair is allowed if used for business.

faqs.q: Can a mall developer claim ITC on construction if the mall is let out on rent?
faqs.a: Safari Retreats (SC, 2024) applied a functionality ('plant') test that allowed such a claim, and the Revenue's review was dismissed in May 2025. But the Finance Act 2025 retrospectively amended section 17(5)(d) (w.e.f. 01.07.2017) to put a let-out building outside 'plant'. So the claim now depends on challenging that retrospective amendment — take a considered view, disclose the position, and track the litigation on the amendment.

faqs.q: Is ITC available on employee health insurance?
faqs.a: Blocked under section 17(5)(b) unless the employer is **obligated to provide it under any law** (e.g. certain COVID-era mandates) or it is for onward taxable supply.

faqs.q: Do I reverse ITC on goods given as free samples?
faqs.a: Yes — section 17(5)(h) blocks ITC on goods disposed of by way of gift or free samples. Reverse the input tax attributable to them.

faqs.q: Is ITC on CSR spend allowed?
faqs.a: No, from 01.10.2023 section 17(5)(fa) expressly blocks ITC on goods or services used for activities relating to CSR obligations under section 135 of the Companies Act.

commonMistakes: Treating all construction ITC as available — 17(5)(d) blocks it unless it is plant and machinery
Missing the annual Rule 42/43 true-up and the interest that follows
Claiming ITC on staff welfare (food, cab, insurance) without checking the 17(5)(b) carve-outs
Not reversing ITC on stock write-offs and free issues
Forgetting that repair / insurance / leasing of a blocked motor vehicle is also blocked

caseLaw.name: Chief Commissioner of CGST v. Safari Retreats Pvt Ltd
caseLaw.citation: 2024 INSC 756 / [2024] 167 taxmann.com 73 (SC), Civil Appeal No. 2948 of 2023, decided 03-10-2024 (per Abhay S. Oka J.); Revenue review petition dismissed [2025] 174 taxmann.com 894 (SC), 20-05-2025
caseLaw.facts: A developer of a shopping mall let out on rent had accumulated ITC of over 34 crore on construction; the department relied on section 17(5)(d) to deny it.
caseLaw.issue: Whether ITC on construction of a building intended for letting on rent is blocked by section 17(5)(d), and the meaning of 'plant'.
caseLaw.held: Whether a mall, warehouse or other building is a 'plant' is a factual question decided by a functionality test — the role the building plays in the taxpayer's business. If the building is essential to the activity of supplying services (e.g. letting on rent), it can be a 'plant' and is then outside the section 17(5)(d) bar. Section 17(5)(d) was read down to that extent and the matter remitted. The Revenue's review petition was dismissed on 20.05.2025.
caseLaw.effect: IMPORTANT — largely undone by legislation. The Finance Act 2025 retrospectively amended section 17(5)(d), substituting 'plant or machinery' with 'plant and machinery' with effect from 01.07.2017 and adding an Explanation, to take the benefit of a let-out building outside 'plant'. A challenge to that retrospective amendment is expected. Treat the functionality test as affirmed but its benefit for buildings as neutralised unless and until the amendment is struck down.

caseLaw.name: Union of India v. VKC Footsteps India Pvt Ltd
caseLaw.citation: (2022) 2 SCC 603 / 2021 (52) GSTL 513 (SC) / [2021] 130 taxmann.com 193 (SC), Civil Appeal No. 4810 of 2021 and connected matters, decided 13-09-2021
caseLaw.facts: Refund of accumulated ITC under the inverted duty structure; challenge to Rule 89(5) which excludes input-service credit from the refund formula.
caseLaw.issue: Validity of the Rule 89(5) formula that limits inverted-duty refund to ITC on inputs (goods).
caseLaw.held: The proviso to section 54(3) is a substantive restriction, not just an eligibility condition. Section 54(3)(ii) and Rule 89(5) are valid; the refund of unutilised ITC in an inverted structure is confined to ITC on inputs (goods) and does not extend to input services — the Court cannot read 'inputs' to include 'input services'. It flagged the anomalies in the Rule 89(5) formula for the GST Council to fix (done via Notification 14/2022-CT).
caseLaw.effect: Input-service ITC accumulated under an inverted structure is not refundable — it can only be carried forward or used against output tax.

instrumentsExplained.gist: Notified Finance Act 2025 changes to the section 17(3) Explanation (value of exempt supply) with retrospective effect from 01.07.2017, in force from 01.10.2025.
Notified the Finance Act 2023 insertion of clause (fa) in section 17(5) blocking ITC on CSR expenditure, from 01.10.2023.
Notified the CGST (Amendment) Act 2018 re-cast of section 17(5) — the current structure of clauses (a) to (i) with the motor-vehicle carve-outs — from 01.02.2019.

forms.purpose: ITC reversals under Rules 42/43 and section 17(5) are reported in Table 4(B).
Annual reconciliation of ITC availed, reversed and ineligible — Tables 6, 7 and 8.
forms.when: By 31 December of the next year

cgst-s18.plainEnglish:
**Section 18 deals with ITC when your status changes** — you newly become
liable to register, opt out of composition, or an exempt supply becomes taxable
(credit *comes in*); and the reverse — you opt into composition or your supply
becomes wholly exempt (credit *goes out*).

- **18(1)(a)** — a person who applies for registration within 30 days of becoming
  liable can take ITC on inputs in stock, in semi-finished / finished goods, on
  the day immediately before the date from which he becomes liable to pay tax.
- **18(1)(b)** — a voluntary registrant takes ITC on stock on the day before
  registration is granted.
- **18(1)(c)** — a composition taxpayer switching to normal takes ITC on stock
  and on capital goods (reduced by 5% per quarter of use) on the day before he
  becomes a normal taxpayer.
- **18(1)(d)** — where an exempt supply becomes taxable, ITC on stock relatable
  to that supply and on capital goods (5% per quarter reduction) as on the day
  before it becomes taxable.
- **18(2)** — no ITC under (1) after one year from the date of the tax invoice.
- **18(3)** — on sale, merger, demerger, amalgamation, lease or transfer of a
  business, unutilised ITC can be transferred to the transferee (Rule 41,
  Form ITC-02).
- **18(4)** — switching **into** composition or supplies becoming **wholly
  exempt**: pay an amount equal to ITC on stock and on capital goods (reduced for
  use); any balance in the credit ledger lapses.
- **18(6)** — on supply of capital goods / plant and machinery on which ITC was
  taken, pay the higher of (ITC reduced by 5% per quarter) or tax on the
  transaction value (Rule 40(2) / 44).

complianceChecklist.item: File Form ITC-01 within 30 days of eligibility for any 'credit comes in' claim
Obtain CA / CMA certification where the ITC-01 claim exceeds 2 lakh
Do not claim stock ITC on invoices older than one year (section 18(2))
On switching to composition / full exemption, compute and pay the ITC-03 amount and note the ledger lapse
On disposing of used capital goods, pay the higher of reduced-ITC or tax on transaction value (section 18(6))
On a business transfer, file ITC-02 and have the transferee accept it

keyConcepts.note: For 18(1)(c)/(d) and 18(6) the useful life is taken as 5 years; ITC is reduced by 5% for every quarter or part-quarter of use.

cgst-s18.practicalNotes:
All the "credit comes in" claims require a declaration in **Form GST ITC-01**
within 30 days, certified by a CA / CMA if the claim exceeds 2 lakh.

The "credit goes out" payment under 18(4) is worked out in **Form GST ITC-03**.

For a business transfer, the transferor files **ITC-02** and the transferee
accepts it on the portal; the transfer must be with a specific provision for
transfer of liabilities.

Watch 18(6) on disposal of used capital goods — many taxpayers charge GST only
on the sale value and miss the "ITC reduced by 5% per quarter" comparison.

examples.title: Capital goods on exit — section 18(6)
examples.scenario: A machine was bought for 20,00,000 + 3,60,000 GST (ITC taken). It is sold after 3 years 1 month of use for 8,00,000.
working: Tax on transaction value = 8,00,000 x 18% = 1,44,000
Pay the higher of the two
examples.result: Pay 1,44,000 (tax on transaction value, being higher) and issue a tax invoice.

faqs.q: I registered 45 days after crossing the threshold. Can I claim ITC on opening stock?
faqs.a: No. Section 18(1)(a) allows the stock credit only if the registration application is made **within 30 days** of becoming liable. A late applicant loses the pre-registration stock credit.

faqs.q: How is ITC transferred when I sell my business?
faqs.a: File Form GST ITC-02 specifying the amount; the transferee accepts it on the portal. For a demerger the credit is apportioned in the ratio of the value of assets, and the transfer must carry a specific provision for transfer of liabilities.

faqs.q: What happens to my credit ledger balance when I opt into composition?
faqs.a: Under section 18(4) you first pay an amount equal to ITC on inputs in stock and on capital goods (reduced for use) via Form ITC-03; **any remaining balance in the electronic credit ledger then lapses**.

commonMistakes: Missing the 30-day window for registration and losing opening-stock ITC
Charging GST only on sale value when disposing of used machinery (ignoring the 18(6) comparison)
Forgetting that the credit-ledger balance lapses on entering composition
Claiming ITC-01 stock credit on invoices more than a year old

forms.purpose: Declaration to claim ITC on stock / capital goods when credit becomes available under section 18(1).
Transfer of unutilised ITC on sale, merger, demerger, amalgamation, lease or transfer of a business.
Payment of ITC on stock / capital goods when switching to composition or supplies becoming wholly exempt.
forms.when: Within 60 days of the start of the year / 30 days of exemption

cgst-s19.plainEnglish:
**Section 19 lets a principal take ITC on inputs and capital goods sent for job
work**, even if they go directly from the supplier to the job worker's premises
without first coming to the principal.

- Inputs must be **received back** (or supplied from the job worker's premises)
  within **one year**; capital goods within **three years**. Moulds, dies, jigs,
  fixtures and tools are outside these time limits.
- If not received back / supplied out in time, it is deemed that the principal
  supplied the goods to the job worker on the day they were originally sent —
  tax plus interest becomes payable, and ITC can be reclaimed when the goods
  eventually come back.
- Read with section 143 (job-work procedure) and Rule 45 / Form ITC-04.

complianceChecklist.item: Move goods to the job worker under a delivery challan (Rule 55)
Track receipt-back within 1 year (inputs) / 3 years (capital goods) per challan
File Form ITC-04 (half-yearly above 5 crore turnover, else annually)
Pay tax + interest on inputs / capital goods not returned in time; re-claim ITC on eventual receipt

keyConcepts.note: Any treatment or process undertaken by a person on goods belonging to another registered person — s.2(68).

cgst-s19.practicalNotes:
Send goods under a **delivery challan** (Rule 55), not an invoice. Track the
one-year / three-year clock per challan. File **ITC-04** — half-yearly if
turnover exceeds 5 crore, annually otherwise.

Waste and scrap generated at the job worker's place can be supplied by the job
worker (if registered) or by the principal, on payment of tax.

faqs.q: Do the time limits apply to moulds and dies?
faqs.a: No. The one-year (inputs) and three-year (capital goods) limits do not apply to moulds, dies, jigs, fixtures or tools sent to a job worker.

faqs.q: What if inputs are not returned within one year?
faqs.a: It is deemed that the principal supplied those inputs to the job worker on the date they were sent. Pay tax with interest for that period; you may take ITC again when the goods are received back.

commonMistakes: Sending job-work goods on a tax invoice instead of a delivery challan
Not tracking the return clock and facing a deemed supply
Missing ITC-04 filings

forms.purpose: Statement of goods sent to and received from a job worker.

cgst-s20.plainEnglish:
**Section 20 governs the Input Service Distributor (ISD).** An ISD is a head /
branch office that receives tax invoices for **input services** used by multiple
GST registrations of the same entity and distributes that ITC to those units.

From **1 April 2025** ISD is **mandatory** for distributing common input-service
credit, including the ITC on inward supplies liable to reverse charge (the RCM
tax is first paid by the recipient unit / ISD and then distributed).

- Distribute through an **ISD invoice** (Rule 54(1)).
- Credit of CGST / SGST / IGST is distributed as IGST to units in other States
  and as CGST + SGST to units in the same State.
- Distribution is in the ratio of the **turnover** of the relevant units in the
  relevant period (Rule 39).
- Credit attributable to one unit goes only to that unit; credit common to all
  goes to all in the turnover ratio.
- Excess or wrong distribution is recovered from the unit with interest under
  section 21.

complianceChecklist.item: Obtain a separate ISD registration (section 24)
Route all common input-service invoices (and RCM on such services) through the ISD from 1 April 2025
Issue ISD invoices under Rule 54(1) for every distribution
Distribute in the turnover ratio of the relevant units (Rule 39)
File GSTR-6 by the 13th of the following month

keyConcepts.note: An office of the supplier that receives input-service invoices and distributes the credit to units under the same PAN — s.2(61).

cgst-s20.practicalNotes:
Take a **separate ISD registration** (section 24 makes it compulsory). File
**GSTR-6** monthly by the 13th; the recipient units see the distributed credit in
GSTR-6A / their GSTR-2B.

The 1 April 2025 change ends the earlier "cross-charge vs ISD" debate for common
input services — ISD is now the prescribed route. Cross-charge under section 25(4)
(distinct persons) still applies to internally-generated services.

examples.title: ISD distribution ratio
examples.scenario: Head office (ISD) receives an audit-fee invoice with 90,000 IGST that relates to all three units. Turnover in the relevant period: Unit A (Maharashtra) 6 crore, Unit B (Gujarat) 3 crore, Unit C (Maharashtra, same State as ISD) 1 crore.
working: Total turnover = 10 crore
Unit A: 90,000 x 6/10 = 54,000 → distributed as IGST
Unit B: 90,000 x 3/10 = 27,000 → distributed as IGST
Unit C: 90,000 x 1/10 = 9,000 → distributed as CGST 4,500 + SGST 4,500 (same State as ISD)
examples.result: Issue three ISD invoices; report in GSTR-6 for the month.

faqs.q: Is ISD compulsory now?
faqs.a: Yes, for distributing common **input-service** credit (including RCM) from 1 April 2025. Before that, an entity could use cross-charge instead.

faqs.q: Can an ISD distribute credit on goods?
faqs.a: No. ISD distributes credit on **input services** only. Common goods are dealt with by the unit that receives them or by stock transfer between distinct persons.

commonMistakes: Claiming common input-service ITC at the head office GSTIN instead of distributing it
Distributing on a basis other than turnover
Not registering as an ISD while still distributing credit

instrumentsExplained.gist: Part of the amendments making ISD mandatory for common input-service credit; the section 2(61) / section 20 recast was notified for 01.04.2025.

forms.purpose: Monthly return of an ISD showing credit received and distributed.
Auto-drafted details of inward supplies to the ISD (view-only).

cgst-s21.plainEnglish:
**Section 21 is the recovery provision for excess ISD distribution.** Where an
Input Service Distributor distributes credit in contravention of section 20 and
that results in **excess credit** to one or more recipients, the excess is
recovered from those recipients **with interest**, using the machinery of
sections 73 or 74 (as applicable).

In short: a mistake at the ISD level is corrected in the hands of the unit that
got the extra credit, not (only) at the ISD.

complianceChecklist.item: Each recipient unit reconciles ISD credit booked to ISD invoices and GSTR-6A / 2B monthly
Flag and reverse any excess ISD credit before it is picked up in audit

cgst-s21.practicalNotes:
Because recovery lands on the recipient unit, each unit should reconcile the ISD
credit it books to the ISD invoices and to GSTR-6A / GSTR-2B every month, and
raise any mismatch with the ISD promptly.

faqs.q: If the ISD distributes wrongly, who pays?
faqs.a: The recipient unit that received the excess credit repays it with interest — recovery is under section 73 / 74. The ISD may also face penalty for the contravention of section 20.

commonMistakes: Assuming ISD errors stay with the ISD — the recovery is from the recipient unit

cgst-s22.plainEnglish:
**Section 22 sets the registration threshold.** A supplier must register in every
State / UT from which a taxable supply is made if **aggregate turnover** in a
financial year exceeds:
- **40 lakh** for a supplier engaged **exclusively in goods** (20 lakh for
  special-category States and a few notified States);
- **20 lakh** for services or mixed suppliers (10 lakh for special-category
  States).

Aggregate turnover is **all-India, PAN-level** and includes exempt, export and
inter-State supplies (excluding taxes and inward RCM).

Existing registrants under the earlier laws (VAT, service tax, excise) were
migrated. On transfer of a business as a going concern, the transferee is liable
to register from the date of transfer.

complianceChecklist.item: Track aggregate turnover at PAN level across all States month by month
Apply the correct threshold (40 / 20 / 10 lakh) based on goods-only vs mixed and State category
Register in every State from which a taxable supply is made once the limit is crossed
Apply within 30 days of becoming liable (section 25(1))

keyConcepts.note: PAN-level all-India value of taxable + exempt + export + inter-State supplies, less taxes and inward RCM — s.2(6).
The States mentioned in Article 279A(4)(g) (Arunachal Pradesh, Manipur, Meghalaya, Mizoram, Nagaland, Sikkim, Tripura, Uttarakhand) — lower thresholds.

cgst-s22.practicalNotes:
The 40-lakh goods threshold (Notification 10/2019-CT) does **not** apply to a
person making intra-State supplies in certain States, to persons required to
register compulsorily under section 24, to those supplying ice cream, pan masala
or tobacco, and to voluntary registrants.

Because turnover is PAN-level, a business with units in several States must
register in each once the **all-India** figure crosses the limit, even if one
State's turnover is small.

examples.title: PAN-level threshold
examples.scenario: A trader has a shop in Maharashtra (turnover 30 lakh) and a small branch in Gujarat (turnover 12 lakh), dealing only in goods.
working: Aggregate turnover = 30 + 12 = 42 lakh > 40 lakh
Threshold crossed at PAN level
examples.result: Registration is required in **both** Maharashtra and Gujarat, even though Gujarat's own turnover is only 12 lakh.

faqs.q: Is the threshold 40 lakh or 20 lakh?
faqs.a: 40 lakh applies only if you supply **goods exclusively** and are not otherwise required to register. Any element of service supply (beyond the interest-on-deposits exclusion) brings the threshold down to 20 lakh.

faqs.q: Do exempt supplies count towards the threshold?
faqs.a: Yes. Aggregate turnover includes exempt supplies. A person making only exempt supplies is not liable to register (section 23), but exempt turnover still counts when testing the threshold for a mixed supplier.

commonMistakes: Using the 40-lakh limit while also supplying services
Testing the threshold State-by-State instead of PAN-level
Delaying registration beyond 30 days and losing pre-registration ITC on stock

instrumentsExplained.gist: Raised the registration threshold to 40 lakh for exclusive suppliers of goods, subject to exclusions (specified States, compulsory-registration cases, ice cream / pan masala / tobacco).

forms.purpose: Application for registration.

cgst-s23.plainEnglish:
**Section 23 lists who is NOT liable to register** — and, as amended
(retrospective from 01.07.2017), this section **overrides** sections 22 and 24.

Not liable:
- a person supplying **only** goods or services that are wholly exempt or not
  liable to tax;
- an **agriculturist**, to the extent of supply of produce out of cultivation of
  land;
- persons in a class notified by the Government (e.g. persons making only
  reverse-charge outward supplies; small inter-State service suppliers up to
  20 lakh; job workers in certain cases).

complianceChecklist.item: Confirm all outward supplies are wholly exempt / non-taxable before relying on section 23
Re-test liability the moment any taxable supply is made

keyConcepts.note: An individual or HUF who cultivates land by own / family labour or hired labour under personal supervision — s.2(7).

cgst-s23.practicalNotes:
The 2023 amendment making section 23 **non obstante** to sections 22 and 24
settled a long-running debate: a person supplying **only exempt** goods /
services need not register **even if** they make an inter-State supply or are
otherwise within section 24. This helps small exempt suppliers (e.g. education,
healthcare) making occasional inter-State supplies.

faqs.q: I supply only exempt services but make an inter-State supply. Must I register?
faqs.a: No. After the 2023 amendment, section 23 overrides section 24, so a person supplying **only** exempt goods / services is not liable to register even for inter-State supplies.

commonMistakes: Assuming any inter-State supply forces registration even for an exempt-only supplier (no longer correct)
Treating a partly-taxable supplier as exempt-only

instrumentsExplained.gist: Notified the Finance Act 2025 confirmation of section 23 as an overriding provision, with retrospective effect from 01.07.2017.

complianceChecklist.item: Register before making any inter-State supply of goods, or before starting as a casual / NR taxable person
Casual taxable person: register 5 days in advance and deposit advance tax
Take separate registrations for TDS, TCS and ISD roles

keyConcepts.note: A person who occasionally supplies in a State / UT where he has no fixed place of business — s.2(20).
A person who occasionally supplies but has no fixed place of business or residence in India — s.2(77).

cgst-s24.practicalNotes:
The most common trigger for small businesses is **inter-State supply of goods** —
even one such supply forces registration. For **services**, Notification
10/2017-IT exempts inter-State suppliers up to 20 lakh aggregate turnover from
compulsory registration.

Casual taxable persons (e.g. an exhibitor at a trade fair in another State) must
register at least **5 days** before starting, and deposit **advance tax** equal
to the estimated liability.

faqs.q: I sell goods on Amazon within my own State only. Must I register?
faqs.a: A small relaxation allows suppliers of **goods** making only **intra-State** supplies through an e-commerce operator, with turnover within the threshold, to operate without registration, subject to conditions and an enrolment number. Inter-State supply through the platform still needs registration.

faqs.q: One inter-State sale of goods worth 5,000 — do I register?
faqs.a: Technically yes — section 24 has no threshold for inter-State supply of goods. Plan the first inter-State dispatch around registration.

commonMistakes: Making inter-State supplies of goods without registration
Not depositing advance tax as a casual taxable person
Assuming the 20-lakh threshold applies to inter-State goods (it does not)

instrumentsExplained.gist: Exempts inter-State suppliers of services with aggregate turnover up to 20 lakh (10 lakh for special-category States) from compulsory registration under section 24.

cgst-s25.plainEnglish:
**Section 25 is the procedure and framework for registration.**

- Apply **within 30 days** of becoming liable (a casual / NR taxable person at
  least **5 days** before commencing).
- **State-wise**: one registration per State / UT; multiple **places of business**
  in a State can be under one registration or, at the person's option, separate
  registrations for each place (Rule 11).
- **Voluntary registration** is allowed; all provisions then apply as to a
  registered person.
- **PAN is mandatory** (TAN for a TDS deductor; a NR taxable person may use other
  documents).
- **Aadhaar authentication** is required (section 25(6A)–(6D)); failure leads to
  physical verification and delay, and can restrict refunds and GSTR-1 filing.
- **25(4)/(5)** — separate registrations of one person, and an establishment in
  one State and another in a different State, are **distinct persons** — supplies
  between them are taxable.
- The **proper officer** may grant registration suo motu on survey / enquiry
  (Rule 16), and a **Unique Identity Number** is given to UN bodies, embassies
  etc.

complianceChecklist.item: Apply within 30 days of liability (5 days in advance for casual / NR persons)
Complete Aadhaar / biometric authentication for the promoters / authorised signatory
Keep the principal place of business ready for physical verification
Decide single vs separate registration for multiple places in a State
Recognise inter-registration and inter-State-establishment flows as taxable distinct-person supplies

keyConcepts.note: Separate registrations of one person, and inter-State establishments of one person — treated as different persons for GST — s.25(4)/(5).
A place from where business is carried on, including a warehouse, godown or the place where books are kept — s.2(85).

cgst-s25.practicalNotes:
**Deemed approval**: if the officer does not act within 30 days (Aadhaar
authenticated) / after physical verification, registration is deemed granted.

The **distinct-person** rule (25(4)) is the legal basis for taxing branch
transfers, HO→branch common services (cross-charge) and stock transfers — value
under Rule 28.

Since 2023, **biometric Aadhaar authentication** and physical verification have
been rolled out State by State to curb fake registrations; promoters should be
available for the visit.

faqs.q: Can I have two GST registrations in the same State?
faqs.a: Yes. Since 01.02.2019 a person with multiple places of business in a State may take a separate registration for each place (Rule 11), subject to conditions (no composition for one place if another is normal, and inter-registration supplies attract tax).

faqs.q: What if Aadhaar authentication fails?
faqs.a: Registration is not refused automatically but is subject to physical verification of the place of business, and processing takes longer. Non-authentication can also restrict IGST refunds on exports and the filing of GSTR-1.

commonMistakes: Missing the 30-day window
Ignoring cross-charge / branch-transfer tax between distinct persons
Not completing Aadhaar authentication and then facing refund / GSTR-1 blocks

cgst-s26.plainEnglish: **Section 26 — deemed registration.** A grant of registration / UIN under the SGST or UTGST Act is **deemed** to be a grant under the CGST Act, and a rejection under one is deemed a rejection under the other — so a taxpayer gets a single GSTIN valid for both taxes.

cgst-s27.plainEnglish:
**Section 27 deals with casual taxable persons and non-resident taxable
persons.**

- Registration is valid for the period specified in the application or **90
  days**, whichever is earlier; extendable **once** by a further 90 days.
- At the time of applying, the person must deposit **advance tax** equal to the
  estimated net tax liability for the registration period (further advance for an
  extension).
- The advance tax is credited to the electronic cash ledger and used to pay the
  actual liability; the balance is refundable **only after** all returns for the
  registration period are filed.

complianceChecklist.item: Apply at least 5 days before starting supplies in the other State
Deposit advance tax = estimated net liability for the period
File all returns for the period before claiming the balance refund

faqs.q: How long is a casual registration valid?
faqs.a: The period requested, capped at 90 days, extendable once by another 90 days on payment of additional advance tax.

faqs.q: When do I get the advance-tax balance back?
faqs.a: Only after every return for the casual registration period has been filed. The unused amount is then refundable.

Not filing the final return and losing access to the advance-tax balance

cgst-s28.plainEnglish: **Section 28 — amendment of registration.** Inform the proper officer of any **change in the particulars** of registration within **15 days** (Form REG-14). Core-field changes (legal name, place of business, promoters / partners / directors) need approval; others are updated online. A change in PAN needs a **fresh** registration.

complianceChecklist.item: File REG-14 within 15 days of any change in registration particulars
Take a fresh registration (and ITC-02 transfer) on a PAN / constitution change

cgst-s29.plainEnglish:
**Section 29 covers cancellation and suspension of registration.**

**Cancellation on application / by the officer (29(1))** — business discontinued,
transferred, amalgamated, demerged or disposed; change in constitution; person no
longer liable to be registered.

**Cancellation by the officer for default (29(2))** — contravention of
prescribed provisions; a composition taxpayer not filing returns for a financial
year beyond 3 months from the due date; **any other registered person not filing
returns for a continuous period as prescribed** (six months / two tax periods
under the QRMP scheme); voluntary registrant not commencing business within 6
months; registration obtained by fraud, wilful misstatement or suppression;
non-commencement of business; non-compliance with the prescribed bank-account /
e-invoicing rules.

**Suspension** — pending cancellation proceedings, registration can be suspended;
a suspended person cannot make taxable supplies or file returns and gets no
refund during suspension.

**29(5)** — on cancellation, the person must **pay** (by debit to the cash /
credit ledger) an amount equal to the ITC on stock and on capital goods, or the
output tax on such goods, whichever is higher.

complianceChecklist.item: File all pending returns to avoid suo-motu cancellation
On cancellation, file GSTR-10 within 3 months
Compute and pay the section 29(5) higher-of amount on stock and capital goods
Stop issuing tax invoices once suspended / cancelled

cgst-s29.practicalNotes:
The most frequent trigger is **non-filing of returns**. File a **final return
(GSTR-10)** within 3 months of cancellation. Reverse ITC on closing stock and
capital goods and pay the higher-of amount.

A cancellation for non-filing can be **revoked** (section 30) by filing the
pending returns with tax, interest and late fee.

faqs.q: My registration was cancelled for not filing returns. Can I get it back?
faqs.a: Yes. Apply for revocation under section 30 (Form REG-21) after filing all pending returns with tax, interest and late fee. Time limits and one-time amnesty windows have applied from time to time.

faqs.q: What do I pay on cancellation?
faqs.a: Under section 29(5), an amount equal to the ITC on inputs held in stock and in semi-finished / finished goods and on capital goods (reduced for use), **or** the output tax on those goods, **whichever is higher** — through GSTR-10.

commonMistakes: Continuing to raise tax invoices after suspension
Not filing GSTR-10 and facing a late fee / best-judgement demand
Ignoring the section 29(5) reversal on closing stock

caseLaw.name: Aggarwal Dyeing and Printing Works v. State of Gujarat
caseLaw.citation: 2022 (61) GSTL 288 (Guj) / [2022] 137 taxmann.com 332 (Guj), decided 24-02-2022
caseLaw.facts: Registrations were cancelled by cryptic show-cause notices and orders without reasons.
caseLaw.issue: Validity of cancellation orders that do not disclose reasons or give a real hearing.
caseLaw.held: Cancellation orders must be reasoned and preceded by a proper show-cause notice and hearing; cryptic orders were quashed.
caseLaw.effect: Widely followed by High Courts to set aside mechanical GST registration cancellations.

Final return after cancellation.
forms.when: Within 3 months of cancellation / order date

cgst-s30.plainEnglish:
**Section 30 allows revocation of a cancelled registration** where the
cancellation was done by the officer **on his own motion**.

- Apply in **Form REG-21** within the prescribed time (base period **90 days**
  from the cancellation order, extendable by the officer / Commissioner up to a
  further 180 days).
- Before applying, file **all pending returns** and pay the tax, interest,
  penalty and late fee.
- The officer may revoke, or reject after a show-cause notice and hearing.

complianceChecklist.item: Confirm the cancellation was officer-initiated (not on your own application)
File every pending return with tax, interest, penalty and late fee
File REG-21 within 90 days (seek extension if needed)
After revocation, claim intervening-period ITC under section 16(6) within 30 days

cgst-s30.practicalNotes:
Revocation is only for **officer-initiated** cancellation — not for a
cancellation the taxpayer applied for. The timeline was liberalised in 2023
(90 + 180 days) and periodic amnesty schemes have reopened windows for older
cases. On revocation, ITC for the intervening period can be claimed under
section 16(6) in a return filed within 30 days of the revocation order.

faqs.q: How long do I have to apply for revocation?
faqs.a: 90 days from the date of the cancellation order, which the proper officer / Additional or Joint Commissioner can extend by up to a further 180 days. Amnesty schemes have periodically reopened this for older cancellations.

commonMistakes: Applying for revocation without clearing all pending returns and dues
Missing the revocation window and having to seek fresh registration (losing continuity and ITC)

forms.purpose: Application for revocation of cancellation of registration.

cgst-s31.plainEnglish:
**Section 31 is the tax invoice.**

- **Goods (31(1))** — issue on or before **removal** (where movement is
  involved) or **delivery / making available** (where it is not).
- **Services (31(2))** — issue **within 30 days** of supply (45 days for banks /
  NBFCs / insurers).
- **Continuous supply of goods (31(4))** — on / before each statement or payment.
- **Continuous supply of services (31(5))** — by the due date of payment / on
  receiving payment / on completion of the event.
- **Revised invoices** for the period between the effective date of registration
  and the certificate.
- **Bill of supply** for exempt supplies and by composition taxpayers (31(3)(c)).
- **Receipt voucher / refund voucher / payment voucher** for advances and RCM
  (31(3)(d)–(g)).
- **Self-invoice** for RCM inward supplies from an unregistered supplier
  (31(3)(f)).
- A registered person may **not issue** a tax invoice below a prescribed value
  (consolidated invoice), and e-invoicing / QR-code requirements apply above the
  notified turnover.

complianceChecklist.item: Issue invoices within the section 31 timelines (removal for goods, 30 days for services)
Generate IRNs for all B2B / export invoices if turnover ever crossed 5 crore
Show the correct HSN/SAC digits for your turnover slab (Rule 46)
Issue self-invoices and payment vouchers for RCM from unregistered suppliers
Use a bill of supply (not a tax invoice) for exempt supplies

keyConcepts.note: Invoice Reference Number generated by the Invoice Registration Portal; mandatory for B2B / export above 5 crore turnover.
Document for exempt supplies and composition taxpayers — no tax component — Rule 49.

cgst-s31.practicalNotes:
**E-invoicing** (IRN from the IRP) is mandatory for B2B supplies and exports
where aggregate turnover in any year from 2017-18 exceeded **5 crore**. A B2B
invoice without a valid IRN is **not a valid tax invoice** — the recipient's ITC
is at risk. B2C invoices above the threshold need a **dynamic QR code**.

Content requirements are in **Rule 46** — GSTIN of both parties, HSN / SAC (by
turnover slab), place of supply for inter-State, and (for RCM) a note that tax is
payable on reverse charge.

faqs.q: Do I need e-invoicing?
faqs.a: Yes if your aggregate turnover in **any** financial year since 2017-18 crossed 5 crore. It applies to B2B invoices, credit / debit notes and exports — not to B2C.

faqs.q: By when must a service invoice be issued?
faqs.a: Within 30 days of the supply of service (45 days for banks, NBFCs and insurers). Late issue shifts the time of supply back to completion (section 13).

commonMistakes: Raising B2B invoices without an IRN once above the e-invoicing threshold
Missing HSN digits / place-of-supply on inter-State invoices
Issuing a tax invoice for an exempt supply

advisories.ref: Advisory — e-invoicing threshold and 30-day reporting limit
advisories.gist: E-invoicing applies where aggregate turnover in any year from 2017-18 exceeded 5 crore. Taxpayers with AATO of 10 crore or more must report invoices to the IRP within 30 days of the invoice date.

advisories.ref: Advisory — new IRP portals and B2C e-invoicing pilot
advisories.gist: Multiple Invoice Registration Portals are live; a voluntary B2C e-invoicing pilot has been introduced in select sectors / States.

cgst-s31a.plainEnglish: **Section 31A — facility of digital payment to the recipient.** The Government may require a class of registered persons to **provide the prescribed modes of electronic payment** to the recipient of a supply, and to display the option. Aimed at pushing digital acceptance at the retail level.

cgst-s34.plainEnglish:
**Section 34 is credit and debit notes.**

- **Credit note** — issued by the **supplier** where the taxable value / tax in
  an invoice is found to **exceed** what is due, or goods are returned, or the
  supply is deficient. It reduces the supplier's output tax **only if** the
  recipient **reverses the corresponding ITC**; declare it in GSTR-1 by **30
  November** following the FY (or the annual-return date).
- **Debit note** — issued by the **supplier** where the value / tax is found to
  be **short**. It increases output tax; the recipient's ITC time limit runs
  from the **debit note's** financial year (post-2021).
- One credit / debit note can now cover **multiple invoices**.
- A **financial (commercial) credit note** — with no GST adjustment — is used
  where the section 15(3) discount conditions are not met.

complianceChecklist.item: Issue GST credit notes only where the recipient will reverse ITC; otherwise financial credit notes
Declare credit / debit notes in GSTR-1 within the 30-November limit
Link the recipient's ITC time limit for a debit note to the debit note's FY
