cgst-s34.practicalNotes:
The **recipient's ITC reversal** is the gate for a GST credit note to reduce the
supplier's liability. If the buyer will not / cannot reverse ITC (e.g. an
unregistered buyer, or a lapsed period), the supplier issues a **financial**
credit note and bears the tax. The 30 November cut-off for GST credit notes mirrors
the ITC time limit.

faqs.q: Can I issue a GST credit note for a post-sale discount to a B2C customer?
faqs.a: The tax on a credit note can be reduced only where the recipient reverses ITC — which a B2C customer cannot do. So for B2C discounts, use a financial credit note and do not reduce output tax.

faqs.q: By when must a credit note be declared?
faqs.a: In the GSTR-1 for a month not later than **30 November** following the end of the financial year of the original supply, or the date of filing the annual return, whichever is earlier.

commonMistakes: Reducing output tax on a credit note without the buyer reversing ITC
Missing the 30-November declaration window

cgst-s35.plainEnglish:
**Section 35 — accounts and records.** Every registered person keeps, at the
**principal place of business** (and each additional place, for the records
relating to it), a true and correct account of: production / manufacture; inward
and outward supplies; **stock** of goods; ITC availed; output tax payable and
paid; and other prescribed records (Rule 56–58) — including, for agents, works
contractors, and transporters / warehouse-keepers, additional registers.

Records may be kept **electronically**. They must be retained for **72 months**
from the due date of the annual return for the year (**section 36**), longer if
an appeal / investigation is pending.

Failure to account for goods can lead to a **best-judgement determination of tax**
on the unaccounted goods as if supplied.

complianceChecklist.item: Maintain stock, ITC, output-tax and supply records at each place of business
Keep records for at least 72 months from the annual-return due date
Transporters / warehouse-keepers: enrol and keep consignment records

The stock register and the ITC / output-tax reconciliation are the records most
often examined in audit. **Transporters and warehouse operators** must enrol

faqs.q: How long must GST records be kept?
faqs.a: 72 months (6 years) from the due date of furnishing the annual return for that year — longer if any appeal, revision or investigation is pending (retain for one year after final disposal).

commonMistakes: Destroying records before the 72-month period
Not maintaining a proper stock register

cgst-s36.plainEnglish: **Section 36 — period of retention of accounts.** Keep the books, records and documents required under section 35 (and the rules) for **72 months** from the due date of furnishing the annual return for the year. If any appeal, revision, or other proceeding / investigation is pending, retain them for **one year after its final disposal**, or 72 months, whichever is later.

complianceChecklist.item: Retain GST records for at least 72 months from the annual-return due date
Extend retention where litigation / investigation is pending

cgst-s37.plainEnglish:
**Section 37 governs the statement of outward supplies — GSTR-1 / IFF.**

Every registered person (other than a composition taxpayer, ISD, TDS / TCS
deductor, OIDAR supplier and a few others) files details of outward supplies for
a tax period by the prescribed date. QRMP taxpayers use the **Invoice Furnishing
Facility (IFF)** for the first two months of a quarter and GSTR-1 for the
quarter.

- **No revision** — errors are corrected by amending the entry in a **later**
  period's return.
- **Sequential filing** — GSTR-1 for a period cannot be filed if GSTR-1 for the
  previous period is pending; and GSTR-1 cannot be filed if GSTR-3B for the
  preceding period is not filed (section 37(4)).
- **Time bar** — outward-supply details for a period cannot be furnished after
  **30 November** following the end of the financial year, or the date of filing
  the annual return, whichever is earlier (a 3-year outer bar applies from
  October 2023 amendments notified later).

complianceChecklist.item: Reconcile GSTR-1 to books, e-invoices and e-way bills before filing
File GSTR-1 / IFF by the due date (11th monthly / 13th quarterly / IFF by 13th)
Keep GSTR-3B of the previous period filed so GSTR-1 is not blocked
Amend missed / wrong invoices in the next period, within the 30-November limit

keyConcepts.note: The recipient's static ITC statement built from suppliers' GSTR-1 / IFF — the basis for ITC under section 16(2)(aa).
Invoice Furnishing Facility — optional monthly upload of B2B invoices by QRMP taxpayers for months 1 and 2 of a quarter.

cgst-s37.practicalNotes:
GSTR-1 feeds the recipient's **GSTR-2B** — late or wrong GSTR-1 directly costs
your customers their ITC. Reconcile GSTR-1 to the books and to the e-invoice /
e-way bill data every month before filing.

Since the 2022 changes, GSTR-1 and GSTR-3B are **linked**: GSTR-1 auto-populates
GSTR-3B Table 3, and a mismatch beyond a threshold triggers **Rule 88C** (explain
or pay) and can bar the next GSTR-1.

faqs.q: Can I revise a filed GSTR-1?
faqs.a: No. GST returns cannot be revised. Correct the mistake by amending the invoice / adding the missed invoice in a subsequent period's GSTR-1, within the section 37 time limit.

faqs.q: GSTR-3B of last month is unfiled — can I file this month's GSTR-1?
faqs.a: No. Section 37(4) blocks filing GSTR-1 for a period if GSTR-3B for the preceding period has not been filed. Returns must move in sequence.

commonMistakes: Treating GSTR-1 as revisable
Reporting B2B invoices as B2C and denying customers ITC
Missing the 30-November cut-off for amendments to a prior year

advisories.gist: GSTR-1 / IFF for a period cannot be filed unless GSTR-1 of the previous period and GSTR-3B of the preceding period are filed (section 37(4) / Rule 59(6)).

advisories.ref: Advisory — HSN reporting in GSTR-1 / GSTR-1A
advisories.gist: HSN is reported in Table 12 from a drop-down (manual entry disabled), split into B2B and B2C, with a validation against Table 13; 4 digits for turnover up to 5 crore, 6 digits above.

forms.when: 11th of the next month (monthly) / 13th of the month after the quarter (QRMP)

complianceChecklist.item: Review the 'ITC not available' section of GSTR-2B every month
Take up supplier defaults / mismatches before filing GSTR-3B
Do not claim ITC flagged as restricted under section 38 / 16(2)(ba)

cgst-s38.practicalNotes:
Section 38 is why **GSTR-2B has an "ITC not available" section** and why credit
can be blocked based on the **supplier's** conduct. The recipient should watch
supplier-risk flags in 2B and take up defaults with suppliers before filing.

This section, with section 16(2)(ba), is the statutory hook for future
system-driven ITC restrictions — the operative detail is in the rules and on the
portal.

faqs.q: Can my ITC be blocked because my supplier defaulted?
faqs.a: Yes — section 38 read with section 16(2)(ba) allows the rules to make ITC of a supplier's tax unavailable where the supplier is a defaulter, a new registrant, has a large GSTR-1 vs 3B gap, or is Rule 86B-restricted. GSTR-2B flags such credit as not available.

commonMistakes: Claiming ITC that GSTR-2B flags as restricted
Not monitoring supplier-risk indicators in 2B

advisories.gist: GSTR-2B is generated on the 14th; where the supplier files GSTR-1 late, the invoice moves to the next month's 2B. For QRMP recipients a quarterly 2B is generated.
Recipients can accept / reject / keep pending each inbound invoice in IMS; the accepted set flows into GSTR-2B, giving the recipient control over which invoices feed ITC.

cgst-s39.plainEnglish:
**Section 39 is the return of tax — GSTR-3B (and GSTR-4 / 5 / 6 / 7 for special
categories).**

- A normal taxpayer files a **monthly** return by the **20th**; QRMP taxpayers
  file **quarterly** (22nd / 24th by State) and pay tax monthly by **PMT-06** (by
  the 25th) for months 1 and 2.
- **Tax must be paid** by the due date for the return to be treated as filed;
  **nil returns** must still be filed.
- **Sequential filing** — a return for a period cannot be filed unless the return
  for the previous period is filed (section 39(10)).
- **Time bar** — a return / details cannot be furnished after **3 years** from
  the due date (amendment notified from October 2023 onwards).
- Composition taxpayers file **GSTR-4 annually**; ISD file **GSTR-6**; TDS
  deductors **GSTR-7**; NR taxable persons **GSTR-5**.

complianceChecklist.item: File GSTR-3B and pay the tax by the due date (20th / 22nd / 24th)
QRMP: pay monthly tax by PMT-06 (25th) for months 1 and 2
Keep returns sequential — clear the previous period first
Reconcile GSTR-3B Table 3 to GSTR-1 and Table 4 to GSTR-2B
Respond to any DRC-01B (Rule 88C) notice within 7 days

keyConcepts.note: Quarterly Return Monthly Payment scheme for taxpayers with turnover up to 5 crore — quarterly GSTR-1/3B, monthly PMT-06.

cgst-s39.practicalNotes:
GSTR-3B is where output tax, RCM, ITC and reversals come together and the cash /
credit ledgers are set off (sections 49, 49A, 49B). From 2023, Table 4 of GSTR-3B
was recast so that ITC is reported **net of reversals** with a separate
disclosure of reclaimed ITC.

**GSTR-1 vs GSTR-3B gap** beyond the Rule 88C threshold triggers **DRC-01B**
(explain or pay the differential with interest) and can bar the next GSTR-1.

faqs.q: Is a return 'filed' if I don't pay the tax?
faqs.a: No. Under section 39(7) the tax due as per the return must be paid by the due date; a GSTR-3B submitted without full payment is not a valid return and attracts late fee and interest.

faqs.q: Do I have to file a nil GSTR-3B?
faqs.a: Yes. A return must be filed for every tax period, even if there is no supply and no tax — nil returns can be filed by SMS.

commonMistakes: Submitting GSTR-3B without paying the full tax
Skipping nil returns
Large unexplained GSTR-1 vs GSTR-3B differences

caseLaw.name: Union of India v. Bharti Airtel Ltd
caseLaw.citation: (2022) 4 SCC 328 / [2021] 131 taxmann.com 319 (SC), Civil Appeal No. 6520 of 2021, decided 28-10-2021
caseLaw.facts: Attempt to rectify GSTR-3B of an earlier period for under-claimed ITC.
caseLaw.issue: Whether a filed GSTR-3B can be reopened.
caseLaw.held: GSTR-3B is a valid return; it cannot be rectified for a past period — the remedy is a later return.
caseLaw.effect: No retrospective correction of GSTR-3B; fix errors prospectively.

cgst-s40.plainEnglish:
**Section 40 — first return.** A person who becomes liable to register and does so
must, in the **first return** after registration, declare the **outward supplies
made between the date on which he became liable to register and the date the
registration is granted** — so that the tax on pre-registration supplies (backed
by **revised invoices** under section 31(3)(a) / Rule 53) is captured.

complianceChecklist.item: Issue revised invoices for supplies between the liability date and the registration date
Report those supplies in the first return (section 40)
File ITC-01 for stock ITC as on the day before the effective registration date

cgst-s40.practicalNotes:
Between the liability date and the grant of registration, issue **revised
invoices** for the taxable supplies already made, collect / account for the tax,
and include it all in the first GSTR-1 and GSTR-3B. Also file **ITC-01** for ITC
on stock as on the day before the effective registration date.

faqs.q: I made sales before my registration came through. How do I report the GST?
faqs.a: Issue revised invoices (section 31(3)(a)) for supplies from the date you became liable to register up to registration, and report them in your first GSTR-1 / GSTR-3B under section 40.

commonMistakes: Not accounting for pre-registration taxable supplies in the first return

cgst-s41.plainEnglish:
**Section 41 (substituted from 01.10.2022) is the self-assessed ITC / reversal
mechanism.**

- **41(1)** — every registered person is entitled, subject to conditions, to
  **avail** the self-assessed ITC in his return, credited on a provisional basis
  to the electronic credit ledger.
- **41(2)** — where the **tax on the supply has not been paid** by the supplier,
  the ITC availed by the recipient must be **reversed** along with **interest**;
  the recipient may **re-avail** it when the supplier subsequently pays the tax.

This replaced the old GSTR-2/3 matching-and-reversal machinery. It makes the
recipient's ITC contingent on the supplier actually depositing the tax
(consistent with section 16(2)(c)).

complianceChecklist.item: Run a Rule 37A check each year: identify ITC where the supplier's GSTR-3B is not filed by 30 September
Reverse such ITC by 30 November with interest
Re-avail on the supplier subsequently filing GSTR-3B

cgst-s41.practicalNotes:
The mechanism to identify "supplier has not paid" and to demand reversal is
built through the rules and the portal (Rule 37A — reverse where the supplier has
not filed GSTR-3B by 30 September of the next year, re-avail when he files).
Track Rule 37A reversals every year end.

faqs.q: What is Rule 37A?
faqs.a: Where a supplier has furnished GSTR-1 but not the corresponding GSTR-3B by 30 September of the next financial year, the recipient must reverse that ITC by 30 November; it can be re-availed when the supplier files the GSTR-3B.

commonMistakes: Ignoring the annual Rule 37A reversal exercise

cgst-s42.plainEnglish: **Section 42 [omitted].** The old ITC 'matching, reversal and reclaim' mechanism (provisional ITC, mismatch reports MIS-1/2) was **omitted** from 1 October 2022 and replaced by the GSTR-2B / section 16(2)(aa) / section 41 scheme.

cgst-s43.plainEnglish: **Section 43 [omitted].** The counterpart provision for **matching of credit notes / reduction in output tax liability** was omitted from 1 October 2022, along with section 42.

cgst-s43a.plainEnglish: **Section 43A [omitted].** A never-notified provision that would have prescribed a simplified return and a supplier-linked ITC procedure. It was omitted from 1 October 2022; the GSTR-1 / 2B / 3B framework was adopted instead.

cgst-s44.plainEnglish:
**Section 44 is the annual return — GSTR-9 (and the self-certified reconciliation
GSTR-9C).**

- Every registered person (other than an ISD, TDS / TCS deductor, casual taxable
  person, NR taxable person and OIDAR supplier) files an **annual return** for
  each financial year by **31 December** of the next year.
- Turnover **up to 2 crore** — GSTR-9 is **optional** (by notification each
  year).
- Turnover **above 5 crore** — a **self-certified reconciliation statement
  (GSTR-9C)** must also be filed, reconciling the annual return with the audited
  financial statements. (The requirement of a CA / CMA audit was removed from
  FY 2020-21 — it is now self-certification.)
- **Late fee** for GSTR-9 is capped by turnover slab.

complianceChecklist.item: File GSTR-9 by 31 December (if turnover > 2 crore or you choose to)
File self-certified GSTR-9C where turnover exceeds 5 crore
Complete the four-way turnover and ITC reconciliation before filing
Pay any additional liability through DRC-03

cgst-s44.practicalNotes:
GSTR-9 is a consolidation, **not** a second chance to claim ITC or reduce
liability — those adjustments must already have been made in the monthly returns
up to the section 16(4) / section 37 / section 39 time limits. Additional
liability **can** be paid in GSTR-9 through **DRC-03**.

Reconcile: books turnover ↔ GSTR-1 ↔ GSTR-3B ↔ GSTR-9; and books ITC ↔ GSTR-2B ↔
GSTR-3B ↔ GSTR-9 Tables 6/7/8, before filing.

faqs.q: Is a GST audit still required?
faqs.a: No. The requirement of a GST audit and audited GSTR-9C by a CA / CMA was removed from FY 2020-21. GSTR-9C is now **self-certified** by the taxpayer, for turnover above 5 crore.

faqs.q: Can I claim missed ITC in GSTR-9?
faqs.a: No. GSTR-9 does not allow fresh ITC claims. ITC had to be claimed in a GSTR-3B within the section 16(4) limit. GSTR-9 only reports what was already done and lets you pay extra tax via DRC-03.

commonMistakes: Treating GSTR-9 as a window to claim missed ITC
Not filing GSTR-9C above the 5-crore threshold
Filing GSTR-9 without reconciling to the financial statements

cgst-s45.plainEnglish:
**Section 45 is the final return — GSTR-10.** A registered person whose
registration has been **cancelled** must file a final return **within 3 months**
of the date of cancellation or the date of the cancellation order, whichever is
later.

It reports closing stock and the ITC / tax payable on it under section 29(5).
Non-filing attracts a late fee and a best-judgement assessment under section 62.

complianceChecklist.item: File GSTR-10 within 3 months of cancellation / the cancellation order
Declare closing stock and pay the section 29(5) amount

cgst-s45.practicalNotes:
GSTR-10 is a one-time return. A composition taxpayer files GSTR-4 up to the
cancellation date and then GSTR-10. Reconcile the section 29(5) payable amount
with the last GSTR-3B / stock records.

faqs.q: I never traded but my registration was cancelled — do I file GSTR-10?
faqs.a: Yes. GSTR-10 is required on any cancellation. If there is no stock and no liability, file a nil final return; otherwise a late fee and a section 62 best-judgement order can follow.

commonMistakes: Forgetting GSTR-10 after cancellation and accumulating late fee

cgst-s46.plainEnglish:
**Section 46 is the notice to a return defaulter.** Where a registered person
fails to file a return under section 39, 44 or 45, the proper officer issues a
notice in **GSTR-3A** requiring the return to be filed within **15 days**. If the
person still does not file, the officer may proceed to a **best-judgement
assessment under section 62**.

complianceChecklist.item: Act on a GSTR-3A notice within 15 days
If a section 62 order is passed, file the valid return within 60 / 120 days to get it withdrawn

cgst-s46.practicalNotes:
File the pending return **before** the 15 days expire — once a section 62 order
is passed it stands unless a valid return is filed within 60 days (extendable to
120 days with additional late fee), which withdraws the order.

faqs.q: I got a GSTR-3A notice. What now?
faqs.a: File the outstanding return with tax, interest and late fee within 15 days. If a section 62 best-judgement order has already been passed, filing a valid return within 60 days (or 120 with extra late fee) withdraws it.

commonMistakes: Ignoring the GSTR-3A notice and letting a best-judgement demand crystallise

cgst-s47.plainEnglish:
**Section 47 is the late fee for delayed returns.**

- **GSTR-3B / GSTR-1** — the Act prescribes 100 per day per Act (max 5,000);
  by notification this is rationalised to **50 per day** (20 per day for nil
  returns), CGST + SGST, with turnover-based caps.
- **GSTR-9** — 100 per day per Act, subject to turnover-slab caps introduced from
  FY 2022-23 (25 / 50 / 100 per day per Act by turnover).
- **GSTR-10 (final return)** — capped at 1,000 (CGST + SGST) by notification.
- Late fee is separate from **interest** under section 50 and from any penalty.

complianceChecklist.item: File returns on time to avoid daily late fee
Check for an amnesty notification before clearing a large accumulated late fee
Pay late fee in cash (it cannot be set off from ITC)

Late fee accrues per day of delay and is auto-computed on the portal; it must be
paid in **cash** and cannot be waived by the officer (only by notification).
Periodic amnesty notifications have capped or waived late fee for old pending
returns — check before paying a large accumulated amount.

faqs.q: Can the officer waive my late fee?
faqs.a: No. Late fee under section 47 can only be reduced or waived by a Government notification, not by the proper officer. Amnesty notifications have periodically done this for old returns.

faqs.q: Is late fee the same as interest?
faqs.a: No. Late fee (section 47) is a fixed per-day charge for late filing. Interest (section 50) is 18% p.a. on the net tax paid late. Both can apply together.

commonMistakes: Confusing late fee with interest
Delaying nil returns (still 20 per day)

cgst-s48.plainEnglish: **Section 48 — Goods and Services Tax Practitioners (GSTPs).** A GSTP enrolled under Rule 83 (Form PCT-01, after the eligibility / exam conditions) may, if **authorised by the taxpayer** in Form PCT-05, undertake specified activities — file GSTR-1 / 3B / 4 / 9, deposit into the cash ledger, file refund and amendment applications, appear before authorities, and file an appeal. **Responsibility for correctness remains with the taxpayer**, who must confirm the return.

cgst-s49.plainEnglish:
**Section 49 governs the two ledgers and how tax is paid.**

- **Electronic cash ledger** — money deposited by challan (**PMT-06**); used to
  pay tax, interest, penalty, fee or any other amount. Amounts can be
  **transferred between heads / GSTINs** of the same PAN via **PMT-09**.
- **Electronic credit ledger** — ITC availed; used **only to pay output tax**
  (not interest, penalty, late fee or RCM).
- **Order of set-off (49(5) read with 49A / 49B and Rule 88A)** — **IGST credit
  first** against IGST, then against CGST / SGST in any order; CGST credit against
  CGST then IGST; SGST credit against SGST then IGST; **CGST and SGST credit can
  never be cross-utilised**.
- **49(8)** — order of discharge for a period: **self-assessed tax of previous
  periods → self-assessed tax of the current period → any other amount**
  (demands).
- **49(12)** — the Government may cap the amount of output tax that can be paid
  from the credit ledger (the hook for **Rule 86B** — 99% cap for large
  taxpayers).

complianceChecklist.item: Pay RCM, interest, late fee and penalty from the cash ledger
Apply the correct set-off order (IGST credit first; no CGST↔SGST cross-use)
Clear previous-period self-assessed tax before current-period tax (section 49(8))
Check Rule 86B (1% cash) applicability each month
Use PMT-09 to correct wrong-head deposits instead of filing a refund

keyConcepts.note: The wallet of tax deposited by challan — s.49(1); used for any amount payable under the Act.
The ledger of ITC availed — s.49(2); usable only against output tax.
Large taxpayers must pay at least 1% of output tax in cash (99% cap on credit utilisation), subject to exceptions.

cgst-s49.practicalNotes:
Interest, late fee, penalty and **reverse-charge tax** must be paid in **cash**.
A frequent mistake is trying to discharge RCM from the credit ledger.

**Rule 86A** (blocking of the credit ledger by the officer on reason to believe
the credit is fraudulent) and **Rule 86B** (1% minimum cash payment for taxpayers
with taxable turnover over 50 lakh a month, subject to carve-outs) are the two
credit-utilisation restrictions to watch.

**PMT-09** lets you move a wrongly-deposited amount between major / minor heads
without a refund claim.

examples.title: Set-off order
examples.scenario: Output tax: IGST 1,00,000, CGST 60,000, SGST 60,000. ITC available: IGST 1,50,000, CGST 20,000, SGST 20,000.
working: IGST credit 1,50,000: pay IGST 1,00,000, then CGST 50,000 (balance of IGST credit)
Remaining CGST output 10,000: pay from CGST credit 10,000 (CGST credit left 10,000)
SGST output 60,000: pay SGST credit 20,000, balance 40,000 in cash
examples.result: Cash payable: SGST 40,000. CGST credit 10,000 carried forward.

faqs.q: Can I pay interest from my ITC balance?
faqs.a: No. The electronic credit ledger can be used **only** to pay output tax. Interest, late fee, penalty and reverse-charge tax must be paid in cash.

faqs.q: I deposited tax under the wrong head. Do I need a refund?
faqs.a: Usually not — use Form PMT-09 to transfer the amount between major or minor heads (and between GSTINs of the same PAN) within the cash ledger.

faqs.q: Can I use SGST credit to pay CGST?
faqs.a: Never. CGST and SGST / UTGST credit cannot be cross-utilised. Only IGST credit bridges the two.

commonMistakes: Paying reverse-charge tax by debiting the credit ledger
Cross-utilising CGST and SGST credit
Ignoring the Rule 86B 1% cash requirement

cgst-s50.plainEnglish:
**Section 50 is interest on delayed payment.**

- **50(1)** — interest at **18% p.a.** on tax paid after the due date. By the
  **proviso** (retrospective from 01.07.2017), where the return is filed late,
  interest is charged **only on the portion of tax paid in cash** (net of ITC),
  **unless** the demand arises from proceedings under section 73 / 74.
- **50(3)** — interest at **18% p.a.** (reduced from 24% w.e.f. 01.07.2017 by the
  Finance Act 2022) on ITC that was **wrongly availed and utilised** — Rule 88B
  clarifies that interest runs only where the wrong ITC has been **utilised**,
  from the date of utilisation to the date of reversal / payment.

complianceChecklist.item: Compute interest on late returns on the net cash portion (unless a 73/74 demand)
For wrong ITC, pay interest only if and from when it was utilised
Pay interest in cash; it cannot come from the credit ledger

cgst-s50.practicalNotes:
The **"cash only" proviso** is a major relief — if your GSTR-3B was late but you
had enough ITC, interest is only on the cash component, not the gross tax.

For **wrongly availed ITC**, no interest if it was availed but **not utilised**
(it sat in the credit ledger). Interest bites only on utilisation. "Utilised" is
tested against whether the credit-ledger balance ever fell below the wrong-ITC
amount.

examples.title: Interest on late GSTR-3B
examples.scenario: GSTR-3B for April (tax 5,00,000; ITC available 4,20,000; cash payable 80,000) is filed on 15 June instead of 20 May — 26 days late.
working: Interest under section 50(1) proviso is on the CASH portion only: 80,000
examples.result: Interest ~1,026 (not on the gross 5,00,000), plus late fee under section 47.

faqs.q: Is interest on the gross tax or the net (cash) tax?
faqs.a: For a late-filed return (not a section 73/74 demand), interest under section 50(1) is on the **net cash** portion only, retrospectively from 01.07.2017.

faqs.q: Do I pay interest on ITC I wrongly claimed but never used?
faqs.a: No. Section 50(3) with Rule 88B charges interest only on wrongly availed ITC that has been **utilised**, from the date of utilisation until reversal.

faqs.q: Is the interest rate on wrong ITC 18% or 24%?
faqs.a: 18% from 01.07.2017 — the Finance Act 2022 reduced it retrospectively from the earlier 24%.

commonMistakes: Paying interest on gross tax for a late return when only cash interest is due
Paying interest on wrongly availed but unutilised ITC
Using the old 24% rate for wrong-ITC interest

caseLaw.name: Refex Industries Ltd v. Assistant Commissioner
caseLaw.facts: Interest demanded on the gross output tax for a late GSTR-3B where ITC was available.
caseLaw.issue: Whether interest is on gross tax or on the net cash liability.
caseLaw.held: Interest is payable only on the cash component; the proviso to section 50(1) is clarificatory and retrospective.
caseLaw.effect: Anchored the 'interest on net cash' position later confirmed by the retrospective amendment.

caseLaw.name: Mahadeo Construction Co. v. Union of India
caseLaw.citation: 2020 (34) GSTL 15 (Jhar) / [2020] 116 taxmann.com 262 (Jharkhand), W.P.(T) No. 3517 of 2019, decided 21-04-2020
caseLaw.facts: Interest under section 50 was demanded and recovery initiated for a delay in filing GSTR-3B, without any adjudication, on the footing that it was an 'admitted' liability.
caseLaw.issue: Can interest under section 50 be recovered by coercive action without first adjudicating the amount?
caseLaw.held: Interest is compensatory and arises automatically, but where the taxpayer disputes the period of delay or the quantum (e.g. the ITC-vs-cash split, or whether the return was actually late), that dispute must be decided through a proper proceeding under section 73 / 74 with a hearing. Interest is not 'self-assessed tax' that can be recovered under section 79 without adjudication.
caseLaw.effect: A disputed section 50 interest demand needs a SCN and an order before the department can attach bank accounts or issue DRC-13. Contest the computation at the SCN stage.

instructions.ref: Instruction — recovery of interest on delayed GSTR-3B
instructions.gist: Field formations were directed to recover interest under section 50 on self-assessed tax paid late through GSTR-3B on the net cash basis, following the retrospective proviso, without a separate SCN where the amount is admitted.

cgst-s51.plainEnglish:
**Section 51 is TDS under GST.** Notified deductors — Government departments,
local authorities, Government agencies, PSUs, and certain notified bodies — must
deduct **2% (1% CGST + 1% SGST, or 2% IGST)** from payments to a supplier where
the value of a **taxable** supply under a contract **exceeds 2,50,000**
(excluding GST).

- No deduction where the supplier's location and the place of supply are in a
  State different from the recipient's registration State (to avoid a stranded
  IGST/CGST mismatch).
- The deductor files **GSTR-7** by the **10th**, pays the TDS, and issues a
  **TDS certificate (GSTR-7A)**.
- The supplier sees the credit in the cash ledger and can use or claim refund of
  it.

complianceChecklist.item: Deductor: deduct 2% where taxable contract value exceeds 2,50,000
Deposit TDS and file GSTR-7 by the 10th
Issue GSTR-7A certificates to suppliers
Supplier: reconcile TDS credit in the cash ledger and use / claim refund

The **2,50,000 threshold is per contract**, tested on the taxable value; splitting
a contract to stay under it is not permitted. From 2024, metal-scrap B2B supplies

faqs.q: Is TDS deducted on the GST component?
faqs.a: No. TDS at 2% is on the **taxable value** excluding CGST, SGST, UTGST, IGST and cess shown on the invoice.

faqs.q: When is no TDS deducted despite a large contract?
faqs.a: Where the location of the supplier and the place of supply are in a State / UT different from that of the recipient's registration — deduction there would create an unusable credit.

cgst-s52.plainEnglish:
**Section 52 is TCS by e-commerce operators.** Every ECO (not being an agent)
that collects the consideration for supplies made **through** it by other
suppliers must collect **TCS at 0.5% (0.25% CGST + 0.25% SGST, or 0.5% IGST)** —
reduced from 1% w.e.f. 10.07.2024 — on the **net taxable value** of supplies
(supplies less returns) for the month.

- Deposit by the **10th** and file **GSTR-8**.
- The supplier sees the TCS credit in the cash ledger.
- The ECO also files an **annual statement (GSTR-9B)** and must furnish, on
  notice, details of supplies for scrutiny; discrepancies communicated to the
  supplier must be reconciled.
- TCS does **not** apply to section 9(5) supplies (where the ECO itself pays the
  tax).

complianceChecklist.item: ECO: collect TCS at 0.5% on net taxable value per supplier per State
Deposit and file GSTR-8 by the 10th
File the annual statement GSTR-9B
Reconcile supplier discrepancies communicated under section 52(9)–(11)
Supplier: claim TCS credit from the cash ledger

faqs.q: What is the TCS rate now?

cgst-s54.plainEnglish:
**Section 54 is the refund provision.** A refund claim in **Form RFD-01** must be
filed within **2 years** from the relevant date (defined for each situation in
the Explanation), except for a balance in the electronic **cash ledger**, which
can be claimed any time in the return.

Main refund situations:
- **Export of goods / services** and **supplies to SEZ** — refund of **IGST
  paid** (goods: routed through the shipping bill; no separate RFD-01) or refund
  of **accumulated ITC** where exported under LUT without payment (Rule 89
  formula).
- **Inverted duty structure** — accumulated ITC where the input rate is higher
  than the output rate. Refund is limited to ITC on **inputs (goods)**;
  input-service ITC is **not** refundable (Rule 89(5), upheld in *VKC Footsteps*;
  a revised formula from 2022 gives partial relief).
- **Deemed exports** (Notification 48/2017), **excess payment of tax**, tax paid
  on a supply later held non-taxable, **provisional-assessment** finalisation,
  refund to **UN bodies / embassies**, refund of tax on supplies to CSD, etc.
- **Provisional refund of 90%** for zero-rated claims within 7 days (Rule 91),
  subject to conditions and risk parameters.
- **Unjust enrichment** — refund goes to the **Consumer Welfare Fund** unless the
  claimant proves the incidence of tax was not passed on (a CA certificate is
  needed above 2 lakh; not required for exports / ITC-accumulation refunds).

complianceChecklist.item: File RFD-01 within 2 years of the correct relevant date
Choose LUT vs payment route for exports deliberately (cash-flow impact)
Use the correct Rule 89 formula (89(4) for zero-rated ITC, 89(5) for inverted duty)
Attach a CA certificate where unjust enrichment applies and the amount exceeds 2 lakh
Track the 60-day clock and claim section 56 interest if the refund is delayed

keyConcepts.note: Export and supply to SEZ — s.16 of the IGST Act; carries full ITC, unlike exempt supply.
The date from which the 2-year refund limitation runs — defined situation-by-situation in the Explanation to s.54.
Letter of Undertaking (Form RFD-11) allowing export without payment of IGST, subject to conditions.

cgst-s54.practicalNotes:
- **LUT vs payment route** for exports: LUT (no tax, refund of ITC) preserves
  cash flow; the "pay IGST and get refund" route is simpler operationally but
  locks up cash and is restricted for some sectors.
- **Relevant date** is the trap — for export of goods it is the date the ship /
  aircraft leaves India; for services, receipt of convertible forex or the
  invoice date; for ITC accumulation, the end of the financial year.
- Interest under **section 56** at **6% p.a.** runs if the refund is not paid
  within **60 days** of a complete application (9% where refund arises from an
  order in appeal / adjudication that is upheld).
- Bunching of refund periods across financial years is now allowed
  (Circular 125/44/2019 as clarified).

nodes.text: You have accumulated credit / excess tax and want a refund
Is it a balance in the electronic cash ledger?
Claim any time via RFD-01 / the return — no 2-year limit, no unjust-enrichment test.
Is it a zero-rated supply (export / SEZ)?
Exported with payment of IGST?
Refund of IGST paid — for goods, automatic via the shipping bill; for services, RFD-01.
Refund of accumulated ITC under Rule 89(4) formula, RFD-01, within 2 years of the relevant date.
Is it an inverted duty structure (input rate > output rate)?
Refund of accumulated ITC under Rule 89(5) — inputs (goods) only; no input-service ITC.
Excess tax / non-taxable supply / deemed export / provisional-assessment refund — RFD-01, 2-year limit, unjust-enrichment test may apply.

faqs.q: Can I get a refund of accumulated ITC on input services under the inverted duty structure?
faqs.a: No. Following *VKC Footsteps* (SC, 2021), Rule 89(5) validly restricts the inverted-duty refund to ITC on inputs (goods). A 2022 amendment to the formula gives partial relief but still excludes standalone input-service credit.

faqs.q: What is the time limit for a refund claim?
faqs.a: 2 years from the 'relevant date' (defined for each situation), except a cash-ledger balance, which has no time limit.

faqs.q: When does the department owe me interest on a delayed refund?
faqs.a: Under section 56, at 6% p.a. if the refund is not sanctioned within 60 days of a complete application (9% p.a. where the refund flows from an appellate / adjudication order that becomes final).

commonMistakes: Missing the 2-year limit by using the wrong relevant date
Claiming inverted-duty refund on input-service ITC
Exporting without a valid LUT and then facing an IGST demand
Not claiming section 56 interest on delayed refunds

caseLaw.name: Union of India v. VKC Footsteps India Pvt Ltd
caseLaw.citation: (2022) 2 SCC 603 / 2021 (52) GSTL 513 (SC) / [2021] 130 taxmann.com 193 (SC), Civil Appeal No. 4810 of 2021 and connected matters, decided 13-09-2021
caseLaw.facts: Refund of accumulated ITC under an inverted duty structure; challenge to Rule 89(5), which excludes input-service ITC from the refund formula. The Gujarat HC had allowed input-service credit; the Madras HC had not.
caseLaw.issue: Validity of section 54(3)(ii) and the Rule 89(5) formula that limits the inverted-duty refund to ITC on inputs (goods).
caseLaw.held: The proviso to section 54(3) is a substantive restriction, not merely an eligibility condition. Section 54(3)(ii) and Rule 89(5) are valid; the refund is confined to ITC on inputs (goods) and does not extend to input services — 'inputs' cannot be read to include 'input services'. The Madras HC view prevails. The Court flagged the formula's anomalies for the GST Council (addressed in Notification 14/2022-CT).
caseLaw.effect: Input-service credit accumulated under an inverted structure is not refundable — carry it forward or set it off against output tax.

caseLaw.name: Union of India v. Cosmo Films Ltd
caseLaw.citation: [2023] 149 taxmann.com 268 (SC) / (2023) SCC OnLine SC 480, Civil Appeal No. 290 of 2023, decided 28-04-2023 (Gujarat HC reversed)
caseLaw.facts: Challenge to the 'pre-import condition' in the Advance Authorisation / IGST exemption scheme.
caseLaw.issue: Validity of conditions restricting IGST exemption on inputs imported under Advance Authorisation.
caseLaw.held: The condition was upheld with prospective effect and directions to allow drawback / ITC for the intervening period.
caseLaw.effect: Relevant to exporters structuring duty-free imports and refunds.

caseLaw.name: State of Jharkhand v. BLA Infrastructure (P.) Ltd.
caseLaw.citation: [2026] 182 taxmann.com 405 (SC) / [2026] 114 GST 6 (SC) / [2026] 106 GSTL 4 (SC); SLP (C) Diary No. 56452 of 2025, order dated 9 January 2026
caseLaw.facts: The taxpayer won its appeal against a section 74 demand and sought refund of the section 107(6) pre-deposit by filing an application under section 54(1). The department returned the claim by a deficiency memo. The Jharkhand High Court set the memo aside, treating section 54's two-year limitation as directory. The State appealed.
caseLaw.issue: Is the refund of an appeal pre-deposit a section 54 refund claim at all?
caseLaw.held: No. The Supreme Court held the refund is relatable to section 107(6) read with section 115, not section 54 — the State conceded this and the Court agreed. The High Court's interpretation of section 54 was unnecessary and was set aside to that extent; the pre-deposit was to be refunded with interest within four weeks. The Court expressly did not decide the scope of section 54.
caseLaw.effect: Do not file RFD-01 under section 54 for a pre-deposit refund after winning an appeal — it follows automatically from section 107(6) read with section 115, with interest, and is not subject to section 54's limitation or procedure. Section 54 continues to govern ordinary refunds of tax, ITC and balances.

**Section 55 allows a refund of tax paid on inward supplies to specified
persons** — UN bodies, notified multilateral financial institutions and
organisations, foreign consulates and embassies, and other persons / classes
notified by the Government (e.g. Canteen Stores Department gets a 50% refund).

These bodies are given a **Unique Identity Number (UIN)** instead of a normal
registration and claim the refund of GST charged to them, subject to conditions
and reciprocity.

cgst-s56.plainEnglish:
**Section 56 is interest on delayed refunds.** If tax ordered to be refunded is
not paid within **60 days** of a complete application, interest runs at a rate
notified (currently **6% p.a.**) from the day after the 60 days to the date of
refund.

Where the refund arises from an order of the appellate authority, tribunal or
court that has attained finality and is still not paid within 60 days of that
application, the interest rate is **9% p.a.**

complianceChecklist.item: Diarise the 60-day date from the complete-application date
Claim 6% (or 9%) interest if the refund is delayed

cgst-s60.plainEnglish: **Section 60 — provisional assessment.** Where a taxable person **cannot determine the value or the rate** of tax, he may request the officer (Form ASMT-01) to allow payment on a **provisional** basis. Differential tax carries interest; an excess is refunded with interest.

is accepted, **ASMT-12** closes it; if not, or if no reply is filed, the officer
may proceed to audit (65), special audit (66), inspection (67) or a demand
(73 / 74 / 74A).

**not** a pre-condition to a section 73 / 74 notice.

faqs.q: I got an ASMT-10. Is a demand coming?
faqs.a: Not necessarily. Reply in ASMT-11 with a reconciliation within 30 days; an accepted explanation is closed by ASMT-12. Only an unsatisfactory / absent reply leads to audit or a demand.

commonMistakes: Ignoring an ASMT-10 and letting it convert into a section 73/74 SCN

instructions.ref: Instruction No. 02/2022-GST — SOP for scrutiny of returns
instructions.gist: A standard operating procedure for scrutiny of GSTR-3B — the parameters to be checked (GSTR-1 vs 3B, 2A/2B vs 3B ITC, RCM, e-way bill, ITC reversal), timelines for ASMT-10 / 11 / 12, and escalation to audit / section 73.

instructions.ref: Instruction No. 04/2023-GST — scrutiny for FY 2019-20 onward
instructions.gist: Extended the scrutiny SOP and introduced the automated workflow on the ACES-GST / DGARM back-end for selecting returns and issuing ASMT-10.

forms.purpose: Scrutiny notice / taxpayer's reply / acceptance order.

cgst-s62.plainEnglish:
**Section 62 — best-judgement assessment of non-filers.** Where a person fails to
file a return even after a **section 46** (GSTR-3A) notice, the officer may
assess the tax to the **best of his judgement** in **Form ASMT-13** within **5
years** of the annual-return due date.

The order is **automatically withdrawn** if the person files a **valid return**
within **60 days** of the ASMT-13 (extendable to **120 days** with an additional
late fee) — though interest and late fee remain.

complianceChecklist.item: File the pending returns within 60 / 120 days of an ASMT-13 to get it withdrawn
If beyond 120 days, appeal the ASMT-13 under section 107

cgst-s62.practicalNotes:
The 60/120-day withdrawal window is the key relief — file the actual returns and
the best-judgement demand vanishes. Beyond 120 days the ASMT-13 stands and must
be appealed. From 2023 the withdrawal window was liberalised.

faqs.q: A best-judgement (ASMT-13) order was passed against me. Can I undo it?
faqs.a: Yes — file the actual valid return within 60 days of the ASMT-13 (or 120 days with additional late fee) and the order is deemed withdrawn. Interest and late fee still apply.

commonMistakes: Missing the 60/120-day window and having to litigate a best-judgement demand

forms.purpose: Best-judgement assessment order for a non-filer.

cgst-s63.plainEnglish:
**Section 63 — assessment of unregistered persons** (and those whose registration
was cancelled but who were liable to pay tax). The officer may assess the tax to
the best of his judgement, after a **show-cause notice (ASMT-14)** and hearing,
within **5 years** of the annual-return due date for the relevant year.

complianceChecklist.item: Register the moment liability arises to avoid a section 63 assessment
Reply to an ASMT-14 with turnover computations and any exemption claims

Used against persons who crossed the threshold or made inter-State supplies of
goods without registering, and against traders continuing to supply after

cgst-s64.plainEnglish: **Section 64 — summary assessment in special cases.** With the **Additional / Joint Commissioner's prior permission**, the officer may, on evidence of a tax liability and to **protect the interest of revenue**, pass a summary assessment order (ASMT-16) without the normal procedure, where any delay would adversely affect revenue. The taxable person can apply (ASMT-17) within **30 days** to have it **withdrawn** if it is erroneous.

complianceChecklist.item: On a summary assessment (ASMT-16), file ASMT-17 within 30 days if it is erroneous

cgst-s65.plainEnglish:
**Section 65 — audit by the tax authorities.** The Commissioner / an authorised
officer may audit a registered person for a financial year or part, at the
business premises or in the office, on **15 days' prior notice (ADT-01)**.

- Complete within **3 months** of commencement, extendable by the Commissioner by
  a further **6 months**.
- The taxpayer must provide facilities, records and information and explain
  entries.
- Findings, rights and obligations are communicated in **ADT-02** within **30
  days**; a detected short-payment / wrong ITC then flows into section
  73 / 74 / 74A.

complianceChecklist.item: On ADT-01, assemble the year's reconciliations and supporting records
Respond to each audit observation in writing with documents
Review the ADT-02 findings and decide on voluntary payment (DRC-03) vs contesting a later SCN

cgst-s65.practicalNotes:
"Commencement of audit" = the later of records being made available or the actual
start — this fixes the 3-month clock. Prepare a reconciliation pack (turnover,
ITC, RCM, exports, reversals) before ADT-01, and respond to each audit query in
writing.

faqs.q: How much notice does the department give before a GST audit?
faqs.a: At least 15 working days, in Form ADT-01. The audit must generally be completed within 3 months of commencement (extendable by 6 months).

commonMistakes: Not tracking the 3-month completion clock
Informal / verbal responses to audit queries

forms.purpose: Audit notice / audit findings.

cgst-s66.plainEnglish:
**Section 66 — special audit.** At any stage of scrutiny, inquiry, investigation
or other proceedings, if the officer (with the Assistant Commissioner's prior
approval) is of the opinion that the **value has not been correctly declared** or
the **credit availed is not within normal limits**, he may direct the taxpayer
to get the accounts audited by a **CA or CMA nominated by the Commissioner**.

- Report within **90 days** (extendable by 90 days).
- The **expenses and remuneration** of the special auditor are borne by the
  **Commissioner**.
- The taxpayer gets an opportunity of being heard on the special-audit findings
  before any demand.

complianceChecklist.item: Test whether the ADT-03 direction records a proper opinion on value / abnormal credit
Cooperate with the nominated auditor but reserve objections to the direction

cgst-s66.practicalNotes:
Special audit is directed sparingly and needs a recorded opinion on **value** or
**abnormal credit** — challenge the very basis if it is invoked mechanically.

faqs.q: Who pays for a special audit under section 66?
faqs.a: The Commissioner. The special auditor is nominated by the Commissioner and the audit fee is determined and paid by him, not by the taxpayer.

forms.purpose: Direction for special audit / communication of findings.

cgst-s67.plainEnglish:
**Section 67 — power of inspection, search and seizure.** Where a **Joint
Commissioner or above** has **reasons to believe** that a taxable person has
suppressed transactions / stock / ITC, or that a person is keeping goods that
have escaped tax, or that a transporter / warehouse-keeper is keeping goods that
have escaped tax:
- an officer (not below a rank as authorised) may **inspect** any place of
  business;
- on reason to believe that goods / documents are secreted, may **search and
  seize** them (**INS-01 authorisation**, **INS-02 seizure order**);
- seized documents are returned within **30 days** of the notice; seized goods
  may be **released provisionally** on bond and security (**INS-04**);
- goods of a **perishable / hazardous** nature or subject to depreciation may be
  disposed of;
- the officer may **seal or break open** premises / receptacles.
Search and seizure follow the **Code of Criminal Procedure** (section 165).

complianceChecklist.item: Verify the officers' identity and the INS-01 authorisation at the start of a search
Ensure two independent panch witnesses and obtain the panchnama and seizure list
Do not sign blank / undated statements; take legal advice before section 70 statements
Apply for provisional release of seized goods (INS-04) and return of documents

cgst-s67.practicalNotes:
"Reason to believe" must exist and be **recorded** before authorisation; a search
on a bare suspicion or a fishing inquiry is liable to be quashed. During a
search, note the officers' names and authorisation, insist on two independent
**panch** witnesses, get a copy of the **panchnama** and the seizure list, and do
not sign blank statements. Statements under section 70 are admissible — take
legal advice before making them.

faqs.q: Can officers seize my books during a search?
faqs.a: Yes, if there is recorded reason to believe they are useful for proceedings, but seized documents must be returned within 30 days of any notice unless required for prosecution, and you are entitled to copies / to take extracts.

faqs.q: Can seized goods be released?
faqs.a: Yes — on execution of a bond for the value and furnishing security (bank guarantee) equal to the tax, interest and penalty (Form INS-04). Perishable goods can be released against a bond alone or are disposed of.

commonMistakes: Signing pre-typed statements under pressure
Not obtaining a copy of the panchnama / seizure memo

caseLaw.name: Deepak Khandelwal Pvt Ltd v. Commissioner of CGST, Delhi West
caseLaw.citation: 2023 SCC OnLine Del 4938 / [2023] 154 taxmann.com 118 (Delhi) / 2023 (78) GSTL 158 (Del), W.P.(C) 6739/2021, decided 17-08-2023; Revenue SLP dismissed by the Supreme Court (2024) and review also dismissed
caseLaw.facts: During a search the officers seized cash and silver bars from the premises and retained them; the taxpayer sought their return.
caseLaw.issue: Does the power to seize 'documents or books or things' in section 67(2) extend to cash and other valuables?
caseLaw.held: 'Things' in section 67(2) takes colour from 'documents' and 'books' (ejusdem generis) and covers items useful for or relevant to the proceedings — it does not extend to cash or valuable assets that are not goods liable to confiscation. The seized currency and silver were ordered to be returned.
caseLaw.effect: GST officers cannot seize or retain cash / jewellery / FDRs found in a search. Note a contrary view exists (M.P. High Court in Kanishka Matta), so the point is not finally settled nationally, but the Delhi HC position (SLP dismissed) is the prevailing one.

caseLaw.name: Vallabh Textiles v. Senior Intelligence Officer
caseLaw.citation: 2022 SCC OnLine Del 4508 / [2023] 146 taxmann.com 421 (Delhi) / 2023 (68) GSTL 3 (Del), W.P.(C) 9834/2022, decided 20-12-2022
caseLaw.facts: Around Rs. 1.8 crore was 'deposited' by the taxpayer through DRC-03 during and immediately after an overnight search, allegedly under pressure.
caseLaw.issue: Is tax collected during a search, without the safeguards of CBIC Instruction 01/2022-23, voluntary?
caseLaw.held: Collection of tax during search hours, without giving the taxpayer time to reflect or consult, and without following Instruction 01/2022-23 (which bars recovery during search and requires any payment to be genuinely voluntary), is not a voluntary payment. The amount was ordered to be refunded with interest at 6%.
caseLaw.effect: You are not obliged to pay anything during a search. If pressured, note it in the panchnama, pay nothing, and claim a refund of any coerced DRC-03.

instructions.ref: Instruction No. 01/2022-GST — no coercion during search
instructions.gist: During inspection / search / investigation, officers must not use force or coercion to obtain payment; any tax deposited must be voluntary and through DRC-03, and grievance redressal is available.

Summons under section 70 should be issued with the approval of a senior officer, name the person, state whether he is a witness or under investigation, avoid repeated / late-hour summons, and senior management should be summoned only where their involvement is indicated.

forms.purpose: Search authorisation / seizure order / bond for release of seized goods.

cgst-s68.plainEnglish:
**Section 68 — inspection of goods in movement.** The Government may require the
person in charge of a conveyance carrying goods above a notified value to carry
prescribed **documents** (tax invoice / bill of supply / delivery challan) and
**devices** — the **e-way bill** (Rules 138–138E).

An officer may **intercept** any conveyance to verify the documents / e-way bill;
on a discrepancy, the goods and conveyance are dealt with under **section 129**
(detention) and, where warranted, **section 130** (confiscation).

complianceChecklist.item: Generate an e-way bill for every consignment above 50,000 and fill Part-B
Extend the e-way bill before expiry if transit is delayed
Ensure the vehicle carries the invoice / challan and the e-way bill

cgst-s68.practicalNotes:
**E-way bill** basics: required for movement of goods of consignment value >
**50,000** (some States have a higher intra-State limit); valid for **1 day per
200 km** (part thereof); can be **extended** within 8 hours before / after
expiry; Part-B (vehicle details) must be filled except for short first/last-mile
moves up to 50 km. **e-invoicing auto-generates** Part-A.

faqs.q: What is the e-way bill validity?
faqs.a: One day for every 200 km (or part thereof) of the approximate distance; for over-dimensional cargo, one day per 20 km. It can be extended within 8 hours before or after expiry.

faqs.q: Is an e-way bill needed for goods below 50,000?
faqs.a: Not generally, though it is required regardless of value for inter-State job-work movement and for movement of handicraft goods by an unregistered person, and some States mandate it above a lower intra-State threshold.

commonMistakes: Moving goods on an expired e-way bill
Not updating Part-B on a change of vehicle

forms.purpose: E-way bill / consolidated e-way bill.

cgst-s69.plainEnglish:
**Section 69 — power to arrest.** Where the **Commissioner** has reason to believe
that a person has committed an offence specified in **section 132(1)(a) to (d)**
(fake invoicing, ITC without invoice, tax collected but not paid, wrong refund)
punishable under section 132(1)(i) or (ii) — i.e. amount **exceeding 5 crore** —
he may **authorise** an officer to arrest that person.

- Offences with amount > 5 crore are **cognizable and non-bailable**; the
  arrested person is produced before a Magistrate within **24 hours**.
- Other offences are **non-cognizable and bailable**; the Deputy / Assistant
  Commissioner can grant bail.

complianceChecklist.item: In a large investigation, take criminal-side legal advice early
Assess anticipatory-bail options where arrest is apprehended
Cooperate with summons; do not obstruct officers

cgst-s69.practicalNotes:
Arrest requires the Commissioner's recorded reasons to believe **both** the
commission of the offence and the amount threshold. Per *Radhika Agarwal v. Union
of India* (SC, 3-Judge Bench, 27-02-2025) the reasons to believe must rest on
material and be recorded in writing, the **grounds of arrest must be given in
writing**, the *Arnesh Kumar* / *D.K. Basu* safeguards apply, and coercing a
"voluntary" payment during search or investigation is impermissible (any such tax
is refundable). **Anticipatory bail is available** where arrest is apprehended —
the contrary view in *Choodamani Parmeshwaran Iyer* (2023) stands overruled.

faqs.q: Can I be arrested for a GST demand under appeal?
faqs.a: Arrest under section 69 turns on the Commissioner's reason to believe that a section 132(1)(a)-(d) offence involving more than 5 crore has been committed — not on the status of a civil demand. It must follow the statutory conditions, the CBIC guidelines and the safeguards in *Radhika Agarwal* (SC, 2025); anticipatory bail can be sought where arrest is apprehended.

commonMistakes: Treating a summons as an arrest and panicking, or ignoring it entirely

caseLaw.name: Radhika Agarwal v. Union of India
caseLaw.citation: 2025 LiveLaw (SC) 255, Writ Petition (Crl.) No. 336 of 2018 with connected matters, decided 27-02-2025 (3-Judge Bench: Sanjiv Khanna CJI, M.M. Sundresh and Bela M. Trivedi JJ.)
caseLaw.facts: Challenge to the arrest power and arrest practice under the CGST Act and the Customs Act, and to coerced payments obtained during search / investigation.
caseLaw.issue: Validity and limits of the section 69 arrest power; whether anticipatory bail can be sought before arrest.
caseLaw.held: The arrest power is valid but constrained: material-based 'reasons to believe' recorded in writing, written grounds of arrest, and the Arnesh Kumar / D.K. Basu safeguards all apply; a customs / GST officer is not a police officer but the CrPC discipline is read in. Force or threats to extract a 'voluntary' payment during search / investigation are impermissible and such tax must be refunded. Anticipatory bail under section 438 CrPC IS maintainable — Choodamani Parmeshwaran Iyer (2023) and Bharat Bhushan are overruled on that point.
caseLaw.effect: The controlling authority on GST arrests. Insist on written grounds of arrest; challenge an arrest made without recorded, material-based reasons; recover any coerced 'spot' payment; move for anticipatory bail where arrest is apprehended.

caseLaw.name: Arnesh Kumar v. State of Bihar
caseLaw.citation: (2014) 8 SCC 273 / AIR 2014 SC 2756, Criminal Appeal No. 1277 of 2014, decided 02-07-2014
caseLaw.facts: Guidelines on arrest for offences punishable with up to 7 years' imprisonment.
caseLaw.issue: When is arrest necessary as opposed to issuing a notice of appearance?
caseLaw.held: Arrest must be necessary and justified with reasons recorded under section 41 CrPC; police must fill a checklist and the Magistrate must apply mind before authorising detention.
caseLaw.effect: Applied to GST arrests under section 69 (and affirmed for that context in Radhika Agarwal) to require necessity and recorded reasons.

instructions.gist: Arrest under section 69 must be authorised by the Commissioner on recorded reasons that the person has committed a section 132(1)(a)-(d) offence involving the threshold amount; the grounds of arrest must be explained, medical examination and Magistrate production within 24 hours, and the CBIC's arrest / bail circular followed.

instructions.ref: Instruction No. 01/2025-GST — grounds of arrest in writing
instructions.gist: Following Supreme Court and Delhi High Court rulings, the written grounds of arrest must be furnished to the arrested person (not merely read out), and an arrest memo prepared, before or at the time of arrest.

cgst-s70.plainEnglish:
**Section 70 — power to summon.** The proper officer has the same powers as a
**civil court under the Code of Civil Procedure** to summon any person whose
attendance is considered necessary to **give evidence** or **produce documents**.
Every such inquiry is a **judicial proceeding** under sections 193 and 228 of the
IPC. A summoned person is **bound to attend** and state the truth; non-attendance
is an offence (section 122(3)(d) / 172).

complianceChecklist.item: Attend on the summons date or seek a written adjournment
Carry exactly the documents listed; keep an acknowledged copy of what is handed over
Read the statement before signing; ask for a copy; do not sign blank sheets

cgst-s70.practicalNotes:
A person summoned under section 70 is being called to **give evidence / produce
documents**, not as an accused (no FIR precedes a section 69 arrest). Attend on
the date (or seek an adjournment in writing),
carry the documents listed, answer what is asked, ask for a copy of your
statement, and do not sign blank pages. Statements recorded under section 70 are
admissible in adjudication and prosecution.

faqs.q: Can I refuse a section 70 summons?
faqs.a: No. Attendance is compulsory and backed by contempt-of-court powers. You may seek a short adjournment in writing for a genuine reason, and you may be accompanied / advised by counsel as courts have increasingly permitted.

faqs.q: Am I an 'accused' if summoned?
faqs.a: No. A summons under section 70 is to a witness. That said, take the statement seriously — it is admissible and often forms the basis of the SCN.

commonMistakes: Ignoring a summons
Making an unconsidered statement without reviewing records

instructions.ref: Instruction No. 03/2022-23 (GST-Investigation) — issue and conduct of summons
instructions.gist: Summons are to be issued judiciously with senior approval, specify the documents required, record statements fairly, provide a copy where sought, and not be used as a substitute for a routine letter seeking information.

cgst-s71.plainEnglish: **Section 71 — access to business premises.** Any officer authorised by the **Additional / Joint Commissioner** may access any place of business of a registered person to **inspect books, records, computers and documents** for audit / scrutiny / verification. The person must produce records, trial balance, audited statements, income-tax returns, cost-audit / GST-audit reports, and afford access, **within 15 working days** of the demand.

complianceChecklist.item: On an access / records demand, provide the trial balance, audited accounts, ITRs and reconciliations within 15 working days

cgst-s73.plainEnglish:
**Section 73 is the demand provision for cases NOT involving fraud** — tax not
paid / short paid / erroneously refunded / ITC wrongly availed for **any reason
other than** fraud, wilful misstatement or suppression of facts.
(For periods **up to FY 2023-24**; from FY 2024-25, section 73 and 74 are
replaced by the common **section 74A**.)

- **Show cause notice** at least **3 months** before the time limit; **order**
  within **3 years** from the due date of the annual return for the year (or from
  the date of erroneous refund).
- **Penalty** — **10% of tax or 10,000, whichever is higher** in the order.
- **No penalty** and **no notice** if the tax with interest is paid **before**
  the SCN (voluntary payment via DRC-03).
- **No penalty** if paid within **30 days** of the SCN.
- Once paid, all proceedings for that matter are deemed concluded.

complianceChecklist.item: On finding an error, pay tax + interest via DRC-03 before any notice to avoid penalty
If an SCN is received, evaluate paying within 30 days (no penalty under 73)
Check the 3-year limitation on any section 73 order
Keep DRC-03 acknowledgements and reconcile them in GSTR-9

keyConcepts.note: The form for voluntary payment of tax / interest / penalty, before or after a notice — cash or credit ledger as applicable.
The summary of the show-cause notice; DRC-07 is the summary of the order.

cgst-s73.practicalNotes:
Section 73 is the "benign" track. If you spot an error, pay tax + interest via
**DRC-03** before any notice — no penalty at all. If a notice comes, paying
within 30 days still means no penalty.

**Time limit under 73** (3 years from the annual-return due date) is shorter than
74's 5 years — a section 73 notice issued beyond 3 years is time-barred, and
"invoking 74" only to buy time (without real fraud) is regularly struck down.

examples.title: Voluntary payment before notice
examples.scenario: During a year-end review, a company finds it under-reported output tax by 4,00,000 for last year.
working: Pay 4,00,000 tax + interest under section 50(1) via DRC-03 before any SCN
Section 73(6): no penalty; no notice will be issued for that matter
examples.result: Exposure closed with tax + interest only, no penalty.

flowchart.title: Section 73 vs 74 vs 74A — which demand track?

nodes.text: Tax is found short-paid / wrongly refunded / ITC wrongly availed
Does the demand relate to FY 2024-25 or later?
Section 74A applies — a single track; the higher penalty and 5-year limit apply only where fraud / suppression is established.
Is there fraud, wilful misstatement or suppression of facts to evade tax?
Section 73 — 3-year limit; penalty 10% or 10,000; NIL penalty if paid before SCN or within 30 days of SCN.
Section 74 — 5-year limit; penalty up to 100%; reduced to 15% (pre-SCN), 25% (within 30 days of SCN), 50% (within 30 days of order).

faqs.q: If I pay before the show-cause notice, is there any penalty under section 73?
faqs.a: No. Payment of tax with interest before the SCN closes the matter with no penalty and no notice (section 73(5)/(6)).

faqs.q: Can the department issue a section 73 notice after 3 years?
faqs.a: No. The order must be passed within 3 years of the annual-return due date, and the SCN at least 3 months before that. A late section 73 notice is time-barred.

commonMistakes: Ignoring a small error until it becomes a notice with penalty
Not checking limitation on the demand order
Paying under DRC-03 but not linking it to the SCN / order

caseLaw.name: G.R. Infra Projects Ltd. v. State of Madhya Pradesh
caseLaw.citation: Civil Appeal No. 11277 of 2026 (SLP(C) No. 33594 of 2025), decided 19-08-2026
caseLaw.facts: An SCN dated 13.06.2025 was issued for FY 2018-19. The annual return for 2018-19 was due 31.12.2019 and was extended by successive notifications to 31.12.2020, so the section 73 three-year outer limit ran to 31.12.2023. The department issued the notice under section 74 (fraud) to get the longer period; the High Court upheld it.
caseLaw.issue: How the COVID limitation exclusion applies to the section 73 outer date, and whether a stale section 73 demand can be re-labelled under section 74.
caseLaw.held: The Supreme Court's suo motu order excludes 15.03.2020 to 28.02.2022; the part of that falling inside the 2018-19 three-year window is 1 year 2 months, which is added to 31.12.2023 — taking the outer date to 28.02.2025. The SCN issued on 13.06.2025 was beyond that and time-barred under section 73. Switching to section 74 did not help, because the notice did not particularise any fraud (see the section 74 note). Appeal allowed; SCN and the High Court order set aside.
caseLaw.effect: For the early years, the COVID exclusion adds a fixed 1 year 2 months to the section 73/74 outer date — it is not open-ended. Work out the exact limit and check any 2017-18 to 2020-21 SCN against it.

instructions.ref: Instruction No. 01/2022-GST — deposit during search / inspection
instructions.gist: No recovery of tax should be made during search, inspection or investigation by force or coercion; any payment must be voluntary through DRC-03, and a taxpayer who later complains of coercion is to be heard.

instructions.ref: Instruction No. 05/2023-GST — SCN and adjudication discipline
instructions.gist: Show-cause notices must clearly state the grounds and quantification, allow adequate reply time, grant a personal hearing, and be adjudicated within the section 73 / 74 limitation; bunched multi-year notices should be avoided where limitation differs.

advisories.ref: Advisory — DRC-01 and DRC-03 on the portal
advisories.gist: SCNs and orders are issued with the DRC-01 / DRC-07 summary electronically; payments are made in DRC-03 and can be mapped to a confirmed demand through DRC-03A so the demand is marked paid.

cgst-s74.plainEnglish:
**Section 74 is the demand provision for FRAUD cases** — tax short-paid / wrongly
refunded / ITC wrongly availed **by reason of fraud, wilful misstatement or
suppression of facts to evade tax** (for periods **up to FY 2023-24**).

- **SCN** at least **6 months** before the limit; **order** within **5 years**
  from the annual-return due date (or the erroneous-refund date).
- **Penalty** — **equal to the tax** (100%).
- **Reduced penalty** — **15%** if tax + interest + 15% penalty is paid **before
  the SCN**; **25%** if paid within **30 days of the SCN**; **50%** if paid within
  **30 days of the order**.
- The onus of establishing fraud / suppression is on the **department**; mere
  non-payment or a bona fide interpretation is not "suppression".

complianceChecklist.item: Test whether the SCN actually pleads and particularises fraud / suppression
Raise limitation and the mis-invocation of section 74 in the reply
Evaluate the 15% / 25% / 50% settlement ladder against litigation risk

keyConcepts.note: Deliberate non-disclosure of material facts with intent to evade tax — not mere omission; the Explanation to s.74 narrows it further.

cgst-s74.practicalNotes:
"Suppression" has a settled meaning — a **deliberate** withholding of information
with intent to evade. A routine ITC mismatch, a disclosed position, or an issue
already in the public domain does not attract section 74. Challenge the very
invocation of section 74 at the reply stage; if the extended period fails, the
whole demand for the earlier years falls.

examples.title: Reduced penalty ladder
examples.scenario: A section 74 SCN demands tax of 20,00,000. The taxpayer decides not to litigate.
working: Before SCN: 20,00,000 + interest + 3,00,000 (15%)
Within 30 days of SCN: 20,00,000 + interest + 5,00,000 (25%)
Within 30 days of order: 20,00,000 + interest + 10,00,000 (50%)
examples.result: Acting at the SCN stage saves 15 lakh of penalty versus contesting and losing.

faqs.q: Is every ITC mismatch a section 74 (fraud) case?
faqs.a: No. Section 74 requires fraud, wilful misstatement or suppression **to evade tax**. A bona fide mismatch, a disclosed position, or a legal interpretation dispute belongs under section 73 (or 74A from FY 2024-25 without the aggravated penalty).

faqs.q: If I pay within 30 days of the section 74 SCN, what is the penalty?
faqs.a: 25% of the tax (plus tax and interest). Paying within 30 days of the **order** reduces it to 50%.

commonMistakes: Accepting a section 74 tag on a bona fide dispute
Missing the 25%-within-30-days window

caseLaw.name: G.R. Infra Projects Ltd. v. State of Madhya Pradesh
caseLaw.citation: Civil Appeal No. 11277 of 2026 (SLP(C) No. 33594 of 2025), decided 19-08-2026
caseLaw.facts: A section 74 SCN dated 13.06.2025 for FY 2018-19 recited only 'fraud or concealment of facts', with no particulars. When challenged, the State tried to elaborate the allegations through its counter affidavit in the writ petition. The High Court upheld the notice.
caseLaw.issue: Whether a section 74 SCN can stand when it alleges fraud / suppression only in bare terms, with the substance supplied later by the department's court pleadings.
caseLaw.held: No. A notice invoking the extended period must set out, from its own contents, the material facts that led the officer to infer fraud, wilful misstatement or suppression; a 'bland statement' and a mechanical use of the statutory words will not do, and the use of 'fraud OR concealment' showed the officer was himself unsure of the ground. A counter affidavit cannot cure a notice that is void for non-application of mind — its validity must be found within its four corners. The SCN was also time-barred under section 73 even after the COVID exclusion (outer date 28.02.2025; notice 13.06.2025). Appeal allowed; SCN and the High Court order set aside; the State barred from further proceedings.
caseLaw.effect: A section 74 SCN that only parrots 'fraud / suppression' without particulars is bad in law, and the department cannot repair it later through its pleadings. Attack the notice itself at the reply stage — if the extended period fails, the whole demand for the earlier years falls.

caseLaw.name: Torrent Power Ltd. v. Union of India
caseLaw.citation: R/Special Civil Application No. 12175 of 2024 & connected matters (Gujarat High Court), decided 14-08-2026
caseLaw.facts: Section 74 SCNs and an order were issued on the corporate-guarantee valuation question, alleging that the guarantors had 'suppressed' facts by not declaring a value in GSTR-1/3B. The taxability of a no-consideration guarantee was itself an open interpretational question, and the facts were known to the department.
caseLaw.issue: Whether non-declaration in the returns, in a genuine interpretational dispute, amounts to 'wilful suppression' under section 74.
caseLaw.held: No. Following Pushpam Pharmaceuticals and Uniworth Textiles, 'suppression' needs a deliberate, positive act to evade — where the facts are known to both sides and the liability turns on a disputed reading of the law, mere failure to declare is not suppression. Invoking section 74 (and, in one matter, for a pre-GST guarantee) was arbitrary and showed non-application of mind; the SCNs and order were quashed and the taxpayers were not relegated to appeal.
caseLaw.effect: An interpretational dispute with the facts on record is not a section 74 case. This is another data point for challenging a 'suppression' tag at the reply / writ stage.

caseLaw.name: Pushpam Pharmaceuticals Co. v. Collector of Central Excise, Bombay
caseLaw.facts: Central Excise — invocation of the 5-year extended period on the ground of 'suppression of facts'.
caseLaw.issue: Meaning of 'suppression of facts' in the proviso to section 11A that unlocks the extended limitation.
caseLaw.held: 'Suppression of facts' means a deliberate non-disclosure of correct information to escape payment of duty; it is qualified by the words around it ('fraud, collusion, wilful mis-statement') and does not cover a mere failure to disclose or a bona fide belief that a levy does not apply.
caseLaw.effect: The governing test for 'suppression' under section 74 of the CGST Act as well — followed in G.R. Infra Projects and Torrent Power (below).

caseLaw.name: Union of India v. Bundl Technologies Pvt Ltd (Swiggy)
caseLaw.citation: [2022] 136 taxmann.com 112 (Karnataka) / 2022 (61) GSTL 145 (Kar), W.A. No. 3660 of 2021 (Division Bench), decided 16-03-2022 (affirming the single-judge order of 14-09-2021)
caseLaw.facts: During a DGGI investigation into alleged wrong ITC, about Rs. 27 crore was paid through DRC-03 at around 4 a.m. and the next day; no SCN was ever issued and the taxpayer had not self-ascertained any liability.
caseLaw.issue: Can the department retain an amount 'paid' during investigation before any SCN, treating it as tax under section 74(5)?
caseLaw.held: A payment during investigation, without a self-ascertainment under section 74(5) and without a SCN, is an involuntary deposit, not tax. The right to seek its refund is independent of the investigation and the two cannot be linked. The department was directed to consider the refund.
caseLaw.effect: Read with CBIC Instruction 01/2022-23 — no recovery during search / investigation, and any deposit made under pressure is refundable. Section 74(5) 'self-ascertainment' must be a genuine, voluntary act by the taxpayer.

cgst-s74a.plainEnglish:
**Section 74A (from FY 2024-25) merges sections 73 and 74 into one demand
track.**

- A **single limitation** — order within **42 months** from the due date of the
  annual return (or the erroneous-refund date); SCN issued so as to leave the
  taxpayer adequate time.
- A **minimum tax threshold of 1,000** below which no notice is issued.
- **Penalty** — the **normal** penalty (10% or 10,000) applies **unless** the
  case involves fraud / wilful misstatement / suppression, in which case the
  **100% penalty** and the **reduced-penalty ladder (15 / 25 / 50%)** apply.
- Voluntary pre-notice payment and payment within the specified windows carry the
  same relief structure as before.

The effect: for genuine errors the taxpayer gets the mild section-73 treatment;
the aggravated consequences arise only where the department **establishes** fraud
— removing the incentive to label everything as fraud to get the longer period.

complianceChecklist.item: For FY 2024-25 onward, track demands under section 74A (42-month limit)
Contest any fraud / suppression allegation to keep the penalty at 10%
Use the pre-notice / 30-day / 60-day payment windows for penalty relief

cgst-s74a.practicalNotes:
For any demand relating to FY 2024-25 onward, section 74A is the operative
provision — section 73 / 74 continue only for the earlier years. The single
42-month limit and the single form set (DRC-01 / 03 / 07) simplify tracking.

faqs.q: Do sections 73 and 74 still exist?
faqs.a: Yes, for tax periods up to FY 2023-24. From FY 2024-25, section 74A is the single demand provision, applying the higher penalty only where fraud / suppression is established.

faqs.q: What is the limitation under section 74A?
faqs.a: The order must be passed within 42 months of the due date for filing the annual return of the relevant financial year (or the date of the erroneous refund).

commonMistakes: Applying the section 73 3-year / section 74 5-year limits to FY 2024-25 demands

instructions.gist: For tax periods from FY 2024-25, demands are to be raised under the single section 74A track with the 42-month limitation; the higher penalty is to be proposed only where fraud / wilful misstatement / suppression is specifically alleged and evidenced.

cgst-s75.plainEnglish:
**Section 75 has the general procedural safeguards for all demands.**

- If an appellate authority / court stays the SCN, the stay period is excluded
  from limitation.
- Where section 74 is set aside on the fraud point, the demand is **re-determined
  under section 73** (deemed).
- **Opportunity of hearing** is mandatory where requested or where an adverse
  order is contemplated; **maximum 3 adjournments**.
- The order **cannot exceed** the amount or the grounds in the SCN.
- The order must be issued within the section 73 / 74 / 74A limitation.
- **Interest under section 50 is payable** whether or not specified in the order.
- Where a **penalty is imposed under section 73 / 74 / 74A, no separate penalty
  under other provisions** for the same act.
- **75(12)** — **self-assessed tax** (declared in GSTR-1 but not paid in GSTR-3B)
  is recoverable **directly under section 79** without any SCN.

complianceChecklist.item: Always request a personal hearing in the SCN reply
Check that the order stays within the SCN's amount and grounds
Keep GSTR-1 and GSTR-3B aligned to avoid section 75(12) direct recovery

cgst-s75.practicalNotes:
**Section 75(12) + Rule 88C** is why an unpaid liability disclosed in your own
GSTR-1 can be recovered straight away — always keep GSTR-1 and GSTR-3B aligned.

Insist on a personal hearing (75(4)); an order passed without one, where an
adverse decision was contemplated, is routinely set aside.

faqs.q: Can a demand order be larger than the show-cause notice?
faqs.a: No. Section 75(7) bars the order from exceeding the amount or travelling beyond the grounds stated in the SCN.

faqs.q: Is a personal hearing always required?
faqs.a: It must be given if the taxpayer asks for it in the reply, or whenever an adverse order is contemplated. Denial of hearing is a standard ground to quash the order.

commonMistakes: Not asking for a hearing and then losing the natural-justice ground
Leaving self-assessed GSTR-1 tax unpaid in GSTR-3B

instructions.gist: A personal hearing must be granted before an adverse order under section 73 / 74 / 74A / 76 even if not specifically requested, wherever an adverse decision is contemplated (section 75(4)); orders passed without a hearing are being remanded.

cgst-s76.plainEnglish:
**Section 76 — "tax collected but not paid to the Government".** Any amount
**collected as tax** must be paid to the Government, **whether or not** the
supply was taxable. If not paid, an SCN is issued and the amount is recovered
with interest and a penalty **equal to the amount** (or 10,000, whichever is
higher). There is **no time limit** for a section 76 demand.

complianceChecklist.item: Deposit any amount collected as 'tax', even on exempt / non-taxable supplies
Stop showing tax on invoices once registration is cancelled / a supply becomes exempt
