cgst-s76.practicalNotes:
This bites where a person shows "GST" on an invoice for an exempt / non-GST
supply, or continues to collect tax after cancellation. If you wrongly collected
tax, deposit it — you cannot keep it, and the customer's remedy is a refund under
section 54.

faqs.q: I mistakenly charged GST on an exempt supply. Can I keep it?
faqs.a: No. Section 76 requires any amount collected as tax to be deposited with the Government, whether or not the supply was taxable. The customer can claim a refund.

commonMistakes: Retaining tax wrongly collected from customers

cgst-s77.plainEnglish: **Section 77 — tax wrongly paid.** A registered person who paid **CGST + SGST** treating a supply as intra-State, which is **subsequently held to be inter-State**, is entitled to a **refund** of the CGST + SGST on paying the correct IGST. **77(2) — no interest** is payable on the delayed IGST in that situation. (IGST section 19 is the mirror provision.)

complianceChecklist.item: Pay the correct head first (IGST or CGST+SGST)
Claim refund of the wrong head within 2 years of paying the correct one
Do not pay interest on the corrective payment (section 77(2) / IGST 19(2))

cgst-s77.practicalNotes: Rule 89 and Circular 162/18/2021 clarify: the 2-year limitation for the refund of the wrongly-paid tax runs from the date the correct tax is **paid**. So pay the IGST first, then claim the CGST+SGST refund within 2 years of that payment.

faqs.q: I charged CGST+SGST but it should have been IGST. Do I owe interest?
faqs.a: No. Section 77(2) (and IGST section 19(2)) expressly exclude interest where tax paid under the wrong head is corrected. Pay the IGST and claim a refund of the CGST+SGST.

cgst-s78.plainEnglish:
**Section 78 — initiation of recovery.** Any amount payable under an order must be
paid **within 3 months** of the order; recovery proceedings begin only after that.
The proper officer may, for reasons recorded in writing, require payment in a
**shorter period** in the interest of revenue.

complianceChecklist.item: Diarise the 3-month date from any demand order
File the section 107 appeal with 10% pre-deposit within the window to stay recovery

cgst-s78.practicalNotes:
The 3-month breathing space is important — it is the window to file an appeal
under section 107 with the pre-deposit (10%), which stays recovery of the
balance. A demand for payment in less than 3 months must be a **speaking**
order.

faqs.q: How long do I have to pay a demand order before recovery starts?
faqs.a: 3 months from service of the order, unless the officer records reasons for a shorter period. Filing an appeal with the pre-deposit within that window stays recovery of the disputed balance.

commonMistakes: Letting the 3 months lapse and facing bank-attachment recovery

complianceChecklist.item: Respond to a DRC-13 garnishee notice immediately (to the department and the third party)
Where an appeal / stay is pending, place that on record to resist recovery
Consider a section 80 instalment application for genuine cash-flow difficulty

cgst-s79.practicalNotes:
The garnishee route (DRC-13 to your bank / customers) is the department's fastest
tool. If recovery is initiated during the appeal window or after a stay
application, move quickly — courts have set aside coercive recovery done before
the 3-month period or before disposal of a stay application.

faqs.q: Can the department attach my bank account for a disputed demand?
faqs.a: Not while the 3-month payment window under section 78 is running, and not (as a rule) where an appeal with the pre-deposit is pending — that operates as a stay of the balance. Coercive recovery in those situations is regularly quashed.

faqs.q: Can I pay a confirmed demand in instalments?
faqs.a: Yes — section 80 allows the Commissioner to grant up to 24 monthly instalments with interest, but not for self-assessed tax shown in a return.

commonMistakes: Not filing the appeal + pre-deposit in time, leaving recovery unopposed
Ignoring a garnishee notice served on a customer / bank

cgst-s80.plainEnglish: **Section 80 — payment of tax in instalments.** On an application, the **Commissioner** may allow a taxable person to pay any amount due (**other than self-assessed tax shown in a return**) in **up to 24 monthly instalments** with interest, subject to conditions. Default on one instalment makes the **whole balance** due at once.

complianceChecklist.item: Instalments are for confirmed demands, not for self-assessed return liability
Keep every instalment on time — one default accelerates the whole amount

cgst-s81.plainEnglish: **Section 81 — transfer of property to be void.** Where a person, after any amount has become due from him, **creates a charge on or parts with any of his property** with the intention of defrauding revenue, that transfer is **void** as against the tax claim — unless it is for adequate consideration, in good faith, without notice of the pendency, or with the officer's prior permission.

cgst-s82.plainEnglish: **Section 82 — tax to be the first charge.** Any amount payable by a taxable person under the Act is a **first charge** on his property, **overriding** other laws — **except** the Insolvency and Bankruptcy Code, 2016. So in a CIRP / liquidation, the IBC waterfall (section 53) prevails over the GST first charge.

faqs.q: Does the GST first charge beat a bank's security interest?
faqs.a: As a rule yes, section 82 overrides other laws — but **not** the IBC. In insolvency, GST dues rank as operational-creditor claims in the section 53 waterfall, below secured financial creditors.

cgst-s83.plainEnglish:
**Section 83 is provisional attachment to protect revenue.** During the pendency
of proceedings under Chapters XII (assessment), XIV (inspection / search /
seizure / arrest) or XV (demands), the **Commissioner**, if of the opinion that
it is **necessary** to protect revenue, may by order in **Form DRC-22**
provisionally attach any property, including a **bank account**, of the taxable
person (and, post-2021, of certain persons under section 122(1A)).

- The attachment **lapses after one year**.
- The affected person can file objections under **Rule 159(5)** within 7 days and
  seek release.

complianceChecklist.item: On a DRC-22, check whether any qualifying proceeding is actually pending
File Rule 159(5) objections within 7 days and seek a hearing
Track the 1-year lapse date

cgst-s83.practicalNotes:
The Supreme Court in *Radha Krishan Industries* laid down strict limits: there
must be **pending proceedings**, a **tangible basis** for the opinion, the power
is **draconian** and to be used sparingly, and the reasons must be recorded and
communicated. A mechanical or pre-emptive attachment (before any proceeding, or
of a third party's account) is liable to be quashed.

faqs.q: Can my bank account be attached before any show-cause notice?
faqs.a: Only if proceedings under Chapter XII, XIV or XV are actually pending and the Commissioner records a tangible, reasoned opinion that attachment is necessary to protect revenue. A pre-proceedings or unreasoned attachment is invalid (*Radha Krishan Industries*).

faqs.q: How long does a provisional attachment last?
faqs.a: It ceases to have effect after one year from the date of the DRC-22 order, unless lifted earlier on objections.

commonMistakes: Not filing timely objections against a provisional attachment

caseLaw.name: Radha Krishan Industries v. State of Himachal Pradesh
caseLaw.citation: (2021) 6 SCC 771 / [2021] 127 taxmann.com 26 (SC), Civil Appeal No. 1155 of 2021, decided 20-04-2021 (per Dr D.Y. Chandrachud J.)
caseLaw.facts: Bank accounts and receivables were provisionally attached under section 83 during an investigation; the High Court declined to interfere, citing the alternative appeal remedy.
caseLaw.issue: The scope and limits of the section 83 power, and whether the writ court should have entertained the challenge.
caseLaw.held: Section 83 is a draconian power, to be strictly construed. It requires (a) proceedings actually pending under the specified sections, (b) an opinion, formed on tangible material and recorded in writing, that attachment is necessary to protect the revenue — not merely convenient, and (c) proportionality: a live link between the attachment and its purpose. Rule 159(5) gives the person a right to object and be heard, which must be honoured. A writ court can and should interfere where the attachment is without jurisdiction or breaches natural justice, despite the appeal remedy.
caseLaw.effect: The leading authority on section 83 — used to quash attachments made without pending proceedings, without recorded tangible reasons, or without a hearing on the taxpayer's objection.

instructions.ref: Instruction / Guidelines on provisional attachment under section 83
instructions.gist: Provisional attachment is to be resorted to only in a few cases where necessary to protect revenue, on the Commissioner's recorded formation of opinion, with proceedings under Chapter XII / XIV / XV actually pending; it should preferably be of immovable property or a fixed deposit rather than a running current account, must not hamper normal business, is limited to the amount at risk, and lapses in one year (following *Radha Krishan Industries*).

cgst-s84.plainEnglish: **Section 84 — continuation of recovery proceedings.** Where a demand is **reduced** in appeal / revision, recovery already initiated continues for the **reduced** amount (a fresh notice is not needed); where it is **enhanced**, a fresh notice is issued only for the enhanced portion. Intimation is in Form APL-04 / DRC-25.

cgst-s107.plainEnglish:
**Section 107 — appeal to the Appellate Authority.**

- Any person aggrieved by a decision / order of an adjudicating authority may
  appeal **within 3 months** (department: **6 months**); the Appellate Authority
  may condone a delay of up to **1 further month**.
- **Pre-deposit** — the admitted amount in full, **plus 10% of the disputed tax**
  (capped; reduced to **7% with a lower cap for orders that are only penalty
  under section 129**; the cap was revised down by the Finance Act 2024). On
  payment of the pre-deposit, **recovery of the balance is stayed**.
- The appeal is filed in **APL-01**; the Authority passes a **speaking order**,
  generally **within 1 year** where possible, and cannot **remand**.
- No adjournment beyond **3 times**.

caseLaw.name: State of Jharkhand v. BLA Infrastructure (P.) Ltd.
caseLaw.citation: [2026] 182 taxmann.com 405 (SC) / [2026] 114 GST 6 (SC) / [2026] 106 GSTL 4 (SC); SLP (C) Diary No. 56452 of 2025, order dated 9 January 2026
caseLaw.facts: A demand was confirmed against the taxpayer under section 74. It filed a first appeal, made the section 107(6) pre-deposit to maintain it, and won. It then applied under section 54(1) for refund of the pre-deposit; the department returned the claim by a deficiency memo. The Jharkhand High Court set the memo aside, holding that a successful appellant's right to the pre-deposit back is a vested right and that section 54's two-year limitation is only directory. The State appealed to the Supreme Court.
caseLaw.issue: When an appeal succeeds, does the refund of the section 107(6) pre-deposit run through the section 54 refund machinery, or does it flow from the appeal provisions themselves?
caseLaw.held: It flows from section 107(6) read with section 115, not section 54. The State conceded this and the Court agreed — the refund is a statutory consequence of the appeal being allowed, so the High Court's exercise of interpreting section 54 was unnecessary and was set aside to that extent. The appeal was disposed of with a direction to refund the pre-deposit with interest, in accordance with law, within four weeks. The Court did not rule on the scope of section 54.
caseLaw.effect: A taxpayer who wins its appeal is entitled to the section 107(6) pre-deposit back with interest under section 115 as a matter of course — it is not a section 54 refund claim, so the two-year limitation, the RFD-01 process and deficiency-memo objections have no application to it. Being a Supreme Court order it binds all authorities and settles a recurring dispute over which provision governs pre-deposit refunds.

cgst-s108.plainEnglish:
**Section 108 — powers of the Revisional Authority.** The Revisional Authority may
**suo motu**, or on information, call for and examine the record of any
proceeding and, if the order of a subordinate officer is **erroneous and
prejudicial to the interests of revenue** (also considering non-consideration of
facts / law), **revise** it after a hearing.

Limits: cannot revise while an **appeal is pending** or the appeal period is
open, cannot revise an order already the subject of an appeal decision on the
point, and the power lapses after **3 years** from the order (with time
exclusions).

cgst-s109.plainEnglish:
**Section 109 constitutes the Goods and Services Tax Appellate Tribunal
(GSTAT).** The Tribunal has a **Principal Bench** at New Delhi and **State
Benches**; each bench has judicial and technical (Centre / State) members.

The Principal Bench hears matters involving **place of supply**; other matters go
to the State Benches. The Tribunal is the second appellate forum (after the
Appellate Authority) and the last **fact-finding** authority — further appeals
lie to the **High Court** (on a substantial question of law) and the **Supreme
Court**.

caseLaw.citation: [2026] 182 taxmann.com 405 (SC) / [2026] 114 GST 6 (SC) / [2026] 106 GSTL 4 (SC); SLP (C) Diary No. 56452 of 2025, order dated 9 January 2026
caseLaw.facts: The taxpayer lost a section 74 demand, appealed, made the section 107(6) pre-deposit and won. It sought refund of the pre-deposit under section 54(1); the department returned the claim by a deficiency memo. The Jharkhand High Court set the memo aside and, in doing so, read section 54's two-year limitation as directory. The State appealed to the Supreme Court.
caseLaw.issue: Which provision governs the refund of a pre-deposit once the appeal succeeds — section 54, or the appeal provisions?
caseLaw.held: The refund is relatable to section 107(6) read with section 115, not section 54 — a point the State conceded and the Court accepted. Because the refund follows automatically from the appeal succeeding, the High Court's interpretation of section 54 was unnecessary and was set aside to that extent. The pre-deposit was directed to be refunded with interest, in accordance with law, within four weeks. The scope of section 54 was left open.
caseLaw.effect: Interest on a pre-deposit refund runs under section 115 (at the section 56 rate) from the date of payment to the date of refund, as a statutory consequence of winning the appeal — the taxpayer does not have to route it through a section 54 claim or its limitation period. A Supreme Court order, binding on all authorities.

The HC formulates the question and decides it; it may award costs.

faqs.a: Not necessarily. Under section 120, the department may have refrained only because the amount was below the litigation threshold; it can still contest the same issue in a later year or another taxpayer's case.

cgst-s121.plainEnglish: **Section 121 — non-appealable decisions and orders.** No appeal lies against an order to **transfer proceedings**, to **seize or retain** books and documents, **sanctioning prosecution**, or allowing **payment in instalments** under section 80.

cgst-s122.plainEnglish:
**Section 122 is the general penalty section.**

**122(1)** — 21 listed offences (supply without invoice, invoice without supply,
tax collected but not paid within 3 months, ITC availed without receipt of goods
/ services, fraudulent refund, falsified records, failure to register, etc.).
Penalty: **10,000 or the amount of tax evaded / ITC wrongly availed / refund
wrongly claimed, whichever is higher**.

**122(1A)** (from 01.01.2021) — a person who **retains the benefit** of certain
122(1) offences (fake invoicing, wrong ITC pass-on) and at whose instance the
transaction is conducted is liable to a penalty **equal to the tax evaded / ITC
wrongly passed on**. This reaches beneficial owners and masterminds.

**122(1B)** — an **e-commerce operator** that allows an unregistered / ineligible
person to supply through it, or misreports supplies — penalty of **10,000 or the
tax involved, whichever is higher**.

**122(2)** — for a registered person, penalty of **10% of tax (min 10,000)** in
non-fraud cases and **100% of tax (min 10,000)** in fraud cases — aligns with
sections 73 / 74.

**122(3)** — **25,000** penalty on a person who aids an offence, deals with goods
liable to confiscation, receives supplies in contravention, fails to appear on
summons, or fails to issue / account for an invoice.

complianceChecklist.item: Issue tax invoices for every supply and account for every invoice issued
Register on time; keep the prescribed records at the registered place
Do not pass on or avail ITC without an actual supply
Appear in response to summons under section 70

cgst-s122.practicalNotes:
Where a penalty is levied under **section 73 / 74 / 74A**, a separate penalty
under section 122 for the **same act** is barred (section 75(13)). So section 122
matters mostly for **standalone** penalties (e.g. registration failure,
record-keeping) and for the **122(1A) beneficiary** penalty which can be imposed
in addition to the demand on the invoice-issuer.

faqs.q: Can I be penalised under section 122 and section 74 for the same evasion?
faqs.a: No. Section 75(13) bars a separate section 122 penalty for the same act once a penalty is imposed under section 73 / 74 / 74A. But the 122(1A) penalty on a **beneficiary** who is not the noticee can stand on its own.

faqs.q: Who does section 122(1A) target?
faqs.a: The person who retains the benefit of, and at whose instance, a fake-invoice / wrong-ITC transaction is carried out — typically the beneficial owner behind a bogus supplier or the recipient who orchestrated the fake credit.

commonMistakes: Assuming section 122 cannot apply once a 73/74 demand is raised (true for the noticee, not for a 122(1A) beneficiary)
Ignoring record-keeping and registration penalties as 'minor'

cgst-s122a.plainEnglish:
**Section 122A (from 01.10.2023) — penalty for failure to register certain
machines** used in the manufacture of goods notified for a **special procedure**
(currently pan masala, tobacco and similar products — Rule 6 of the special
procedure and Form SRM).

For every unregistered machine: a penalty of **1,00,000**, and the machine is
**liable to seizure and confiscation** — though not confiscated if the penalty is
paid and the machine is registered within 3 days.

complianceChecklist.item: Notified manufacturers: register every packing / filling machine in SRM-I
File SRM-II monthly

faqs.q: Does section 122A apply to all manufacturers?
faqs.a: No — only to manufacturers of goods notified under the special procedure (pan masala, gutkha, chewing tobacco, unmanufactured tobacco, etc.).

**Section 122B (from 01.04.2025) — penalty for contravening the track-and-trace
mechanism** under **section 148A**. Where a person fails to comply with the
unique identification marking, record-keeping or reporting requirements of a
notified track-and-trace scheme, the penalty is **1,00,000 or 10% of the tax
payable on the goods, whichever is higher** (in addition to any other penalty).

cgst-s123.plainEnglish: **Section 123 — penalty for failure to furnish an information return.** Where a person required to furnish an information return under section 150 fails to do so within the period in the notice, a penalty of **100 per day** applies, up to a maximum of **5,000**.

Provided that the penalty imposed under this section shall not exceed five thousand rupees

cgst-s125.plainEnglish:
**Section 125 is the general (residuary) penalty** — any contravention of the Act
or rules for which **no separate penalty** is provided: penalty **up to
25,000**.

complianceChecklist.item: Rectify procedural lapses promptly and voluntarily
Cite section 126 against a disproportionate section 125 penalty for a technical breach

cgst-s125.practicalNotes:
Section 125 is often invoked for procedural lapses (late Form filings, minor
record issues). It is capped at 25,000 (CGST) and read with section 126 (no
penalty for minor / bona fide / technical breaches).

faqs.q: Can a small procedural slip attract 25,000 penalty?
faqs.a: Section 125 permits up to 25,000, but section 126 requires the officer to consider the nature and gravity of the breach; no penalty is to be imposed for a minor breach or an omission easily rectifiable and made without fraudulent intent.

cgst-s126.plainEnglish:
**Section 126 — general discipline for penalties.**
- **No penalty** for a **minor breach** (tax involved < 5,000) or an
  **easily-rectifiable documentation error** made without fraudulent intent or
  gross negligence.
- Penalty must be **proportionate** to the degree and severity of the breach.
- The officer must give a **hearing** and a **speaking order** with the facts and
  the reasons.
- A person who **voluntarily discloses** a breach before its discovery may get a
  **reduced** penalty.
- This section does **not** apply where the penalty is a **fixed sum or a fixed
  percentage** (e.g. 122, 129, 47 late fee).

complianceChecklist.item: Invoke section 126 against discretionary penalties for technical / bona fide breaches

cgst-s126.practicalNotes:
Because section 126 is disapplied for **fixed** penalties, it does not help
against section 129 (detention) or section 47 (late fee). It is a real defence
against discretionary penalties under sections 122(2) / 125.

faqs.q: Does section 126 protect me from a section 129 penalty on a minor e-way bill error?
faqs.a: No. Section 126 expressly does not apply to penalties that are a fixed sum or a fixed percentage — and section 129 is such a penalty. Relief from a section 129 penalty for a genuine clerical e-way bill error comes from case law and CBIC Circular 64/38/2018, not section 126.

commonMistakes: Relying on section 126 against fixed penalties (129, 130, 47) where it does not apply

cgst-s127.plainEnglish: **Section 127 — power to impose a penalty in certain cases.** Where the proper officer is of the view that a person is liable to a penalty that is **not covered by a section 62 / 63 / 64 / 73 / 74 / 74A / 129 / 130** proceeding, he may issue an order imposing that penalty **after a hearing**.

This is the basis for the periodic **amnesty** notifications.

cgst-s128a.plainEnglish:
**Section 128A (from 01.11.2024) is the GST amnesty** — a **waiver of interest
and penalty** for demands under **section 73** for **FY 2017-18, 2018-19 and
2019-20**.

Where a section 73 notice / statement / order for those years does **not** allege
fraud, the taxpayer who pays the **full tax** by the notified date (30 March
2025, with the payment window operating up to 30 June 2025 as clarified) gets the
**interest and penalty waived** and the proceedings closed.

- Not available where the demand is only of interest / penalty (no tax), or for
  erroneous refunds, or for section 74 cases.
- Any amount already paid towards tax counts; amounts paid towards
  interest / penalty are **not refunded**.
- Applications are filed in **SPL-01 / SPL-02**.

complianceChecklist.item: Identify open section 73 demands for FY 2017-20 without a fraud allegation
Quantify the pure tax component
Pay the tax and file SPL-01 / SPL-02 within the notified window
Withdraw any appeal / writ on the same issue

faqs.q: Which years and which demands does section 128A cover?
faqs.a: Section 73 (non-fraud) demands for FY 2017-18, 2018-19 and 2019-20. Not section 74 cases, not erroneous-refund demands, and not demands that are interest/penalty only.

faqs.q: Do I get back interest I already paid?
faqs.a: No. Section 128A waives unpaid interest and penalty on payment of the tax; amounts already paid towards interest / penalty are not refunded.

cgst-s129.plainEnglish:
**Section 129 is detention, seizure and release of goods and conveyances in
transit** where they are moved in **contravention** of the Act / rules (typically
an e-way bill defect).

Release is on payment of:
- **owner comes forward** — **penalty of 200% of the tax** payable on the goods
  (or 2% of value / 25,000 for exempt goods, whichever is less);
- **owner does not come forward** — **penalty of 50% of the value** of the goods
  (or 200% of tax if higher);
- or on furnishing **security** equal to that amount.

An order must be passed within **7 days** of the detention notice; if the penalty
is not paid within **7 days** of the order, **section 130 confiscation** may
follow. From 01.01.2022 section 129 is a **standalone penalty** — the tax is not
separately demanded here (it is dealt with in the normal return / demand stream).

complianceChecklist.item: Generate a valid e-way bill for every movement above 50,000 and keep it current (extend before expiry)
Carry the invoice / delivery challan and e-way bill with the consignment
On detention, photograph goods + documents and reply to MOV-07 within the time given
Push for the 500+500 treatment where the error is clerical (cite Circular 64/38/2018)

cgst-s129.practicalNotes:
Courts and **CBIC Circular 64/38/2018** distinguish **minor / clerical** e-way
bill errors (wrong PIN code, minor address / document-number error, one digit in
the vehicle number) — for which only a token **500 + 500** penalty applies —
from substantive contraventions (no e-way bill, expired e-way bill, undervaluation,
mismatch of goods). Photograph the goods and documents at detention and reply to
the MOV-07 notice promptly.

working: Owner comes forward → penalty 200% of tax = 3,60,000
But if the delay is genuine (breakdown, documented) and there is no intent to evade, courts have set aside or reduced the penalty
examples.result: Pay 3,60,000 to release and then litigate, or seek release on security and challenge the MOV-09 order.

flowchart.title: Goods detained under section 129 — what now?

nodes.text: Goods / vehicle detained; MOV-06 detention order and MOV-07 notice served
Is it only a minor / clerical e-way bill error (Circular 64/38/2018 list)?
Only 500 CGST + 500 SGST penalty (MOV-09); insist on this.
Do you accept the contravention and want quick release?
Pay the 129 penalty (200% of tax / 50% of value) via DRC-03; goods released; you may still appeal.
Seek release on bond + security (MOV-08), reply to MOV-07, and challenge the MOV-09 order in appeal / writ.

faqs.q: Is tax also demanded under section 129?
faqs.a: Not since 01.01.2022. Section 129 is now a **penalty-only** provision for the transit contravention; the tax on the supply flows through the normal return / demand process.

faqs.q: My e-way bill had a typo in the vehicle number. Full penalty?
faqs.a: No. Per CBIC Circular 64/38/2018, minor errors — including a wrong vehicle number of one or two digits, a wrong PIN, or a minor error in the consignee's name / address — attract only a 500 + 500 penalty, provided the other details are correct and there is no tax-evasion intent.

commonMistakes: Letting an e-way bill expire in transit without extending it
Paying the full 200% penalty on a clerical error without contesting
Not replying to the MOV-07 notice within the 7-day window

caseLaw.name: Assistant Commissioner v. Satyam Shivam Papers Pvt Ltd
caseLaw.citation: 2022 (60) GSTL 3 (SC) / [2022] 134 taxmann.com 241 (SC), SLP(C) No. 21132 of 2021, decided 12-01-2022 (Telangana HC order affirmed with costs)
caseLaw.facts: Goods detained for an expired e-way bill where the delay was caused by traffic / a public disturbance, with no intent to evade.
caseLaw.issue: Whether penalty under section 129 is sustainable absent any intent to evade tax.
caseLaw.held: The detention and penalty were unjustified where the expiry was due to circumstances beyond control and there was no attempt to evade; costs were imposed on the department.
caseLaw.effect: Leading authority that mens rea / evasion intent matters for section 129 in genuine transit-delay cases.

instrumentsExplained.gist: Notified the 01.01.2022 recast of sections 129 and 130 — de-linking, higher penalties, the 7-day timelines and separate treatment of confiscation.

forms.purpose: Detention order / notice / penalty order for goods in transit.
Bond for provisional release of detained goods.

cgst-s130.plainEnglish:
**Section 130 is confiscation of goods / conveyances and levy of penalty** where
a person, **with intent to evade tax**: supplies / receives goods in
contravention with intent to evade; does not account for goods; supplies goods
without registration; contravenes the Act with intent to evade; or uses a
conveyance to carry goods in contravention (unless the owner proves it was
without his knowledge).

- The owner is given an **option to pay a fine in lieu of confiscation** (not
  exceeding the market value less the tax), **plus** the tax, penalty and other
  charges.
- A **notice and hearing** are mandatory (section 130(4)).
- Since 01.01.2022, section 130 is **de-linked** from section 129 — confiscation
  is a separate, more serious step requiring proof of **intent to evade**.

complianceChecklist.item: On a section 130 notice, contest the 'intent to evade' finding specifically
Insist on a proper hearing before any confiscation order
Evaluate the redemption-fine option against the appeal route

cgst-s130.practicalNotes:
The de-linking matters: the department can no longer jump straight to
confiscation from a section 129 detention. *Synergy Fertichem* (Gujarat HC) and
subsequent rulings require a **finding of intent to evade** and a proper
adjudication before confiscation. Contest the "intent to evade" element head-on.

faqs.q: Can goods be confiscated just because the e-way bill was missing?
faqs.a: No. Section 130 requires **intent to evade tax**, a show-cause notice and a hearing. A missing / expired e-way bill without more is a section 129 matter, not automatic confiscation (*Synergy Fertichem*).

commonMistakes: Treating a section 130 notice like a routine section 129 penalty

caseLaw.name: Synergy Fertichem Pvt Ltd v. State of Gujarat
caseLaw.citation: 2020 (33) GSTL 3 (Guj) / [2019] 111 taxmann.com 313 (Guj), decided 23-12-2019
caseLaw.facts: Confiscation proceedings initiated straight after detention for an e-way bill lapse.
caseLaw.issue: When can section 130 confiscation be invoked as against section 129 detention?
caseLaw.held: Section 130 requires an independent finding of intent to evade tax; it cannot be invoked mechanically on the back of a section 129 detention.
caseLaw.effect: The reference point for challenging premature confiscation; reinforced by the 2022 de-linking amendment.

cgst-s131.plainEnglish: **Section 131 — confiscation or penalty not to interfere with other punishments.** A confiscation or penalty under the Act does **not** prevent any **other punishment** under this or any other law for the same facts.

cgst-s132.plainEnglish:
**Section 132 lists the criminal offences and punishments.**

Offences include: supply without invoice to evade tax; issuing an **invoice
without supply** (fake invoicing) and availing ITC / refund on it; availing ITC
**without any invoice**; collecting tax and not paying it within 3 months;
obstructing an officer; tampering with evidence; and abetment.

**Punishment scales with the amount** of tax evaded / ITC wrongly availed /
refund wrongly taken:
- **> 5 crore** — up to **5 years** and fine (**cognizable and non-bailable**);
- **2–5 crore** — up to **3 years** and fine;
- **1–2 crore** — up to **1 year** and fine.
- Certain offences (obstruction, tampering, falsifying records) — up to 6 months
  regardless of amount.

**Threshold for prosecution** raised to **2 crore** (Finance Act 2023) except for
fake invoicing. Repeat offence — up to 5 years. Prosecution needs the
**Commissioner's sanction** (section 132(6)).

complianceChecklist.item: Never issue or accept an invoice without an underlying supply
Deposit any tax collected within 3 months
Cooperate with summons / investigation; take legal advice early where amounts are large
Consider compounding under section 138 where prosecution is threatened and the offence is compoundable

cgst-s132.practicalNotes:
Prosecution is separate from the tax demand — it can proceed even while the
demand is under appeal, though courts weigh the outcome of adjudication.
**Compounding** under section 138 is available for most offences (not for fake
invoicing above the threshold, and not for repeat offenders) on payment of a
compounding amount.

**Arrest** under section 69 is possible only for the offences in 132(1)(a)–(d)
where the amount exceeds **5 crore** (cognizable and non-bailable); the CBIC
arrest guidelines and *Arnesh Kumar* principles apply.

faqs.q: What is the monetary threshold for GST prosecution?
faqs.a: Generally **2 crore** of tax evaded / ITC or refund wrongly taken (raised by the Finance Act 2023), **except** for the offence of issuing invoices without supply, where the lower thresholds still apply.

faqs.q: Can I be arrested for a GST offence?
faqs.a: Only for the offences in section 132(1)(a) to (d) where the amount exceeds 5 crore — these are cognizable and non-bailable. Arrest requires the Commissioner's authorisation and must follow the CBIC guidelines and Supreme Court safeguards.

faqs.q: Can a GST offence be compounded?
faqs.a: Yes, under section 138 for most offences, on payment of a compounding amount (now 25%–100% of the tax, within a floor and ceiling). Fake invoicing above the threshold and repeat offences cannot be compounded.

commonMistakes: Treating a large ITC-mismatch investigation as a pure tax dispute and ignoring the prosecution risk
Assuming every evasion above 1 crore is prosecutable (threshold is now 2 crore except fake invoicing)

caseLaw.name: Radhika Agarwal v. Union of India
caseLaw.citation: 2025 LiveLaw (SC) 255, Writ Petition (Crl.) No. 336 of 2018 with connected matters, decided 27-02-2025 (3-Judge Bench: Sanjiv Khanna CJI, M.M. Sundresh and Bela M. Trivedi JJ.)
caseLaw.facts: Batch of petitions challenging the power of arrest and the arrest practice under the CGST Act and the Customs Act, and the availability of anticipatory bail to a person summoned/apprehending arrest.
caseLaw.issue: Validity and limits of the section 69 arrest power; whether a person can seek anticipatory bail before arrest under the GST / Customs Acts.
caseLaw.held: The power of arrest under both Acts is valid but hedged with safeguards — the officer must have material-based 'reasons to believe' recorded in writing, the grounds of arrest must be furnished in writing, and the CrPC safeguards and Arnesh Kumar / D.K. Basu discipline apply; force and threats to coerce a 'voluntary' payment during search or investigation are impermissible and any tax so paid must be refunded. Anticipatory bail under section 438 CrPC IS maintainable where arrest is apprehended — the two-Judge rulings in State of Gujarat v. Choodamani Parmeshwaran Iyer (2023) and Bharat Bhushan (Del HC) holding that the only remedy is an Article 226 writ are overruled.
caseLaw.effect: The leading authority on GST / Customs arrest. A person apprehending arrest can move for anticipatory bail; coerced 'spot' payments are recoverable; an arrest without recorded, material-based reasons and written grounds is bad.

caseLaw.name: State of Gujarat v. Choodamani Parmeshwaran Iyer
caseLaw.citation: 2023 SCC OnLine SC 851 / [2023] 153 taxmann.com 267 (SC), SLP(Crl) Nos. 4212-4213 of 2019, decided 17-07-2023
caseLaw.facts: The respondent, summoned under section 70 in a GST evasion inquiry, obtained protection from arrest from the Gujarat High Court; the State appealed.
caseLaw.issue: Whether a person summoned under section 70 and apprehending arrest under section 69 can invoke section 438 CrPC for anticipatory bail.
caseLaw.held: No. As no FIR is registered before the section 69 arrest power is invoked, the person is not an 'accused' and cannot invoke section 438 CrPC; the only remedy against apprehended pre-trial arrest is a writ under Article 226.
caseLaw.effect: OVERRULED on the anticipatory-bail point by the 3-Judge Bench in Radhika Agarwal v. Union of India (2025) — anticipatory bail is now available. Cite Radhika Agarwal, not this case, for the current position.

cgst-s138.plainEnglish: **Section 138 — compounding of offences.** Most GST offences can be **compounded** by the Commissioner, on payment of a **compounding amount** — now between **25% and 100% of the tax involved**, subject to a floor and ceiling. **Cannot** be compounded: the offence of issuing invoices without supply (fake invoicing) above the threshold, a person who was allowed to compound once for an offence above 1 crore, a person convicted for an offence above 1 crore, and offences under other Acts. cgst-s140.plainEnglish:
**Section 140 — transitional credit.** It allowed a registered person to carry
forward, into the electronic credit ledger, the **CENVAT credit / VAT credit**
closing balance from the pre-GST returns, and credit on **stock held on 1 July
2017**, subject to conditions — claimed through **Form TRAN-1** (and TRAN-2 for
traders without duty-paying documents).

The window was reopened by the Supreme Court in *Union of India v. Filco Trade
Centre* (2022) for **2 months** (Sept–Nov 2022, later extended). Most transitional
credit litigation is now about the **validity of the TRAN-1 claim** and technical
glitches.

complianceChecklist.item: For any pending TRAN-1 dispute, establish admissibility under both the old and the new law
Distinguish a technical-glitch denial (relievable) from a substantive one

cgst-s140.practicalNotes:
Largely of historical / litigation interest now. Where a TRAN-1 credit is under
challenge, the key questions are: was the credit **admissible** under the earlier
law and under GST; was the claim **filed** in the (re)opened window; and is the
denial based on a **technical glitch** (relievable) or a **substantive**
ineligibility.

faqs.q: Can I still file TRAN-1?
faqs.a: The general window has closed. It was reopened once for all taxpayers (Sept–Nov 2022) pursuant to *Filco Trade Centre*. Fresh claims now are only through litigation on specific facts.

caseLaw.name: Union of India v. Filco Trade Centre Pvt Ltd
caseLaw.citation: [2022] 140 taxmann.com 535 (SC), decided 22-07-2022 (main order); extended by [2022] 142 taxmann.com 89 (SC), 02-09-2022
caseLaw.facts: The Revenue's SLPs against many High Court decisions allowing late TRAN-1 filing were pending; taxpayers had been unable to file or revise TRAN-1 / TRAN-2 because of portal failures and the statutory time limit.
caseLaw.issue: Whether the transitional-credit window under section 140 should be reopened for everyone.
caseLaw.held: The GSTN was directed to open the common portal for filing / revising TRAN-1 and TRAN-2 for two months — eventually 01.10.2022 to 30.11.2022 — for all aggrieved taxpayers, whether or not they had litigated and whether or not their case went before an ITGRC. The officer then has 90 days to verify and pass an order; verified credit is reflected in the electronic credit ledger. All questions of law on section 140 decided by the High Courts were kept open.
caseLaw.effect: Gave every taxpayer a one-time window (now closed) to file or correct transitional credit. Claims filed in that window stand; fresh claims outside it are only on specific facts through litigation.

caseLaw.name: Adfert Technologies Pvt Ltd v. Union of India
caseLaw.citation: 2019 SCC OnLine P&H 5701 / [2019] 111 taxmann.com 27 (P&H) / 2020 (32) GSTL 726 (P&H), CWP No. 30949 of 2018, decided 04-11-2019; Revenue SLP dismissed by the Supreme Court on 28-02-2020, [2020] 115 taxmann.com 249 (SC)
caseLaw.facts: Taxpayers could not carry forward accumulated CENVAT / VAT credit because TRAN-1 could not be filed or revised in time due to portal glitches.
caseLaw.issue: Can unutilised transitional credit be denied for a technical failure to meet the TRAN-1 deadline?
caseLaw.held: Unutilised input tax credit earned under the earlier laws is a vested right and 'property' under Article 300A; it cannot be taken away for a procedural or technical lapse where the taxpayer was otherwise entitled. The department was directed to permit filing / correction of TRAN-1.
caseLaw.effect: The leading pre-Filco authority that transitional credit is a substantive right, not a concession that lapses with a form deadline. The SC's dismissal of the Revenue SLP (28-02-2020) affirms it.

forms.purpose: Declaration to carry forward pre-GST credit / claim credit on transitional stock.

cgst-s143.plainEnglish: **Section 143 — job work procedure.** A registered **principal** may send inputs / capital goods to a job worker (and onward to another job worker) **without payment of tax**, under intimation and subject to conditions. Inputs must come back / be supplied out within **1 year**, capital goods within **3 years** (not moulds / dies / jigs / fixtures / tools). If not, it is a **deemed supply** from the date they were sent, with tax and interest. The principal may supply the goods **directly from the job worker's premises** if he declares that place as an additional place of business (or the job worker is registered / notified).

extended the section 73 limitation for 2018-19 and 2019-20) on grounds that (i)
the Council did not "recommend" before the notification and (ii) force majeure had
ended. The issue is before the Supreme Court — the outcome affects the validity
of a large tranche of demands. Preserve the limitation ground in any affected
matter.

faqs.q: My section 73 order for FY 2019-20 relies on a 168A extension — is it valid?
faqs.a: That is exactly the question pending before the Supreme Court (validity of Notifications 9/2023 and 56/2023-CT). Raise the limitation / 168A challenge in your reply and appeal; do not let it go by default.

commonMistakes: Not raising the 168A limitation challenge and losing it by acquiescence

instrumentsExplained.gist: Extended the section 73 limitation for FY 2018-19 and 2019-20 relying on section 168A — validity challenged and pending before the Supreme Court.

cgst-s169.plainEnglish: **Section 169 — service of notice.** A notice / order / communication is validly served by: hand delivery / courier to the person or his representative; **registered / speed post with acknowledgment** to the last known place of business / residence; **email** to the registered email; **making it available on the common portal**; publication in a newspaper; or, if none is practicable, affixing it at the last known place of business / on the notice board of the office. Service is deemed on **tendering / publishing / uploading**.

cgst-s169.practicalNotes: Uploading to the portal is valid service — but courts have repeatedly set aside orders where the notice was **only** placed under 'Additional Notices and Orders' (a tab many taxpayers miss), holding that the mode must be **effective**, especially for the first notice.

faqs.q: I never saw the SCN — it was only on the portal. Is the order valid?
faqs.a: Uploading is a recognised mode under section 169. But where it was buried under 'Additional Notices' and no other mode was tried, several High Courts have set aside the ex-parte order and remanded, treating the service as ineffective.

cgst-s170.plainEnglish: **Section 170 — rounding off of tax.** The amount of tax, interest, penalty, fine or any other sum payable, and the refund / ITC, is **rounded off to the nearest rupee** (50 paise and above rounded up).

cgst-s171.plainEnglish:
**Section 171 — anti-profiteering.** Any reduction in the rate of tax, or the
benefit of ITC, must be **passed on to the recipient by a commensurate reduction
in prices**.

- The **National Anti-profiteering Authority (NAA)** examined complaints;
  from **1 December 2022** the function moved to the **Competition Commission of
  India (CCI)**, and the **sunset date for accepting new applications was
  1 April 2025** — after which no fresh anti-profiteering complaints are
  entertained.
- The Authority could order the price reduction, a **refund to consumers with
  18% interest** (or deposit to the Consumer Welfare Fund), a **penalty** and, in
  extreme cases, cancellation of registration.

complianceChecklist.item: On any rate cut or new ITC benefit, document a commensurate price reduction (SKU-level)
Retain pre- and post-change pricing evidence for pending / legacy matters

cgst-s171.practicalNotes:
No prescribed **methodology** — the absence of statutory computation rules was a
main litigation ground (the Delhi High Court in *Reckitt Benckiser / Hindustan
Unilever* upheld the provision's validity in 2024 but the methodology debate
continues). With the 1 April 2025 sunset, section 171 is now essentially a
**legacy** provision — existing orders and appeals continue, but no new
investigations begin.

faqs.q: Is anti-profiteering still in force?
faqs.a: The obligation in section 171 remains on the statute, but the authority stopped accepting **new** applications from 1 April 2025. Pending cases and appeals (now before the CCI / GSTAT) continue.

commonMistakes: Absorbing a rate cut as margin without a price reduction (legacy exposure)

caseLaw.name: Reckitt Benckiser India Pvt Ltd v. Union of India
caseLaw.citation: [2024] 158 taxmann.com 675 (Del) / 2024 SCC OnLine Del 615, batch of ~107 writ petitions (lead W.P.(C) 7743/2019), decided 29-01-2024
caseLaw.facts: Batch challenge by ~107 companies (Hindustan Unilever, Nestle, Patanjali, Reckitt and others) to the constitutional validity of section 171 and anti-profiteering Rules 122, 124, 126, 127, 129, 133 and 134, and to the absence of a prescribed computation methodology.
caseLaw.issue: Validity of the anti-profiteering framework under Articles 19(1)(g) and 300A.
caseLaw.held: Section 171 and the rules were upheld as constitutionally valid — section 171 is a consumer-welfare / benefit-passing measure, not a price-fixing mechanism, and does not violate Article 19(1)(g) or 300A. Individual orders of the Authority remain open to challenge on merits / methodology, and the Court cautioned against arbitrary or mechanical exercise of the power.
caseLaw.effect: Settles the vires question; SKU-level methodology and quantum disputes continue in individual appeals (now before the GST Appellate Tribunal / Principal Bench).

cgst-s172.plainEnglish: **Section 172 — removal of difficulties.** The Government could, for **5 years** from 1 July 2017 (i.e. up to 30 June 2022), by order, remove any difficulty in giving effect to the Act, consistent with its provisions. Several **Removal of Difficulties Orders** (on annual-return dates, appeal timelines, transitional credit) were issued under this power.

igst-s1.plainEnglish: **Section 1 of the IGST Act — short title, extent and commencement.** Extends to the whole of India; in force from **1 July 2017**.

keyConcepts.note: Defined term — tap in the text to see the definition.

igst-s2.plainEnglish:
**Section 2 of the IGST Act defines the terms special to inter-State / cross-
border GST**, and adopts the CGST Act definitions for the rest.

Key IGST-specific definitions:
- **"export of goods"** — taking goods out of India to a place outside India.
- **"export of services"** — supplier in India, recipient outside India, place
  of supply outside India, payment in convertible forex (or INR where permitted
  by RBI), and the two are **not merely establishments of a distinct person**.
- **"import of goods / services"** — bringing goods into India / recipient in
  India, supplier outside India, place of supply in India.
- **"intermediary"** — a broker / agent who **arranges or facilitates** a supply
  of goods / services **between two persons**, but does not supply it on his own
  account.
- **"location of the supplier / recipient of services"**, **"fixed
  establishment"**, **"online information and database access or retrieval
  (OIDAR) services"**, **"online money gaming"**, **"specified actionable
  claim"**, **"non-taxable online recipient"**, **"zero-rated supply"** (s.16).

complianceChecklist.item: Test each cross-border service against the 5 export conditions in s.2(6)
Assess whether a support arrangement is 'intermediary' (Circular 159/15/2021)
Confirm forex realisation (FIRC / BRC) for export-of-service refund claims

keyConcepts.note: Arranges / facilitates a supply between two other persons; does not supply on own account — IGST s.2(13). Place of supply = supplier's location (s.13(8)(b)).
Five conditions in IGST s.2(6); failing any one makes the service a domestic (taxable) supply.

igst-s2.practicalNotes:
The definition of **"intermediary"** decides whether a back-office / marketing /
support arrangement for a foreign group company is an **export** (place of supply
= recipient's location) or an **intermediary service** (place of supply = India,
taxable). CBIC Circular 159/15/2021 lists the tests: two supplies, a main and an
ancillary; arrangement / facilitation; not on own account.

**Export of services** fails if the Indian entity and the foreign recipient are
"merely establishments of a distinct person" (Explanation 1 to section 8) — i.e.
a branch billing its own head office.

faqs.q: My company does marketing support for its US parent. Is it an export?
faqs.a: It is an export only if the service is provided on the company's **own account** to the parent as recipient. If the company merely **arranges / facilitates** supplies between the parent and Indian customers, it is an 'intermediary' — place of supply is India and GST applies. Circular 159/15/2021 has the tests.

commonMistakes: Treating an intermediary service as an export
Claiming export benefit on a branch-to-head-office billing

caseLaw.name: Dharmendra M. Jani v. Union of India
caseLaw.citation: [2023] 151 taxmann.com 271 (Bom), Writ Petition No. 2031 of 2018 — Division Bench split verdict (Ujjal Bhuyan J. holding s.13(8)(b) ultra vires, 09-06-2021; Abhay Ahuja J. holding it valid, 16-06-2021); resolved by the referral (third) judge, G.S. Kulkarni J., on 18-04-2023
caseLaw.facts: Challenge to the constitutional validity of taxing 'intermediary' services under section 13(8)(b) read with section 8(2) of the IGST Act, where the recipient / principal is located outside India.
caseLaw.issue: Whether section 13(8)(b) (place of supply of intermediary services in India) and section 8(2) are constitutionally valid.
caseLaw.held: After a split verdict of the Division Bench, the referral (third) judge upheld sections 13(8)(b) and 8(2) as legal, valid and constitutional, but read them as operative only for the purposes of the IGST Act — they cannot be pressed into service to levy CGST/SGST. The double-taxation debate and contrary views of other High Courts remain unresolved, and a legislative amendment / Supreme Court reference is possible.
caseLaw.effect: Intermediary services with an Indian-located supplier remain taxable in India as an inter-State supply; the 'export of services' route is not available. Structure and documentation of the arrangement matter.

igst-s3.plainEnglish: **Section 3 of the IGST Act — appointment of officers.** The Board may appoint officers for IGST purposes; officers appointed under the CGST Act are **authorised to be the proper officers** for IGST.

igst-s4.plainEnglish: **Section 4 of the IGST Act — authorisation of State / UT tax officers.** Officers of State / UT tax are authorised as proper officers for IGST, subject to conditions the Government notifies (cross-empowerment for IGST).

igst-s5.plainEnglish:
**Section 5 is the charging section for IGST** — the mirror of CGST section 9.

- IGST on all **inter-State** supplies (except alcoholic liquor) on the
  section 15 value, at notified rates (up to 40%).
- IGST on **imports of goods** is levied and collected under the **Customs Tariff
  Act** at the point of customs clearance, on the value **plus basic customs
  duty**.
- Petroleum products — from a date to be notified.
- **Reverse charge (5(3), 5(4))** and **e-commerce (5(5))** — same scheme as
  CGST section 9, for inter-State supplies and imports of services.

complianceChecklist.item: Pay IGST under RCM on every import of service in cash in GSTR-3B
Issue self-invoices for imported services
Reconcile IGST paid at customs (Bills of Entry) with GSTR-2B ITC

igst-s5.practicalNotes:
**Import of services** is always an inter-State supply → IGST under reverse
charge, paid in cash by the recipient, ITC claimed subject to sections 16/17. The
time of supply is the earlier of payment or **60 days** from the foreign
supplier's invoice (CGST section 13(3)).

IGST on **import of goods** is not paid through GSTR-3B — it is paid at customs
and appears in GSTR-2B (from ICEGATE) as ITC.

faqs.q: How is IGST on imported goods paid?
faqs.a: At the time of customs clearance under the Customs Tariff Act, on the assessable value plus basic customs duty (and other duties). It is not routed through GSTR-3B; the ITC flows into GSTR-2B from the Bill of Entry data.

faqs.q: Do I pay IGST on services imported from my foreign vendor?
faqs.a: Yes, under reverse charge (section 5(3)), in cash, in your GSTR-3B; then claim ITC subject to sections 16 and 17. Issue a self-invoice.

commonMistakes: Missing RCM on imported software / SaaS / management fees
Claiming customs IGST ITC without a Bill of Entry in 2B

igst-s6.plainEnglish: **Section 6 of the IGST Act — power to grant exemption from IGST**, mirroring CGST section 11. IGST exemption notifications track the CGST ones (the 9/2017 and 2/2017 IT(R) series).

igst-s7.plainEnglish:
**Section 7 — inter-State supply.** A supply is **inter-State** where the
**location of the supplier** and the **place of supply** are in **different**
States / UTs, or one is in a State and the other in a UT, or the supply is an
**import**, an **export**, a supply to / from an **SEZ**, or a supply in the
**territorial waters / EEZ**, or **any supply not intra-State** and not otherwise
covered.

Supplies to or by an **SEZ unit / developer** are **always inter-State** (hence
IGST / zero-rated), even if physically within the same State.

complianceChecklist.item: Determine place of supply first, then compare with the supplier's location for inter/intra call
Treat all SEZ supplies as inter-State / zero-rated
If tax paid under the wrong head, claim refund under section 77 and pay the correct head (no interest — section 77(2))

igst-s7.practicalNotes:
The inter-State vs intra-State call decides **CGST+SGST vs IGST** — a wrong call
means tax paid under the wrong head, a refund claim under section 77 / IGST
section 19, and interest exposure (mitigated: no interest where the correct tax
is paid after paying the wrong one — section 77(2) / IGST 19(2)).

faqs.q: I supplied to an SEZ unit in my own State. IGST or CGST+SGST?
faqs.a: IGST — a supply to an SEZ unit / developer is always treated as inter-State (section 7(5)(b)), and is zero-rated under section 16 (supply under LUT without tax, or with IGST and refund).

commonMistakes: Charging CGST+SGST on an SEZ supply
Charging IGST on an intra-State supply where the place of supply is local

igst-s8.plainEnglish:
**Section 8 — intra-State supply.** A supply is **intra-State** where the
supplier's location **and** the place of supply are in the **same** State / UT —
attracting **CGST + SGST/UTGST**.

**Exclusions** (never intra-State): supply to / by an **SEZ**; **import** of
goods until they cross the customs frontier; supplies to a **tourist** under
section 15; and supplies where the supplier is in India and the place of supply
is outside India.

**Explanation 1** — an establishment of a person in one State and another in a
different State (or in a UT, or as an SEZ unit) are **distinct persons**;
Explanation 2 — a person with an establishment in India **and** outside India is
treated as distinct establishments.

igst-s8.practicalNotes:
Explanation 1 is the legal hook for **cross-charge**: an Indian head office
providing services (management, HR, common IT) to its branches in other States
makes an inter-State supply between distinct persons — value under Rule 28. Since
1 April 2025 common **input-service** credit must be distributed via **ISD**;
cross-charge continues for **internally-generated** services.

faqs.q: Do I need to cross-charge my branches for head-office costs?
faqs.a: For **internally generated** services (use of common employees, management oversight) — yes, value under Rule 28 (invoice value accepted where the branch has full ITC). For **procured** common input services — route the ITC through an ISD from 1 April 2025.

commonMistakes: Not cross-charging common management / HR / IT services to branches
Over-valuing cross-charge where the branch has full ITC

igst-s9.plainEnglish:
**Section 9 — supplies in territorial waters.** Where the location of the
supplier or the place of supply is in the **territorial waters** (up to 12
nautical miles), it is deemed to be in the **coastal State / UT** nearest to the
appropriate baseline. This mainly affects offshore supplies, ports and vessels.

complianceChecklist.item: For offshore / port / vessel supplies, map the location to the nearest coastal State

keyConcepts.note: Defined term — tap in the text to see the definition.

igst-s9.practicalNotes:
Beyond 12 nm (the EEZ / continental shelf up to 200 nm) special notifications
extend the Acts for specific activities (petroleum operations). For most
businesses this section is relevant only for coastal shipping, port services and
offshore contracts.

igst-s10.plainEnglish:
**Section 10 — place of supply of goods (other than imports / exports).**

- **10(1)(a)** — where movement is involved: the location where the movement
  **terminates for delivery** to the recipient.
- **10(1)(b) — bill-to / ship-to**: where goods are delivered to a third person
  on the direction of the buyer, the place of supply is the **buyer's principal
  place of business** (the "bill-to" party), by legal fiction.
- **10(1)(c)** — no movement: the location of the goods at delivery.
- **10(1)(ca)** (from 2023) — supply to an **unregistered person**: the address
  on the invoice; if none, the supplier's location.
- **10(1)(d)** — goods assembled / installed at site: the place of installation.
- **10(1)(e)** — goods supplied on board a conveyance: the location where they
  are **taken on board**.

complianceChecklist.item: For third-party deliveries, treat it as two supplies and fix the place of supply for each
For B2C sales, capture the recipient's address on the invoice (section 10(1)(ca))
For site installation, tax at the place of installation

keyConcepts.note: Defined term — tap in the text to see the definition.

igst-s10.practicalNotes:
The **bill-to / ship-to** rule (10(1)(b)) is the one that trips up dropship and
third-party-delivery models — there are **two supplies** (supplier→bill-to,
bill-to→ship-to), each with its own place of supply, and the first one's place of
supply is the bill-to party's location regardless of where the goods physically
go.

examples.title: Bill-to / ship-to
examples.scenario: A (Maharashtra) sells goods to B (Karnataka) but delivers them, on B's instruction, to C (Tamil Nadu).
working: Supply 1: A → B. Place of supply = B's location (Karnataka) by section 10(1)(b) → A charges IGST
Supply 2: B → C. Movement terminates in Tamil Nadu → place of supply Tamil Nadu → B charges IGST
examples.result: Two IGST supplies; A must register / bill correctly to Karnataka even though goods never enter Karnataka.

faqs.q: Goods shipped to a different State than the buyer's — which State's tax?
faqs.a: For the supplier→buyer leg, section 10(1)(b) fixes the place of supply as the **buyer's** location (the party who directed the delivery), not where the goods physically go. It is usually an IGST supply.

commonMistakes: Charging tax by reference to the ship-to State instead of the bill-to State
Missing the second supply in a bill-to/ship-to chain

igst-s11.plainEnglish:
**Section 11 — place of supply of imported / exported goods.**
- **Import** — the location of the **importer**.
- **Export** — the location **outside India**.

So imported goods have a place of supply where the importer is registered, which
matches the State where IGST credit on the Bill of Entry is taken.

complianceChecklist.item: Declare the correct importer GSTIN on every Bill of Entry

igst-s11.practicalNotes:
Simple but important for ITC: IGST paid at customs is creditable to the GSTIN of
the **importer** shown on the Bill of Entry — ensure the correct GSTIN is
declared on the BoE, especially for multi-State importers.
commonMistakes: Wrong GSTIN on the BoE, stranding the customs-IGST credit

For immovable-property / event services, tax at the property / event location
Assess whether a site presence needs registration in that State

faqs.q: Hotel stay — which State's GST?
faqs.a: The State where the hotel is located (section 12(3)(b)), regardless of where the guest or the guest's company is registered. So the guest's company cannot take ITC of that CGST+SGST if it is not registered in that State — a known ITC leakage on travel.

igst-s13.practicalNotes:
**13(8)(b)** — an intermediary in India serving a foreign principal has place of
supply **in India** → the service is **not an export** and IGST is payable. This
is the single biggest cross-border classification issue for Indian back-offices
and agents (see *Dharmendra Jani*).

For **export of services**, place of supply must be **outside India** — so a
service caught by 13(3)/(4)/(5)/(8) with an Indian nexus fails the export test.

faqs.q: Indian agent earning commission from a foreign company — export?
faqs.a: No. Section 13(8)(b) places the supply of an intermediary at the **supplier's** (India) location, so it is a domestic taxable supply, not an export — even though the commission is received in forex.

commonMistakes: Treating intermediary commission from abroad as an export
Ignoring the 'destination of goods' rule for cross-border goods transport

igst-s14.plainEnglish:
**Section 14 — special provision for OIDAR services** supplied from outside India
to a **non-taxable online recipient** (an unregistered person, Government, local
authority or individual receiving the service for a non-business purpose).

The **overseas supplier** must take **simplified registration** and pay IGST. If
the supplier operates through an **intermediary / electronic platform**, that
platform is deemed the supplier and is liable — unless it satisfies all the
conditions to show it is a mere conduit.

**14A** — a parallel special provision for **online money gaming** supplied from
outside India to a person in India, with a **single simplified registration** and
the power to block access to non-compliant platforms.

complianceChecklist.item: Foreign OIDAR B2C suppliers: take simplified registration, file GSTR-5A
Indian businesses: pay RCM on imported OIDAR / digital services

keyConcepts.note: Online information and database access or retrieval services — delivered over the internet, essentially automated — IGST s.2(17).

igst-s14.practicalNotes:
OIDAR = services delivered over the internet with **minimal human intervention**
(cloud, streaming, e-books, online advertising space, SaaS). B2B OIDAR is under
**RCM** (the Indian recipient pays); B2C OIDAR is on the **foreign supplier**
under section 14. The 2023 amendment widened "non-taxable online recipient" to
include unregistered persons receiving for business purposes too.

faqs.q: A foreign SaaS company bills Indian consumers — who pays GST?
faqs.a: The foreign company, under section 14, after taking a simplified GST registration in India and filing GSTR-5A. For Indian **business** customers, the customer pays under RCM instead.

commonMistakes: Foreign digital suppliers not registering for B2C India sales
Indian businesses missing RCM on cloud / advertising / software subscriptions

forms.purpose: Return of an OIDAR service provider located outside India.

igst-s14a.plainEnglish: **Section 14A of the IGST Act — special provision for online money gaming supplied from outside India.** A supplier of **online money gaming** located outside India to a person in India must take a **single simplified registration**, pay IGST, and may have platform access **blocked** for non-compliance. GST on online money gaming is on the **full face value** of bets / deposits at **28%** (from 1 October 2023).

igst-s16.plainEnglish:
**Section 16 — zero-rated supply.** Exports of goods / services and supplies to
an **SEZ unit / developer for authorised operations** are **zero-rated** — the
outward supply bears **no tax**, but **full ITC** is preserved (unlike an exempt
supply).

Two routes:
- **(a) LUT / bond** — supply without paying IGST, and claim **refund of
  unutilised ITC** (Rule 89(4) formula); or
- **(b) with payment** — pay IGST and claim **refund of the IGST paid** (for
  goods, automatically via the shipping bill).

The **payment route** is restricted for some suppliers (those who received
inputs under concessional / exemption notifications, and certain risky
exporters). A supply to an SEZ is zero-rated only to the extent of **authorised
operations** (an endorsement from the SEZ officer is needed).

complianceChecklist.item: File the LUT (RFD-11) before the start of each financial year
Do not reverse ITC on zero-rated supplies — claim the refund instead
Obtain the SEZ endorsement for authorised operations
Track forex realisation within 9 months (Rule 96B)

keyConcepts.note: Zero-rated = no output tax + full ITC + refund. Exempt = no output tax but ITC blocked / apportioned. Getting this wrong costs the ITC.

igst-s16.practicalNotes:
- File the **LUT (RFD-11)** at the start of each financial year.
- Realise export proceeds within the FEMA period (generally **9 months**);
  non-realisation can require reversal / payment of the IGST refund with interest
  (Rule 96B).
- **Deemed exports** (Notification 48/2017) are **not** zero-rated — tax is paid
  and either the supplier or the recipient claims a refund.

faqs.q: Is an export an exempt supply?
faqs.a: No. Exports and SEZ supplies are **zero-rated** under section 16 — they carry full ITC and a refund entitlement. Treating them as exempt (and reversing ITC under Rule 42) is a costly mistake.

faqs.q: SEZ supply — do I need anything from the SEZ unit?
faqs.a: Yes — an endorsement from the specified officer of the SEZ that the supply was received for authorised operations, which is required for the refund.

commonMistakes: Reversing ITC on exports as if they were exempt
Exporting without a valid LUT and facing an IGST demand
Missing forex realisation and the Rule 96B refund reversal

igst-s17.plainEnglish:
**Section 17 — apportionment of tax and settlement of funds.** The machinery for
splitting IGST between the Centre and the States:
- IGST used by a taxpayer to pay **CGST** is transferred to the Centre; IGST used
  to pay **SGST** is transferred to the destination State.
- IGST on B2C supplies and on ITC that will be used for SGST is apportioned to
  the State of **consumption**.
- A provisional apportionment is made monthly and adjusted; the balance in the
  IGST pool is settled between the Centre and States on the Council's formula.

This is largely a **Government-to-Government** provision — not a taxpayer
compliance obligation — but it is why place of supply matters so much (it
directs revenue to the right State).

complianceChecklist.item: Get place of supply right so IGST is apportioned to the correct State

igst-s20.plainEnglish:
**Section 20 — application of CGST Act provisions to IGST.** The CGST Act
provisions on scope of supply, composite / mixed supply, time and value of
supply, ITC, registration, tax invoice, accounts, returns, payment, TDS / TCS,
assessment, audit, inspection, demands, refunds, appeals, offences, advance
ruling and miscellaneous matters **apply to IGST**, so far as may be, **mutatis
mutandis**.

Some carve-outs / modifications: the **ITC set-off order** (IGST credit first),
the **maximum rate is 40%** (vs 20% CGST), the **penalty amounts are doubled** in
some provisions (since IGST = CGST + SGST), and there is **no separate composition
scheme** under IGST.

complianceChecklist.item: Apply CGST procedure to IGST matters (returns, ITC, demands, appeals)
Use the doubled penalty ceilings for IGST where relevant

faqs.q: Are States still being compensated?
faqs.a: The 5-year compensation guarantee ended on 30 June 2022. The cess continues to be collected (extended to March 2026) but now services the loans taken during 2020-22 to bridge the compensation shortfall, not fresh compensation.

cess-s8.plainEnglish:
**Section 8 of the Compensation Cess Act is the charging section for the GST
Compensation Cess** — levied on the supply of goods and services **specified in
the Schedule** (mainly tobacco and tobacco products, pan masala, aerated waters,
motor vehicles above certain specifications, coal).

- Levied on the **same value** as GST (section 15 of the CGST Act), or on a
  **specific / quantity** basis for some goods (e.g. per 1,000 sticks of
  cigarettes), at rates in the notified Cess rate schedule.
- **Not payable** by a composition taxpayer.
- On **imports**, cess is collected at customs under the Customs Tariff Act.
- **ITC of cess** can be used **only to pay cess** — it cannot cross to CGST /
  SGST / IGST.

complianceChecklist.item: Charge cess on every Schedule item, in addition to GST
Use the correct basis (ad valorem or specific / per-unit) per the Cess rate schedule
Ring-fence cess ITC — use only against output cess
Reconcile cess paid at customs (imports) with cess ITC in GSTR-2B

keyConcepts.note: A cess over and above GST on notified 'sin' / luxury goods, to fund State compensation — levied under the GST (Compensation to States) Act, 2017.

cess-s8.practicalNotes:
The compensation-cess period was extended (originally to June 2022, then to March
2026) to service the back-to-back loans taken to compensate States during COVID.
Its future beyond that is a GST Council / GoM agenda item.

**Cess credit ring-fencing** is the practical trap — a business that pays cess on
inputs (e.g. coal) but makes no cess-liable outward supply cannot use that
credit against GST; it accumulates or is refundable only in limited situations
(zero-rated supplies).

examples.title: Cess on a motor vehicle
examples.scenario: A dealer sells a large SUV (length > 4m, engine > 1500cc, ground clearance qualifying) for 20,00,000.
working: Compensation cess @22% (illustrative top slab) = 4,40,000
Total tax = 10,00,000 on a 20,00,000 vehicle
examples.result: Cess is charged in addition to 28% GST; the buyer's cess ITC (if a business) is usable only against output cess.

faqs.q: Can I use compensation-cess ITC to pay my GST?
faqs.a: No. ITC of compensation cess can be used **only** to pay compensation cess. It cannot be set off against CGST, SGST, UTGST or IGST.

faqs.q: Is the compensation cess going away?
faqs.a: The levy was extended to 31 March 2026 to repay the compensation-period borrowings. What happens after that (merge into GST, a new levy, or lapse) is under GST Council consideration.

commonMistakes: Setting off cess credit against GST
Missing cess on aerated waters / tobacco / large vehicles / coal
Using the wrong (ad valorem vs specific) basis

caseLaw.name: Union of India v. Mohit Minerals Pvt Ltd
caseLaw.citation: (2019) 2 SCC 599 / [2018] 98 taxmann.com 449 (SC), Writ Petition (C) No. 1152 of 2017 (with connected matters), decided 03-10-2018
caseLaw.facts: Challenge to the compensation cess on the supply of coal, including on stock on which Clean Energy Cess had already been paid.
caseLaw.issue: Constitutional validity of the Compensation Cess Act and the levy on coal.
caseLaw.held: The Compensation Cess Act is constitutionally valid; the cess is a distinct levy and set-off of the earlier Clean Energy Cess is not a matter of right.
caseLaw.effect: Confirms the validity of the compensation cess (distinct from the 2022 ocean-freight ruling of the same name).

cess-s11.plainEnglish:
**Section 11 of the Compensation Cess Act — other provisions relating to cess.**
It applies the machinery of the **CGST Act and the IGST Act** (returns, payment,
ITC, assessment, demands, refunds, offences, penalties, etc.) to the compensation
cess, **mutatis mutandis**.

faqs.a: No. Cess is reported in the cess columns of the regular GST returns (GSTR-1, GSTR-3B) and maintained as a separate balance in the electronic ledgers, under section 11 which imports the CGST/IGST machinery.

faqs.q: Do I need a valuation study for branch transfers?
faqs.a: Not if the receiving branch is eligible for full ITC — Rule 28's second proviso deems the invoice value to be the open market value. A study is only needed where the recipient has restricted / no ITC.

faqs.q: We gave a free corporate guarantee for a subsidiary's loan. Is GST payable?
faqs.a: As notified, Rule 28(2) values it at 1% per annum of the guaranteed amount, or the actual fee if higher. The Gujarat HC (Torrent Power, 2026) has read down 'whichever is higher' — so where a fee is charged, value it at the fee; the deemed 1% applies only where nothing is charged — and has barred the 1% for periods before 26.10.2023. If the subsidiary has full ITC the tax is revenue-neutral but must still be invoiced.

commonMistakes: Building elaborate cost-plus valuations where the invoice-value proviso applies
Ignoring GST on inter-company guarantees

caseLaw.name: Torrent Power Ltd. v. Union of India
caseLaw.citation: R/Special Civil Application No. 12175 of 2024 & connected matters (Gujarat High Court), decided 14-08-2026
caseLaw.facts: Holding companies gave corporate guarantees to banks for their subsidiaries, mostly without a commission. The department demanded GST on a deemed 1% per annum of the guaranteed amount under Rule 28(2), including for guarantees executed before Rule 28(2) came in (26.10.2023) and pre-GST, and issued section 74 SCNs alleging suppression.
caseLaw.issue: Validity of the Rule 28(2) '1% per annum or actual consideration, whichever is higher' valuation, and whether it can apply to guarantees given before 26.10.2023.
caseLaw.held: Rule 28(2) is upheld, but the words 'whichever is higher' are struck down as arbitrary (Article 14 / 19(1)(g)) — value is the actual consideration where a fee is charged, otherwise the deemed 1%. The 1% deemed value cannot be levied for any period before 26.10.2023 (impermissible retroactive levy), though it applies from that date if the guarantee continues. Corporate guarantees without consideration are still taxable supplies between related persons; they are 'business' and not actionable claims. Section 15(4) is intra vires. Section 74 SCNs premised only on non-declaration in a genuine interpretational dispute were quashed. Circulars 204/16/2023 and 225/19/2024-GST set aside to the extent inconsistent.
caseLaw.effect: Where a guarantee fee is actually charged, that fee is the value — the department cannot demand the deemed 1% on top. No 1% demand for periods before 26.10.2023. Gujarat HC — binding in Gujarat, persuasive elsewhere; a Revenue SLP is expected, so confirm the position and any stay.

cgst-r31d.plainEnglish:
**Rule 31D — value of notified goods on retail sale price (RSP).** For the goods notified under **section 15(5)** — **pan masala (2106 90 20)** and **tobacco products of headings 2401–2404** — the value of supply is **deemed to be the RSP declared on the pack, less the tax component**, overriding the transaction-value rules of this Chapter.
- **Tax back-calculation (31D(2))**: Tax = (RSP × total tax rate %) ÷ (100 + total tax rate %).
- **RSP (Explanation (b))** = the maximum price at which the packaged goods may be sold to the ultimate consumer, **inclusive of all taxes, duties, cess**. Where several RSPs are printed, the **highest** applies (c); an increased RSP at any stage replaces the earlier one (d); area-specific RSPs apply to sales in that area (e).

cgst-r32.plainEnglish:
**Rule 32 — value in specific cases (optional).** 
- **32(2)** foreign-exchange / money changing — a slab formula, or 1% / 0.5% / etc. of the gross amount.
- **32(3)** air-travel agent — 5% of the basic fare (domestic) / 10% (international).
- **32(4)** life insurance — gross premium less the investment / savings portion, or 25% of the first-year premium and 12.5% thereafter, or 10% for single-premium annuity.
- **32(5) margin scheme** — a dealer in **second-hand goods** who does not claim ITC on the purchase may pay GST only on the **margin** (sale price minus purchase price); a negative margin is ignored.
- **32(6)** value of a **token / voucher / coupon** = the money value of the goods / services redeemable.

cgst-r37.plainEnglish: **Rule 37 — reversal for non-payment within 180 days.** Where the recipient fails to pay the supplier the **value plus tax** within **180 days** of the invoice date, the ITC availed is added to the **output tax liability** for the period **in which the 180 days expire**, with **interest under section 50**. It is **re-availed** when the payment is made — with no time limit on re-availment. RCM supplies are excluded.

complianceChecklist.item: Run creditor ageing monthly; reverse ITC on invoices past 180 days
Pay interest under section 50 on the reversal
Re-avail on payment

cgst-r42.plainEnglish: **Rule 42 — reversal of common ITC on inputs and input services.** Monthly: total ITC (T) → less ITC exclusively for non-business (T1), exclusively for exempt (T2), and blocked ITC (T3) → credit to the ledger is C1 = T − (T1+T2+T3). Of C1, ITC exclusively for taxable / zero-rated (T4) is fully available. Common credit **C2 = C1 − T4**. Reverse: **D1 = C2 × (exempt turnover ÷ total turnover)** and **D2 = 5% of C2** (deemed non-business). Eligible common credit **C3 = C2 − (D1 + D2)**. An **annual** recomputation is done by **30 November** of the next year; a shortfall is paid with interest, an excess is re-credited.

complianceChecklist.item: Tag every ITC as T1/T2/T3/T4 or common at booking
Compute D1 + D2 every month and reverse in Table 4(B)(1)
Do the annual recomputation by 30 November and pay any shortfall with interest

cgst-r43.plainEnglish: **Rule 43 — reversal of common ITC on capital goods.** Capital-goods ITC used partly for exempt supply is spread over a **useful life of 5 years (60 months)**. Common capital-goods credit **Tc** → monthly attributable credit **Tm = Tc ÷ 60** → the exempt portion **Te = Tm × (exempt turnover ÷ total turnover)** is added to output tax each month with interest, for the remaining life. A capital good moving from exclusively-exempt / exclusively-taxable to common use (or vice versa) is brought into / taken out of Tc with the 5%-per-quarter adjustment.

cgst-r46.plainEnglish: **Rule 46 — contents of a tax invoice.** Consecutive serial number (≤16 characters); date; **GSTIN and address of supplier and recipient** (recipient's name / address / State for B2C above 50,000); **HSN / SAC** (4 digits for turnover ≤ 5 crore B2B / mandatory 6 digits above 5 crore, 8 for exports / specified goods); description, quantity, unit, value, taxable value, rate and amount of each tax; place of supply for inter-State; whether tax is on **reverse charge**; signature / digital signature; and, where applicable, the **IRN and QR code**. A supplier can issue a **consolidated invoice** for B2C supplies below 200 where the recipient does not want an invoice.
